qText: A 50-year-old male patient known case of carcinoma lower lip. Picture given below. He was undertaken for wide local excision with neck dissection. The defect arising in the lower lip after surgery is more than 2/3rd of the length of the lip. What should be the appropriate intervention for reconstruction in this case?
expl: Explanation: With larger defects of the lower lip, reconstruction requires either large cheek flaps to be advanced to repair the defect or the use of free tissue transfer. The common forms of cheek flap include the bilateral Gillies fan flaps or the Bernard-Webster cheek flap reconstruction. Abbe flap is based on the main artery of the orbicularis Oris, the Labial artery. A portion of uninvolved lip is rotated across the mouth and placed into the surgical defect of the involved lip. After 10 to 14 days, the flap is divided. The defect of the uninvolved lip from which the flap has been taken is sutured primarily. Gillies fan flap borrow tissue from the cheek and adjacent sites.

qText: A 45-year-old female patient presented with midline neck swelling since 4 months. USG local part is suggestive of nodule in the left lobe of thyroid gland. Hemi thyroidectomy was done in this patient. Postoperative histopathology report was suggestive of cells with salt and pepper chromatin arranged in sheets, nests or trabeculae in an organoid fashion. Cells were positive of calcitonin, CEA, chromogranin, and synaptophysin. Histopathology picture is given below. What is the type of thyroid neoplasm is seen here?
expl: Explanation: Medullary carcinoma thyroid is a malignant tumour showing C cell differentiation. It constitutes 5 to 10 % of all thyroid malignancy. Histologically it shows cells with salt and pepper chromatin arranged in sheets, nests or trabeculae in an organoid fashion. Necrotic is infrequent. C cell hyperplasia can be seen in surrounding thyroid tissue adjacent to the invasive tumour. Cells are positive for calcitonin , chromagranin, CEA, synaptophysin . Amyloid deposits are also seen. Papillarycarcinoma ( Option A ): shows cells arranged in monolayer papillae with characteristic nuclear features such as orphan Annie nuclei . It shows metaplasia squamous cytoplasm. Follicular carcinoma ( Option B ): shows cells arranged in follicles, solid or trabecular fashion. They lack the typical nuclear features. Anaplastic carcinoma (Option D): have pleomorphic large cells with high nuclear to cytoplasm ratio. Key Takeaway: Medullary thyroid Carcinoma: Salt & Pepper Chromatin & Amyloid Deposits Synaptophysin & Chromogranin Positive.

qText: Which of the anatomical site is marked with arrow in the given image?
expl: The piriform fossa, also known as the pyriform sinus, is a pear-shaped recess on either side of the laryngeal inlet, and is part of the hypopharynx. It's located posterolaterally to either side of the laryngeal opening, and is bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold, and laterally by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane. This sinus is a common place for food particles to become trapped; if foreign material becomes lodged in the piriform fossa of an infant, it may be retrieved nonsurgically. If the area is injured (e.g., by a fish bone), it can give the sensation of food stuck in the subject's throat.

qText: What radiological sign is identifiable in the provided X-ray image?
expl: Explanation: The given X-ray images (AP and lateral views) show a radiopaque foreign body in the upper oesophagus, with a characteristic double ring appearance . This finding is highly suggestive of an ingested button battery , a medical emergency requiring urgent removal. The double ring sign is due to the two concentric metal components of the button battery: Outer metal casing Inner insulating ring The lateral view helps distinguish between a coin (homogeneous opacity) and a button battery (double ring appearance) . Radiology of foreign bodies in trachea/ oesophagus: Coin in the oesophagus is identified by a circular-shaped opacity seen on AP view and appears slit-like on lateral view . Coin in trachea: Slit-like on AP view and Circular opacity on lateral view. Button battery: It can get dislodged in the oesophagus following accidental ingestion. Peripheral double contour ring (or) Halo sign seen on X-ray distinguishes button battery from a coin in the oesophagus. Explanation for other options: Steeple Sign (Option A): is it refers to the subglottic narrowing seen in croup on an AP neck X-ray. String Sign (Option B): is it refers to the narrowing of the terminal ileum in Crohn's disease , seen in contrast studies. Thumb Sign (Option C): is it refers to swelling of the epiglottis in epiglottitis , giving the appearance of a "thumb" on lateral neck X-ray. Reference: Oesophagal foreign body - coin | Radiology Case | Radiopaedia.org Disk Battery Ingestion - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

qText: Steeple sign on X-ray neck AP view is seen in?
expl: The "steeple sign" on an X-ray of the neck (AP view) is indicative of acute laryngotracheobronchitis, commonly known as croup. Croup is characterized by inflammation of the upper airway, specifically the larynx and trachea, leading to narrowing of the subglottic region and causing the characteristic steeple-like appearance on X-ray. Other options: A. Acute epiglottitis: Acute epiglottitis causes inflammation and swelling of the epiglottis, which leads to a " thumbprint sign" on X-ray , not the steeple sign. C. Laryngomalacia: Laryngomalacia is a congenital condition where the soft tissues of the larynx collapse during inspiration, causing a characteristic " omega-shaped" epiglottis on X-ray, not the steeple sign. D. Laryngeal web: A laryngeal web is a congenital condition where there is a membrane or web-like structure across the larynx , which may cause respiratory difficulty, but it does not result in the steeple sign on X-ray.

qText: A 70-year-old male who had been chewing tobacco for past 50 years, presents with a 6 months history of fungating soft papillary lesion in the oral cavity picture given below lymph nodes are not palpable. Biopsy from the lesion shows benign appearing papilloma with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis. Most likely diagnosis is ?
expl: Explanation: Verrucous carcinoma is a low-grade SCC that appears as a cauliflower-like exophytic tumor. There are three forms of verrucous carcinomas; all of them are recognized in areas of maceration. Verrucous carcinoma of the oral cavity, known as oral floridpapillomatosis, involves large areas of oral mucosa in elderly male tobacco chewers. Verrucous carcinoma of the anogenital region, called giant cell condyloma of Buschke Löwenstein , occurs on the glans penis of young uncircumcised males and on the perianal region in both sexes. Plantar verrucous carcinoma, also called epithelioma cuniculatum , usually involves the skin underlying the first metatarsal head, making numerous deep crypts filled with horny material and pus, and ultimately penetrates the plantar fascia. Management is surgical excision with an appropriate margin of healthy tissue. Key Takeaway: Verrucous Carcinoma : low grade SCC Giant cell condyloma Papilloma with hyperkeratosis Mx with Surgical Excision.

qText: A 40-year-old female patient known case of papillary carcinoma thyroid was advised radioiodine ablation after total thyroidectomy. All of the following statements about preparation of patient for radioiodine ablation are true except?
expl: Explanation: The following are necessary to be done before radioiodine ablation or scan. Patient is weaned off form iodine containing drugs like cough suppressant and iodine contrast based imaging. (Option B) Food stuff such as sea foods and iodinated salts should be avoided for 3 to 4 weeks. It is mandatory to stop tablet thyroxine so that serum thyroid level is elevated to more than 30 micro IU /ml. (Option C) Amount of residual thyroid is calculated using thyroid uptake probe at 4, 6 and 24 hours after 20 micro curie 131 I application. (Option D) Normal dosage of 131I used to ablation residual thyroid tissue is in the range of 30 to 70 mCi . ( Option A ) Following ablation patient is put on suppressive doses of tablet thyroxine. A post therapy whole body scintigraphy is performed 5 to 7 days after ablation. Selection of patient for radio iodine ablation: Patient with I 131 concentrating in distant metastasis. Patient with multicentric, multifocal, and microscopic differentiated thyroid malignancy. All patients with follicular, papillary and mixed carcinoma of more than 1.5 cm in size with or without capsular invasion. Patient with residual thyroid disease in which revision surgery is not possible. Who should not be ablated: Patient with low risk factors including papillary carcinoma with tumor size 1 to 1.5 cm with no capsular invasion or distant metastasis. Patient with medullary carcinoma because they are based on parafollicular C cells which can't concentrate radioiodine. Hence, they are treated with 131 I labelled meta iodo benzyl guanidine (MIBG). Key takeaway: Normal dosage of 131I used to ablation residual thyroid tissue is in the range of 30 to 70 mCi .

qText: Given below is the X-ray image of a child with a history of ingestion of a coin. What is the most likely site of dislodgement of the foreign body
expl: Explanation: In the given lateral neck X-ray, the coin is seen on its edge, indicating an oesophageal location. In suspected foreign body ingestion, posteroanterior and lateral views of neck and similar views of the chest including abdomen are taken. Xrays reveals most of the radio-opaque foreign bodies. Foreign bodies of the oesophagus lie in the coronal plane in PA view and edge on in the lateral view. It is just the reverse in tracheal foreign bodies because of orientation of vocal cords. Radiolucent foreign bodies may show as an air bubble in cervical oesophagus in X-ray soft tissue lateral view of neck. A disc battery may elude as it may cast a double shadow or stacked coin appearance. Most of the foreign bodies in oesophagus can be removed by oesophagoscopy under general anaesthesia. Fig: Foreign body food passage.(A) PA view showing a coin.(B) Lateral view of the same. Explanation of other options: Larynx (Option A): The typical presentation in a laryngeal foreign body is choking while eating. On x-ray, it may show airway narrowing or obstruction. Fig: Soft tissue lateral view neck showing a fruit seed in the subglottic region of larynx (arrow). Note: The patient needed tracheostomy (black arrow) to relieve obstruction. Trachea (Option B): A coin or a flat foreign body in trachea lies edge on in PA view and flat on lateral view. A key sign of a tracheal foreign body can be an audible slap and palpatory thud. A large foreign body may totally obstruct the airway leading to sudden death unless resuscitative measures are taken urgently. Bronchus (Option D): Bronchial foreign bodies are more common on the right side than the left. In cases of suspected bronchial foreign body, chest X-ray PA view may show segmental or lobar collapse, hyperinflation or even a normal X-ray. A normal x-ray will not rule out the presence of a foreign body.

qText: A 40-year-old female came with a complaint of vertigo for 7 days. An examination was performed in which the patient was asked to keep looking at the examiner's finger while her head was moved briskly and abruptly. It was found that her eyes lagged and showed saccades at the end of head movements. What is this suggestive of?
expl: Explanation: Based on the description given above, the test performed on the patient is called the Head Impulse Test. Head movements required during the head-impulse test to investigate the horizontal canals (top, a-c) and the vertical canals (bottom, d-f) The head impulse test examines the vestibulo-ocular reflex. The VOR helps stabilise gaze on the object during different head movements, so that the image remains centred on the fovea of the retina. The patient is asked to keep looking at an object while his head is moved briskly and abruptly. In a normal patient or in a head-impulse- negative patient, the eyes move in the opposite direction at the same speed as the head movement and will remain fixed on the target. In the absence of VOR or in a Head impulse positive test, the eyes will lag, and there will be jerky catch-up movement called saccades at the end to catch up to the target.

qText: A 70-year-old elderly male presents with a history of dysphagia since 1 month. Dysphagia is associated halitosis, regurgitation of food, and coughing. Barium swallow was done in this patient, picture is given below. All of the following is true about this condition except?
expl: Explanation: The picture of Barium swallow shown above is suggestive of Zenker's diverticulum. Diverticulum is an outpouching from a tubular structure. It forms when there is neuromuscular incoordination while swallowing. In hypopharynx, the most common site of its formation is the Killian dehiscence, which lies between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus , parts of inferior constrictive muscle. It arises from posterior wall hence it is also called posterior pouch. (Option A) It is a pulsing diverticulum as it occurs due to increase in intraluminal pressure. (Option D) A true diverticulum contains all the layers of wall, but zenker's diverticulum contains only mucosa hence it is a false diverticulum. (Option B) Main management of zenker's diverticulum is excision of pouch, Endoscopic stapling diverticulotomy. (Option C) Excision of pouch: The pouch is excised and crico pharyngeal myotomy is done to relax the cricoid pharyngeal sphincter. Endoscopic stapling of the diverticulotomy: This is presently preferred mode of therapy. The surgery aims at converting the cricopharyngeal and pouch cavity into one single cavity to avoid collection of food. This is achieved by cutting the cricopharyngeal bar. Historically it was first done byHe used diathermy to achieve this. Key Takeaway : Zenker Diverticulum is Pulsing False diverticulum caused due to increased intraluminal pressure in the Posterior wall of hypopharynx. Managed with excision & Endoscopic stapling diverticulotomy.

qText: A 30-year-old female patient presented with complain of pain and swelling over floor of mouth, bilateral submandibular region. The entire region was tender and inflamed. expl: Explanation: In the above condition, the swelling involves bilateral submandibular region. It developed following dental extraction. Patient also has uncontrolled diabetes. It involves floor of mouth. All these points lead to diagnosis of Ludwig's abscess. There are four Goldring's criteria to diagnose Ludwig's abscess. It is always cellulitis and not an abscess. If an abscess is present it is known as submandibular abscess and not Ludwig's angina. (Option A) It is always bilateral (Option B) It spreads through tissue space and not through lymphatic. (Option D) It does not involve the submandibular and sublingual glands. (Option C) Management: Incision and drainage : A horizontal incision is kept 2 to 3 cm below the lower border of mandible extending from angle of mandible to the other. Antibiotics covering both aerobes and anaerobes. Key Takeaway: Ludwig's Angina: Bilateral Cellulitis which spread through tissue space without involving salivary glands.

qText: A patient with maxillary cancer underwent the surgical procedure as shown in the image below. Identify the type of maxillectomy performed.
expl: Explanation: Since the surgical image in question shows removal of the entire maxilla along with the orbital floor , this matches the description of a total maxillectomy . Total maxillectomy involves the removal of the entire maxilla along with the orbital floor , especially when the tumor invades the bony orbital floor but not the orbital contents . The procedure builds on subtotal maxillectomy , which already removes the entire maxilla, by including resection of the orbital floor for wider tumor clearance. In total maxillectomy , the orbital rim is removed en bloc with the maxilla, and reconstruction of the orbital floor is essential to preserve both cosmesis and function . Explanation of Other Options: Medial maxillectomy (Option B) is a more limited resection involving only the medial wall of the maxilla. Subtotal maxillectomy (Option C) removes the entire maxilla but not the orbital floor . Infrastructure maxillectomy (Option D) includes the removal of the hard palate, alveolar ridge, and dentition but preserves the orbital floor .

expl: Explanation: The X-ray reveals a radiopaque foreign body within the esophagus, which is a frequent occurrence in children. qText: Which of the following structures are forming boundaries of MacEwen's Triangle?
expl: Explanation: McEwen's Triangle (Suprameatal Triangle): A small depression located posterosuperior to the external acoustic meatus. In adults, the lateral wall of the mastoid antrum corresponds to the suprameatal triangle (MacEwen's triangle) on the outer surface of the skull. This is palpable through the cymba conchae Boundaries : Above : Defined by the supramastoid crest . (Option A) In front : Bounded by the posterosuperior margin of the external acoustic meatus. (Option A) Behind : Marked by a vertical tangent to the posterior margin of the meatus. The superior side of the triangle, the supramastoid crest, is level with the floor of the middle cranial fossa ; The anteroinferior side, which forms the posterosuperior margin of the external acoustic meatus , indicates approximately the position of the descending part of the facial nerve canal; And the posterior side, formed by a posterior vertical tangent to the posterior margin of the external acoustic meatus, is anterior to the sigmoid sinus . Key Takeaway: McEwen's triangle (suprameatal triangle) is defined by the supramastoid crest above, the posterosuperior margin of the external acoustic meatus in front, and a vertical tangent behind, crucial for understanding the anatomy surrounding the tympanic and mastoid regions.

qText: A 35-year-old male presents with a three-day history of severe headache, fever, and nausea. He also reports pain and swelling behind the left ear, along with blood-tinged ear discharge. On examination, there is tenderness and bluish discolouration over the mastoid process of the left temporal bone. CT imaging reveals an empty delta sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The patient most likely has lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis , a known complication of otitis media or mastoiditis . The empty delta sign observed on CT imaging is a characteristic indicator of lateral sinus thrombosis. Lateral sinus thrombosis (Sigmoid sinus thrombosis) An inflammation of the inner wall of the lateral venous sinus with formation of an intrasinus thrombus, often secondary to otitis media or mastoiditis. Clinical features Fever: Hectic "picket-fence" type with rigors Headache: Early mild, later severe due to venous obstruction Griesinger's sign: Mastoid tenderness and swelling with bluish discolouration. This is due to blockage of Mastoid emissary veins which are also drained in the sigmoid sinus In lateral sinus thrombosis, compression of the internal jugular vein (IJV) on the affected side does not change CSF pressure due to obstruction of venous outflow. Tobey-Ayer Test: Assesses this phenomenon via lumbar puncture , measuring CSF pressure changes when the IJV is compressed. Crowe-Beck Test: Observed on fundus (retina) examination, where compression of the jugular vein on the healthy side causes retinal vein engorgement, while compression on the thrombosed side shows no change. Papilledema: Depends on venous obstruction Tenderness along jugular vein if thrombosis extends Investigations: CECT/MRI brain: Empty delta sign (triangular area of central hypodensity with rim enhancement) MR venography: Assess extent and progression X-ray mastoids: Clouding of air cells or bone destruction Treatment Involves performing a modified radical mastoidectomy (MRM) , exposing the lateral sinus a nd removing the thrombus carefully until fresh, healthy bleeding is seen, confirming that the sinus lumen is cleared. Explanation of other options: Meningitis (Option A): Although meningitis can cause headache, fever, and nausea, it does not present with an empty delta sign or the mastoid swelling seen in lateral sinus thrombosis. Brain Abscess (Option C): A brain abscess typically presents with neurological deficits or altered consciousness and would not show an empty delta sign on CT imaging. Extradural Abscess (Option D): While an extradural abscess can cause localized pain and swelling , it does not produce an empty delta sign or the characteristic spread of infection seen in lateral sinus thrombosis.

qText: What is the Battle sign?

Option D: Pitting edema on mastoid -Pitting edema on the mastoid is unrelated to the Battle sign.

qText: Which of the following is the most commonly injured nerve after parotid surgery?
expl: Explanation : The facial nerve is the most commonly injured in parotid surgery as it traverses perpendicularly through the parotid gland. land. The cervical branch of the facial nerve is usually involved leading to Bell's palsy. Following parotid surgery auriculotemporal nerve and the greater auricular nerve can also be injured, but less frequently than the facial nerve. (Option B, D ruled out) Iatrogenic injury to facial nerve The most common cause of facial nerve injury is parotid surgery, followed by mastoid surgery. During mastoid surgery, the site most frequently injured is the second genu of the facial nerve, followed by the vertical segment. Management options include surgical exploration with end-to-end anastomosis and facial nerve grafting Commonly used graft sources include: Greater auricular nerve Sural nerve (preferred for long grafts). Explanation of other options: Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option C): Glossopharyngeal nerve lies deep in the neck and is not related anatomically to the parotid gland. Injury to the nerve causes loss of taste in the posterior one-third of the tongue and loss of the gag reflex.

qText: The figure is showing the structure of chochlear canal. Identify the marked cavity.

Scala vestibuli (1) : Located above the vestibular membrane (Reisnners membrane), continuous with the vestibule at the base of the cochlea. Scala media (2) : Also known as the cochlear duct, located between the basilar and vestibular membranes, contains endolymph. qText: Which of the following structures is responsible for balance and hearing?
expl: Explanation: The vestibule is a part of the inner ear which is responsible for both hearing and balance. Vestibule contains the utricle and saccule, each with a sensory epithelium called the macula. The utricle detects horizontal linear acceleration, while the saccule detects vertical linear acceleration. These structures help the brain maintain static balance and posture. Explanation of other options: Semicircular canal (Option A): The semicircular canals are responsible for maintaining balance; have no role in hearing. Cochlea (Option B), Organ of Corti (Option D): The cochlea is the main organ of hearing, containing the sense organ called Organ of Corti on the basilar membrane.

expl: Presbycusis is sensorineural hearing loss associated with the physiological aging process in the ear calling presbycusis. It usually manifests at the age of 65 years but may do so early if there is hereditary predisposition, chronic noise exposure or generalized vascular disease. qText: A 5 year old boy while having dinner suddenly becomes aphonic and is brought to the casualty with the complaint of respiratory difficulty. What should be the appropriate management?
expl: Heimlich manoeuvre Heimlich manoeuvre is sudden thrust directed upward and backwards below the epigastrium. It squeezes the residual air from lungs, which dislodges the foreign body. This manoeuvre should not be done if there is partial obstruction. Cricothyroidotmy or emergency tracheostomy is done if Heimlich maneuver fails. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 377, 378

qText: The Hallpike maneuver is used to assess which of the following conditions?
expl: Explanation: The Hallpike maneuver , also known as the Dix-Hallpike test , is primarily used to assess vestibular function . Hallpike maneuver The Hallpike manoeuver is the diagnostic test for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Diagnosis is made by provoking vertigo and nystagmus related to inner ear dysfunction. During the test, the patient's head is rapidly positioned in a specific manner to assess the function of the posterior semicircular canal , which plays a key role in balance. A positive test is indicated by a sudden burst of vertigo accompanied by nystagmus, confirming BPPV. This maneuver is specifically designed for evaluating vestibular disorders and is not used to assess hearing or corneal reflexes. Explanation of other options: Audiometry (Option B), Cochlear function (Option C) : Audiometry and cochlear function evaluates hearing , not balance or vestibular function. Corneal test (Option D) : The corneal reflex assesses sensory and motor pathways for blinking , which is unrelated to vestibular or auditory function

qText: A 30 year old male is having Attic cholesteatoma of left ear with lateral sinus thrombophlebitis. Which of the following will be the operation of choice?
expl: The main treatment of Cholesteatoma is surgery → MRM. Treatment : Surgery is called MRM (Modified Radical Mastoidectomy) also called as TYMPANOMASTOID EXPLORATION. Main aim of MRM is to make ear safe. After making adequate clearance of cholesteatoma, we remove the posterior wall of EAC to open the mastoid cavity into EAC. Most common site of residual cholesteatoma after mastoid surgery is SINUS TYMPANI. MEATOPLASTY : This surgical step is aimed at widening the EAC. It is done by removing the part of Conchal cartilage. qText: A 40-year-old male patient presents with foul-smelling ear discharge. Discharge was scanty in nature; the patient also experienced vertigo intermittently. HRCT of the temporal bone was done, which is suggestive of cholesteatoma in epitympanum and mesotympanum with erosion of the incus. On endoscopy, the tympanic membrane appeared as shown in the picture below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
expl: Explanation: The image shown above suggests an attic retraction pocket with cholesteatoma flakes , suggestive of Cholesteatomatous CSOM (AKA Unsafe CSOM or Atticoantral disease). Cholesteatoma is the presence of keratinising stratified squamous epithelium in any part of the temporal bone where it is usually not present. E.g. middle ear, mastoid, petrous Apex. In its basal layer, cholesteatoma expresses enzymes such as collagenase and acid phosphatase, which cause bony erosion, helping the middle ear infection spread to surrounding areas and leading to various complications. Patient presents here with scant, painless and foul-smelling discharge because of otitis and bone erosion by cholesteatoma and infection with anaerobic organisms. The main management of such CSOM is mastoid exploration with removal of disease from the mastoid , followed by removal of disease from the middle ear. The discharge is mainly due to bone erosion; hence, medical management with local and systemic antibiotics has little effect on the discharge's drying (Option A) . Myringoplasty alone is not sufficient in eradicating the disease from the middle ear and mastoid cavity (Option C) . Radical mastoidectomy is indicated in extensive cholesteatoma following unsafe csom with dead ear (Option D) .

qText: The most common hidden site for residual cholesteatoma after the mastoid surgery in Atticoantral CSOM is
expl: One of the ways the surgical treatment of CSOM is done is Canal wall-up procedures. Here disease is removed by combined approach through the meatus and mastoid but retaining the posterior bony meatal wall intact, thereby avoiding an open mastoid cavity. It gives dry ears and permits easy reconstruction of the hearing mechanism. However, there is a danger of leaving some cholesteatoma behind. The incidence of residual or recurrent cholesteatoma in these cases is very high and therefore long-term follow-up is essential. Some surgeon’s even advise routine re-exploration in all cases after 6 months or so. Canal wall up procedures are advised only in selected cases. In a combined approach or intact canal wall mastoidectomy, disease is removed both permeatally, and through cortical mastoidectomy and posterior tympanotomy approach, in which a window is created between the mastoid and middle ear, through the facial recess, to reach sinus tympani Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.87

qText: Tubercular otitis media is characterized by all except

qText: A 7 year old male presents to emergency with a two day history of worsening ear pain and drainage. On the day prior to presentation, his parents noted redness behind his right ear and that his right ear appeared to be sticking out. He had been well until 10 days ago when he started complaining of a cough and runny nose that progressed to include right ear pain and fever. He was evaluated in the clinic 5 days ago and diagnosed with an acute right otitis media. He was placed on amoxicillin and he initially appeared to improve until two days ago when his ear pain recurred and this is now accompanied by ear drainage, redness behind his right ear and a prominent right pinna which is pointing up and out. The most likely diagnosis is?
expl: Mastoid surface is found to be smooth, red and shiny. This is called the Ironing of the mastoid surface. It is the first sign of Mastoiditis. MASTOIDITIS : It is an infection of the mastoid air cells. It is a complication of ASOM and CSOM. Chief complaint- Pain behind the pinna, Profuse ear discharge On examination- Mastoid surface is found to be smooth, red and shiny. This is called the Ironing of the mastoid surface. It is the first sign of Mastoiditis. Mastoid Tenderness is positive. RESERVOIR SIGN on cleaning, the pus fills immediately again, this is because pus is continously flowing from mastoid to middle ear this is called PULSATILE OTORRHOEA. Light House sign is seen due to this pulsatile otorrhoea. Investigation : X ray mastoid right and left lateral oblique view. It is called Schuller's view. This is the most used x-ray view for mastoids in ENT. This X-ray shows two findings. Clouding of air cells. Coalescence of air cells. qText: A 22-year-old male patient with a known case of CSOM attico-antral type develops Gradenigo syndrome. Which of the following symptoms will not be a part of Gradenigo syndrome?
expl: Explanation: Gradenigo syndrome results from the spread of a middle ear infection into the petrous part of the temporal bone, leading to petrousitis. It is the triad of: Persistent Ear Discharge (Due to involvement of the petrous apex) Diplopia (Due to VI nerve palsy) Retrobulbar Pain (Due to irritation of the Trigeminal ganglion) The air cells of the petrous part of the temporal bone communicate with the mastoid bone. Thus, infection in the mastoid region can transmit to the petrous bone, leading to persistent ear discharge. The 6 th cranial nerve runs in the Dorello's canal at the petrous Apex, and the 5 th nerve lies in the Meckel's canal. So, there is palsy of the VI nerve leading to diplopia. Involvement of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve leads to retrobulbar pain. The Facial nerve is not involved in petrositis; therefore, its palsy is not part of Gradenigo syndrome.

qText: A 28-year-old male with a history of chronic ear discharge and hearing loss undergoes an otoscopic evaluation. The image below shows a large central perforation of the tympanic membrane with visible middle ear structures. What is the most appropriate surgical intervention for this patient?
expl: Explanation: The patient has features of Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM) – Tubotympanic type , evidenced by: Chronic ear discharge Conductive hearing loss Large central perforation of the tympanic membrane without cholesteatoma The most appropriate surgical treatment is Tympanoplasty . Tympanoplasty: Tympanoplasty is a surgical procedure aimed at repairing a perforated eardrum (tympanic membrane) and, in some cases, reconstructing the ossicles (the small bones in the middle ear) to restore hearing function. This surgery is commonly recommended when a perforation does not heal on its own, often due to chronic ear infections or trauma. Anaesthesia: Typically performed under general anaesthesia Surgical Approach: The surgeon may access the eardrum through the ear canal or make an incision behind or in front of the ear, depending on the location and size of the perforation. Graft Material: A graft, often taken from the patient's tissue (such as fascia or cartilage ), is used to patch the eardrum. Additional Procedures: If the ossicles are damaged, procedures like ossiculoplasty (reconstruction of the ossicles) or mastoidectomy (removal of infected mastoid bone) may be performed concurrently. The Wullstein classification categorizes the procedure based on the extent of the defect and the method of reconstruction. Explanation of Other Options: Atticotomy (Option A): Performed for attic cholesteatoma or retraction pockets in the pars flaccida. Not indicated in simple central perforation. Modified radical mastoidectomy (Option B): Indicated in atticoantral disease (cholesteatoma type of CSOM) or unsafe ear. Not required in safe central perforation. Myringoplasty (Option C): It only repairs the tympanic membrane without addressing ossicular continuity, making it inadequate in this case, where middle ear structures are exposed .

qText: A child presented with hearing loss in both the ears. Hearing aid was tried but that did not benefit the child what is the next treatment option in this child:

qText: A patient with CSOM presented to the OPD with seizures, headache and complaints of nausea and vomiting. CT image of patient is given. Identify the clinical condition?
expl: Explanation: CT shows a low-density lesion with a thin, smooth, and uniformly "ring-enhancing" peripheral rim in the temporal region. These findings combined with history of CSOM point towards Temporal Abscess. Complications of Acute and Chronic Otitis Media: Extracranial: Acute and chronic mastoiditis Tympanic membrane perforation Facial nerve palsy Cholesteatoma (Chronic) Subperiosteal abscess Suppurative labyrinthitis Intracranial: Meningitis Brain abscess Lateral/sigmoid sinus thrombosis Otitic hydrocephalus (Pseudotumor cerebri) Explanation of Other Options: Extradural Abscess (Option B) While extradural abscesses can also occur in CSOM, they typically present with less severe symptoms such as localized pain, tenderness, or a discharging sinus rather than seizures or marked raised intracranial pressure. CT would not show a focal abscess. Meningitis (Option C) Meningitis presents with fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status . Seizures can occur, but the CT scan would not show a focal abscess ; instead, you might see meningeal enhancement or sometimes a normal scan. Also, meningitis is a diffuse condition , not localized like a temporal abscess. Petrositis (Option D) Petrositis, or inflammation of the petrous apex, presents with Gradenigo's syndrome - a triad of lateral rectus palsy (diplopia), ear discharge, and retro-orbital pain . It doesn't cause seizures or intracranial signs like a temporal abscess. Key Takeaway: A temporal lobe abscess is a serious intracranial complication of CSOM, often presenting with headache, seizures, and signs of raised intracranial pressure , and is typically confirmed on CT imaging as a ring-enhancing lesion in the temporal lobe.

It is of 4 types : Primary Acquired Cholesteatoma (mc) Secondary Acquired Cholesteatoma Tertiary Acquired Cholesteatoma Congenital Cholesteatoma Congenital Cholesteatoma: We use LEVENSON’S CRITERIA to diagnose congenital cholesteatoma . Treatment : Surgery → MRM ( Modified Radical Mastoidectomy) also called as Tympanomastoid Exploration. qText: Which of the following is present in complicated Otitis media? 1. Bezold Abscess 2. Battle Sign 3. Delta Sign 4. Griesinger Sign
expl: A) Bezold Abscess: It can occur following acute coalescent mastoiditis when pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck. The abscess may (i) lie deep to sternocleidomastoid, pushing the muscle outwards, (ii) follow the posterior belly of digastric and present as a swelling between the tip of mastoid and angle of jaw, (iii) be present in upper part of posterior triangle, (iv) reach the parapharyngeal space Bezold Abscess. B) Battle's Sign: It can be related to otitis media. Battle's sign refers to bruising or discoloration behind the ear, specifically in the mastoid region. It is associated with basilar skull fractures, which can occur as a complication of severe otitis media or mastoiditis C) Delta Sign: "Delta Sign" is commonly used in radiology to describe a characteristic radiographic finding in certain medical conditions, particularly in the context of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST). In the context of CVST, the "Delta Sign" refers to a triangular or delta-shaped filling defect within the dural venous sinuses, most commonly seen in the superior sagittal sinus. This sign is observed on contrast-enhanced imaging, such as computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and indicates the presence of a blood clot or thrombus within the sinus. D) Griesinger's Sign: This is due to thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein. Oedema appears over the posterior part of the mastoid.

qText: Which of the following findings is referred to as Battle's sign?
expl: Explanation: Battle's sign is the presence of bruising over the mastoid process Indicates a basilar skull fracture (temporal bone fractures) This ecchymosis appears behind the ear and typically develops as a late sign following head trauma. Explanation of other options: Periorbital hematoma (Option B): Periorbital hematoma also known as raccoon eyes presents as bruising around the eyes, which is a sign of trauma to the face or base of the skull, but it is not the same battle's sign. Bezold abscess (Option C): Bezold abscess refers to a collection of pus in the neck, often caused by a middle ear infection, and does not relate to the bruising over the mastoid. Perichondritis (Option D): P erichondritis refers to inflammation of the cartilage of the ear, typically caused by infection, but it does not involve bruising behind the ear. qText: Identify the abscess.
expl: Explanation: The abscess described is a zygomatic root abscess , a rare extracranial complication of acute otitis media . It occurs when a mastoid infection erodes the root of the zygomatic process , leading to swelling in the temporo-parietal region. It is an extracranial complication of acute otitis media, though very rare. First described by Friedrich Bezold , who reported the erosion of the zygomatic root due to mastoid abscess. Clinically presents as swelling in the temporo-parietal or zygomatic region , often causing facial asymmetry. The abscess forms secondary to mastoid infection that erodes the zygomatic process . Radiographic imaging of the mastoid is helpful for diagnosis, especially to detect associated cholesteatoma . Treatment: Typically involves modified radical mastoidectomy with drainage of the abscess to prevent further complications. Importance: Early recognition is crucial, as misdiagnosis or delay in treatment can lead to serious morbidity . Explanation of Other Options: Citelli abscess (Option A): Occurs in the occipital region from mastoid infection. Bezold abscess (Option B): Forms in the sternocleidomastoid region due to erosion of the mastoid tip. Luc abscess (Option C): A subperiosteal temporal abscess without intraosseous involvement. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3343403/

qText: What is ideal choice of treatment for a patient with diphtheria and a right vocal fold palsy?
expl: Explanation: In a patient with diphtheria and right vocal fold palsy, thyroplasty type 1 is the most appropriate treatment. Thyroplasty type 1 is a surgical procedure used to improve vocal fold closure in cases of vocal fold paralysis. This procedure involves the insertion of an implant to push the paralysed vocal fold towards the midline, improving voice quality and airway protection. It is especially helpful in cases of vocal fold paralysis caused by infections like diphtheria, which can result in nerve damage affecting vocal fold movement. Explanation of other options: Wait and watch (Option A) : Waiting and watching may be appropriate in some cases of vocal fold paralysis that resolve spontaneously over time. However, given that the patient has vocal fold palsy with potential functional impairment (speech and airway protection), active intervention such as thyroplasty is typically preferred to improve outcomes. Gelfoam injection (Option B) : Gelfoam injection is sometimes used in laryngeal procedures for temporary volume augmentation, but it is not the definitive treatment for vocal fold paralysis. It may not provide long-term results compared to thyroplasty. Fat injection (Option D) : Fat injection, similar to Gelfoam, is another method for increasing vocal fold bulk and improving closure, but it is less commonly used for permanent correction compared to thyroplasty. Fat injections can lead to resorption over time, reducing their long-term efficacy.

qText: What is the preferred treatment for a primipara who is experiencing hearing impairment that has worsened during her pregnancy? The Rinne's test yields negative results in both ears, while the Weber's test shows lateralization to the right side. The otoscopy reveals normal tympanic membranes, and audiometry indicates a dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz.
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation is classic for otosclerosis , a condition where abnormal bone growth fixes the stapes footplate, causing conductive hearing loss . Key diagnostic clues include: Negative Rinne test (bone conduction > air conduction) indicating conductive loss. Weber test lateralizing to the worse-hearing (right) ear. Carhart's notch (bone conduction dip at 2000 Hz) on audiometry. Worsening during pregnancy due to hormonal influences. Stapedotomy is the preferred surgical treatment. It involves creating a small fenestration in the fixed stapes footplate and inserting a prosthesis, effectively bypassing the fixation and restoring sound transmission to the inner ear. Explanation of other options: Sodium fluoride (Option A) : This is a medical therapy used to potentially slow the progression of otosclerotic activity by promoting bone mineralization, but it is not a definitive treatment to restore hearing. Tympanoplasty (Option B): This procedure repairs the tympanic membrane or ossicles in cases of chronic otitis media or trauma. It is not indicated for otosclerosis, where the tympanic membrane is normal. Stapedectomy (Option C): While also a treatment for otosclerosis, the more modern stapedotomy technique is generally preferred as it is less invasive, has a lower risk of complications (e.g., sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo), and offers faster recovery. Key Takeaways: The classic triad for otosclerosis is : conductive hearing loss normal TM Carhart's notch on audiometry. Stapedotomy is the gold standard surgical treatment for otosclerosis.

qText: A young lady presents to OPD with a history of sudden onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness following an episode of acute otitis media two weeks back. On examination, Rinne's test and fistula test were found positive. However, she initially refused treatment and again presented with complaints of worsened hearing loss in the affected ear. Further examination, revealed a negative fistula test. What would be the most likely finding on the Rinne test in this scenario?
expl: Explanation: The patient with otitis media , has developed labyrinthine fistula as a complication, which caused sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) , tinnitus, and vertigo. This will result in a: Positive Rinne's test Positive fistula test: Due to perilymph leak or fistula Since treatment was refused, the condition progressed, resulting in complete labyrinthine destruction or the dead ear. This caused a negative fistula sign. However, the ear now has profound unilateral SNHL, where Rinne's test remains positive (a true positive result). Rinne's Test: The Rinne test compares bone conduction (BC) to air conduction (AC) of sound. In conductive hearing loss , BC > AC (i.e., the sound is heard better through bone conduction). In sensorineural hearing loss , AC > BC (i.e., the sound is heard better through air conduction).

qText: A 38-year-old male presents with suspected diagnosis of suppurative labyrinthitis. A positive Rinne test and a positive fistula sign were recorded on initial examination. The patient refused treatment and returned to the emergency department after 2 weeks complaining of deafness on the same ear. On examination, now the fistula sign was found to be negative. What would be the expected finding on repeating the Rinne test?
expl: The patient was earlier having labyrinthine fistula. Because of no treatment, he developed dead labyrinth. A negative fistula sign in this case indicates a dead labyrinth which implies severe sensorineural hearing loss. In such cases a false negative Rinne's test is most likely. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 26, 48.

qText: A 35-year-old woman presents with complaints of slowly progressive difficulty hearing in the right ear and pulsatile tinnitus. On examination, a reddish mass was seen behind the tympanic membrane, and an audible bruit was heard over the mastoid on auscultation. The Rinne's test was found negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The likely diagnosis in this scenario is a glomus tumor , a vascular middle ear lesion often causing conductive hearing loss reflected by a negative Rinne's test. Glomus tumors Also known as glomus jugulare tumors are skull based jugular foramen tumour. These are vascular lesions that occur in the middle ear, often behind the tympanic membrane. Tumours originate from the dome of the jugular bulb and can extend into the middle ear and surrounding structures. More common in females. The most common blood supply to this tumour is the ascending pharyngeal artery. Clinical features and findings Pulsatile tinnitus Hearing loss IX, X, XI CN involvement Rising sun sign The red vascular tumour behind the tympanic membrane gives the characteristic rising sun sign. Bleeds on touching Brown sign Tumor blanches on siegelisation. Aquino sign Pulsatile mass in the ear, these Pulsations will disappear on pressing carotid arteries Investigations Biopsy is contraindicated. CT scan Shows Phelps sign: Erosion of bony septum between the carotid canal and Jugular foramen MRI Done to rule out intracranial extension. MR Angiography helps to find out the main source of blood supply for the tumour. Pre-operative embolisation will reduce blood loss during surgery. Urinary VMA levels (24 hours) Pune tone audiometry shows CHL Histopathology Show the Zell Ballen pattern, where epithelioid chief cells and sustentacular supporting cells form clusters (Zell Ballen) encircled by extensive vascular sinusoids. Treatment Treatment Of choice is surgery. Alternative: Gamma knife therapy If a similar tumor found to be arising from glomus cells lying around promontory (bulge on the medial of the middle ear). Then this tumor is called glomus tympanicum Explanation of other options: CSOM (Option A) : CSOM is a chronic ear infection, often associated with purulent drainage and ear discomfort. While it can cause hearing loss, the presence of a reddish mass behind the tympanic membrane and pulsatile tinnitus would not be typical for CSOM, which typically presents with a history of recurrent ear infections and persistent drainage. ASOM (Option B) : ASOM is an acute ear infection, typically presenting with severe pain, fever, and sometimes a perforated tympanic membrane. It does not commonly cause pulsatile tinnitus or the specific signs seen in this case, such as the reddish mass and bruit. Mastoiditis (Option C) : Mastoiditis is an infection of the mastoid air cells, often resulting from a prolonged middle ear infection. It presents with fever, pain behind the ear, and swelling over the mastoid. The pulsatile tinnitus and reddish mass behind the tympanic membrane are more consistent with a vascular tumor like a glomus tumor, rather than mastoiditis.

qText: Treatment of choice for the polyp shown in the CT scan is?
expl: The CT scan shows a homogenous mass in one maxillary sinus and ipsilateral nasal cavity. So antrochoanal polyp (Killian’s polyp) is the most likely diagnosis. The treatment of choice for antrochoanal polyp is FESS (Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery). If unavailable, endoscopic polypectomy can be done. Intranasal polypectomy and Caldwell Luc operations were done previously for antrochoanal polyp. Intranasal ethmoidectomy was done previously for ethmoidal polyp. All these are superseded by endoscopic surgeries now. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra , 8 th Edition, pg. no – 200

qText: A 48-year-old man from China presented with hearing loss in right ear. On examination the tympanic membrane was dull and a B type tympanogram was seen. Lymph nodes in the neck are palpable. What is the appropriate management?
expl: Explanation: The above symptoms, particularly in an individual from an endemic region like China, strongly suggests Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC) with associated Eustachian tube obstruction and nodal metastasis. Radiotherapy is the appropriate management Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a rare cancer that starts in the nasopharynx, fossa of Rossenmuller. It can present as unilateral serous otitis media and painless cervical lymphadenopathy , often necessitating radiotherapy as the primary treatment due to its location. Risk Factors: Strong association with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) , genetic predisposition, and diets high in preservatives such as nitrosamines, Geographic centers such as Southern China Presenting symptoms : Painless cervical lymphadenopathy (enlarged neck nodes) - often the first presenting symptom, Otitis media with effusion/Eustachian tube dysfunction, Unilateral hearing loss, Nasal obstruction. Cranial nerve palsy Diagnosis : Nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy is definitive; MRI/CT for staging, PET/CT for metastasis, EBV serologies Treatment : State I-II: radiation alone, Stage III-IV: chemoRT Explanation of Other Options: Grommet insertion + steroids (Option A) While grommet insertion is used for chronic otitis media with effusion, it addresses the symptom (middle ear fluid) but not the underlying malignancy . In the context of a neck mass and unilateral effusion in an adult, it is inappropriate to treat symptomatically without addressing the primary cause. Wait and watch (Option C) Observation is not acceptable in this clinical scenario. Delaying diagnosis or treatment of a potentially aggressive cancer like NPC would compromise outcomes. Radical neck dissection (Option D) While NPC may present with cervical lymphadenopathy, the primary treatment is radiotherapy or chemoradiation , not surgery. Neck dissection is usually not first-line and may be considered only in residual or recurrent nodal disease after radiotherapy. Key Takeaway: In an adult with unilateral middle ear effusion and painless neck swelling , always suspect nasopharyngeal carcinoma . The ideal management is radiotherapy , as NPC is highly radiosensitive.

qText: Which one of the following causes maximum hearing loss:
expl: Explanation: A disrupted ossicular chain with an intact tympanic membrane causes the maximum hearing loss (~55 dB) among the given options. This is because the intact TM reflects sound back out of the ear canal, while the disrupted ossicles prevent efficient transmission of the remaining sound energy to the inner ear. This creates a highly inefficient system. Hearing Loss Degrees in Different Conditions: Tympanic Membrane (TM) perforation → 10-40 dB hearing loss Complete obstruction of External Auditory Canal (EAC) → 30-40 dB hearing loss TM perforation with ossicular discontinuity → 40 dB hearing loss Ossicular discontinuity with intact TM → 55 dB hearing loss Complete fixation of the footplate of the stapes (seen in otosclerosis) → 60 dB hearing loss Explanation of other options: Serous otitis media (Option A) : It is an infection of the middle ear and causes a mild to moderate conductive loss (10-30 dB). Disrupted ossicular chain and disrupted TM (Option C): The perforation allows some sound to enter the middle ear directly, resulting in a lesser hearing loss (~40 dB) than an intact TM with ossicular disruption. Partial footplate fixation (Option D): As in early otosclerosis, causes a mild conductive loss. References: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5023437/ https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5023437/

qText: Identify the type of tympanoplasty?
expl: Explanation: The given image shows that graft is placed directly onto the stapes head which is suggestive of Type III Tympanoplasty. The Wullstein classification, developed by Horst Ludwig Wullstein in 1956, categorizes tympanoplasty proceduresinto the following five types: Type I (Myringoplasty) : Repair of a tympanic membrane (TM) perforation only; ossicular chain is intact. The graft is placed directly onto the edges of the perforation. Type II: Repair of TM perforation with some malleus erosion ; graft connects to malleus or incus. Type III (Myringostapediopexy): Absent malleus and incus, repair of TM perforation with graft placed directly onto the intact stapes head Type IV : Repair of TM perforation with only the stapes footplate intact ; graft covers the oval window, and sound is directed to the round window. Type V : (Fenestration): Used for a fixed stapes (e.g., in otosclerosis); involves creating a new opening (fenestra) in the lateral semicircular canal. Key Takeaway: Type 3 tympanoplasty is used when malleus and incus are absent , and the graft is placed on a mobile stapes head , preserving hearing function.

qText: Which condition presents with both a positive reservoir sign and tenderness over the mastoid?
expl: Explanation: Acute mastoiditis is characterized by the presence of both mastoid tenderness and a positive reservoir sign . Acute Mastoiditis: Acute mastoiditis is an infection of the mastoid including the air cells It usually occur as a complication of acute otitis media. Most common causative organisms: Beta-hemolytic streptococcus Symptoms Persistent or increasing ear pain, especially behind the ear Fever that persists or recurs despite antibiotics Ear discharge: profuse, purulent, or sometimes obstructed Examination Findings Investigations Blood tests: Show polymorphonuclear leukocytosis and a raised ESR. Imaging: X-ray mastoid (Schuller's view): Reveals clouding and coalescence of air cells . CT temporal bone: Demonstrates loss of bony septa and cavity formation in advanced stages. Treatment: Medical: Administer IV antibiotics for 48 hours ; if no improvement, proceed to surgery. Surgical: Cortical mastoidectomy (Schwartz operation) is performed. Explanation of other options: Otosclerotic lesion (Option A): Otosclerosis typically presents with progressive conductive hearing loss due to stapes fixation, but does not cause mastoid tenderness or a reservoir sign. Intratympanic glomus tumor (Option C): Intratympanic glomus tumors present with pulsatile tinnitus and a reddish mass behind the tympanic membrane, yet mastoid tenderness and reservoir sign are absent. Chronic suppurative otitis media (Option D): Chronic suppurative otitis media shows persistent purulent ear discharge and tympanic membrane perforation, but mastoid tenderness and reservoir sign are usually absent unless complicated by cholesteatoma or acute mastoiditis.

qText: The best description of Gelle's test
expl: Gelle's test Compares intensity of bone-conducted tuning fork sound, without and with, raising pressure on the tympanic membrane with Siegel's speculum. Normally, Gelle's test is positive because intensity of hearing decreases when air pressure is raised in external auditory canal. In ossicular fixation or ossicular discontinuity, increased air pressure makes no changes in the sound intensity(Gelle's negative). Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 27.

qText: Type B tympanogram is seen associate with which of the following conditions?
expl: Explanation: A type B tympanogram indicates poor middle ear compliance, which is typically associated with fluid in the middle ear as seen in serous otitis media . This flat-shaped tympanogram suggests that the middle ear is filled with fluid, preventing the eardrum from moving normally in response to changes in air pressure. It is one of the most common findings in middle ear effusion. Explanation of other options: Ossicular dislocation (Option A) : This condition typically results in a hypercompliant tympanogram, showing an Ad curve (type Ad), rather than a flat B curve. Otosclerosis (Option B) : Otosclerosis is associated with stapes fixation and reduced middle ear compliance. It results in an As tympanogram (shallow curve) due to reduced mobility of the ossicular chain, not a flat B curve. Normal ear (Option D) : A normal ear produces a type A tympanogram, indicating normal compliance and middle ear pressure. Reference: Otitis media with effusion Jerger classification system for tympanogram

qText: Which of the following statements is false about sodium fluoride regarding its use in the treatment of otosclerosis?
expl: SODIUM FLUORIDE Mechanism of action: Inhibitor of osteoclast activity and so a stabilizer of bone turnover. It also leads to increased calcium deposition in otospongiotic foci and decreased bone remodelling. It inhibits the proteolytic enzymes in the cochlea. Uses: Sodium fluoride is the treatment of choice in Schwartz sign positive patients which represents the active stage of the disease. It is also used in cochlear otosclerosis. Contraindications: Chronic nephritis, Flourosis, in pregnant and lactating women and in children. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1074.

qText: A 45-year-old woman reports gradually worsening hearing loss over several years. Audiometry shows conductive hearing loss, and she is diagnosed with otosclerosis. What is the preferred surgical treatment for this condition?
expl: Explanation: Stapedectomy with the placement of a prosthesis is the surgical treatment of choice for Otosclerosis. Otosclerosis: Treatmen t Medical Otosclerosis has no definitive medical cure. Sodium fluoride has been used to promote maturation of active lesions and prevent further cochlear damage, but its efficacy is controversial, and it is generally not recommended. Surgical The treatment of choice for otosclerosis is stapedectomy or stapedotomy with prosthesis placement. In this procedure, the fixed stapes is removed, and a prosthesis is inserted between the incus and oval window. Common prostheses include Teflon, stainless steel, platinum-Teflon, or titanium-Teflon pistons. Fig: (A) Before removal of stapes. (B) Stapes removed and replaced by a Teflon piston. Other options: Stapes mobilization: No longer done these days as it gives temporary results; refixation being quite common. Lempert's fenestration operation: Not done now. Hearing aid: Patients who refuse surgery or are unfit for surgery can use a hearing aid.

qText: True about stapedial reflex is:
expl: Explanation: The stapedial reflex is absent in cases of otosclerosis . The Stapedial Reflex (Acoustic Reflex): It involves the contraction of the stapedius muscle in response to a loud sound. Mechanism in Otosclerosis: In otosclerosis, the footplate of the stapes becomes fixed (ankylosis) to the oval window. Consequently, the stapedius muscle cannot move the stapes, resulting in an absent reflex. This is often one of the earliest signs of the disease. Reflex Arc: Afferent (Sensory): Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) Efferent (Motor): Facial nerve (CN VII) It is also absent in severe sensorineural hearing loss and facial nerve paralysis (proximal to the nerve to stapedius). Explanation of Other Options: Facial nerve is afferent (Option A): Incorrect. The Facial nerve (CN VII) is the efferent limb that innervates the stapedius muscle. Vestibulocochlear nerve is efferent (Option B): Incorrect. The Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) is the afferent limb that carries sound information to the brainstem. Protective reflex for middle ear function (Option C): Incorrect. While the action takes place in the middle ear, it is a protective reflex for the inner ear (cochlea). The contraction dampens the transmission of loud sounds (especially low frequencies) to the cochlea to prevent acoustic trauma.

qText: Rinne test is negative in all except
expl: In this test air conduction of the ear is compared with its bone conduction. A vibrating tuning fork is placed on the patient's mastoid and when he stops hearing, it is brought beside the meatus. If he still hears, AC is more than BC. Alternatively, the patient is asked to compare the loudness of sound heard through air and bone conduction. Rinne test is called positive when AC is longer or louder than BC. Sensorineural hearing loss associated with physiological aging process in the ear is called presbycusis, thus having a positive Rinne test. qText: Which of the following are indications for cochlear implant? 1.Otosclerosis 2.Congenital hearing loss 3.Fixed malleus 4.Aminoglycosides induced hearing loss
expl: Explanation: Severe sensorineural hearing loss from birth (congenital) or caused by aminoglycoside toxicity are both recognized indications for a cochlear implant. Cochlear Implant Indications: Sensorineural hearing loss is the primary indication for cochlear implantation. Specifically, congenital severe-to-profound hearing loss and hearing loss caused by aminoglycoside ototoxicity are classic indications. Cochlear implants are recommended for patients who do not gain sufficient benefit from conventional hearing aids . Mechanism of Action: The cochlear implant bypasses damaged cochlear hair cells and directly stimulates the auditory (8th cranial) nerve , allowing sound perception. The electrode array is surgically positioned within the scala tympani of the cochlea. A functioning auditory nerve and intact central auditory pathways are essential prerequisites for the procedure. Components of a Cochlear Implant: External Component: Includes a speech processor and a transmitter , which capture and encode sound. Internal Component: Surgically implanted under the skin and consists of a receiver/stimulator unit with an electrode array that interfaces with the cochlea. Candidate Criteria for Cochlear Implantation: Ideal candidates for a cochlear implant typically meet the following criteria: Bilateral severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss Minimal or no improvement with conventional hearing aids No medical conditions that contraindicate surgery Realistic expectations regarding outcomes Strong family and social support to assist with post-implant rehabilitation Sufficient cognitive ability to effectively use and benefit from the device Components: Key takeaway: Preoperative Evaluation: Audiological assessment to determine the degree and type of hearing loss. Imaging: High-resolution CT (HRCT) and MRI to assess the cochlear structure, cochlear nerve, and identify any central nervous system abnormalities. Surgical Approach: Two main techniques are used to access the cochlea: Facial recess approach - via the facial recess Pericanal approach - via the external auditory canal (EAC) The electrode array is inserted into the scala tympani , typically through the round window from the middle ear. Postoperative Management: The cochlear implant is usually activated 3-4 weeks after surgery . Postoperative evaluation is performed using HRCT ; MRI is generally contraindicated due to the implant. Contraindications: Cochlear aplasia (Michel aplasia) - absence of the cochlea Absence or damage of the cochlear nerve or lesions affecting the central auditory pathways

qText: Carhart's notch is seen in which of the following conditions:
expl: Explanation: Carhart's Notch is a classic, though not pathognomonic, audiometric finding in Otosclerosis . It appears as a false depression in bone conduction thresholds at 2000 Hz . It is thought to be due to the fixation of the stapes footplate, which disrupts the normal ossicular resonance. This "notch" often disappears after successful stapes surgery. Explanation of other options: Ossicular Discontinuity (Option B): It causes conductive hearing loss but does not produce Carhart's notch. Oto syphilis (Option C): It causes sensorineural hearing loss, not associated with Carhart's notch. Serous otitis media (Option D): It causes conductive hearing loss, but the pattern is typically flat across frequencies, not a specific notch at 2 kHz. Key Takeaways: Carhart's Notch (2 kHz dip in BC) → Classic finding in Otosclerosis .

expl: Congenital syphilis is of two types: the early form, manifesting at the age of 2 or the late form, manifesting at the age of 8-20 years. qText: For which of the subsequent conditions is Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) implemented?
expl: Explanation: A Bone Anchored Hearing Aid (BAHA) works via bone conduction , bypassing the external auditory canal and middle ear to directly stimulate the cochlea. It is ideally suited for conditions where these structures are absent, malformed, or chronically diseased, such as congenital external auditory atresia . Indication: Chronic ear discharge . Single-sided hearing loss. Children with microtia , anotia, canal atresia. Conductive or mixed hearing loss (e.g., otosclerosis, tympanosclerosis) with contraindications for surgery. Following MRM (large mastoid cavity). Excessive feedback or discomfort from AC hearing aids. Age of implantation: >5yrs Surgical Procedure : Adults typically have a single-stage surgery with a 3-month osseointegration wait. Children usually undergo a two-stage procedure, with the fixture placed first and the abutment connected after 6 months. Explanation of other options: Sensorineural hearing loss (Option A): Results from inner ear or neural damage. Since the cochlea is damaged, bone conduction is also impaired, making BAHA ineffective. Conventional hearing aids or cochlear implants are used. Acoustic neuroma (Option B): A tumor affecting the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). Treatment involves surgery or radiation, not BAHA. Otitis media (Option D): A middle ear infection or effusion. This is typically a temporary conductive hearing loss treated medically or with grommets. BAHA is not indicated. Key Takeaways: BAHA is indicated for conductive or mixed hearing losses where the cochlear function is preserved. It is a excellent solution for congenital aural atresia, chronic otitis externa, or single-sided deafness.

qText: A 23-year-old male presents with nasal discharge, as depicted in the image on a handkerchief. Which feature of the discharge helps in identifying it as CSF rhinorrhoea?
expl: Explanation: The Halo sign is a key indicator of CSF rhinorrhea. It appears when nasal discharge on a tissue or handkerchief forms a central clear layer of fluid surrounded by a ring of blood, creating a halo pattern. This suggests cerebrospinal fluid leakage into the nasal cavity, commonly from a skull base fracture near the ethmoid sinuses. CSF Rhinorrhea: CSF rhinorrhea is the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the nose, usually due to trauma or iatrogenic injury. The leak commonly occurs through the skull base, involving structures such as the cribriform plate, crista galli, and fovea ethmoidalis . C auses: The most common cause of CSF rhinorrhoea is iatrogenic. Often from cribriform plate injury during functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS). Traumatic h ead injuries including Le Fort II/III fractures, ethmoid or nasal fractures are the second most common cause. Clinical features: Clear, watery nasal discharge that increases with bending, straining, or in the morning. Traumatic leaks may mix with blood, producing the halo/target/double halo sign on filter paper. Unlike nasal secretions, CSF gushes suddenly and cannot be sniffed back. Diagnosis: Beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein: Highly specific and sensitive tests for CSF in nasal discharge. Nasal endoscopy: Can help localize the leak. Imaging: CT or MR cisternography can identify the site of the leak. Explanation of other options: Rising sun sign (Option B) : The Rising Sun Sign refers to a red, vascular tumor in the middle ear that erodes the floor and extends into the hypotympanum, giving the appearance of a rising sun behind the intact tympanic membrane. It is characteristic of glomus jugulare tumors. Schwartz sign (Option C) : A reddish blush seen behind the tympanic membrane in otosclerosis , due to increased vascularity of the cochlear promontory. Phelps sign (Option D) : Phelps Sign on CT scan refers to the erosion of the bony septum between the carotid canal and the jugular foramen, often seen in glomus jugulare tumors.

qText: Tympanic membrane rupture is related to which level of blast injury?
expl: Explanation: Blast trauma produces a variety of injuries due to the sudden and extreme pressure changes generated by an explosion. Among the affected organs, the ear is the most vulnerable , especially the tympanic membrane, because of its sensitivity to pressure fluctuations. Blast-related ear injuries are therefore very common and help in classifying the type of blast injury involved. Blast injuries are classified into four levels: Primary blast injury (Level I) (Option A): Caused by the direct effect of blast pressure waves (positive and negative phases). Organs containing air, such as the ear, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract , are most vulnerable. Tympanic membrane rupture is the most common injury, as the eardrum is highly sensitive to rapid pressure changes. Secondary blast injury (Level II) (Option B): Results from flying debris or shrapnel leading to lacerations or penetrating injuries. Tertiary blast injury (Level III) (Option C): Due to the displacement of the body by the blast wind , causing blunt trauma or crush injuries. Quaternary blast injury (Level IV) (Option D): Includes miscellaneous effects such as burns, inhalation injuries, or exposure to toxic substances. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5782944/

qText: A 70-year-old man presents with left-sided deafness and tinnitus. Examination reveals a dull tympanic membrane, palpable neck lymph nodes, and tympanometry showing a type B curve. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The most likely diagnosis is nasopharyngeal carcinoma , presenting with cervical lymphadenopathy, left-sided deafness, tinnitus, and a dull tympanic membrane due to eustachian tube obstruction. Tympanometry shows a type B curve, indicating middle ear effusion secondary to the tumor. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma Nasopharyngeal cancer is a multifactorial disease most common in China. Mostly affects people aged 50 to 70 years, although younger patients can also be affected. Aetiology Epstein-Barr (EB) virus is closely associated with nasopharyngeal cancer. Genetics, particularly HLA-A2 and B47, also play a supportive role. Air pollution, smoking of tobacco and opium, nitrosamines from dry salted fish, smoke from burning of incense and wood have all been incriminated. Clinical features Cervical lymphadenopathy The most common presentation is metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy (secondary neck node). Hearing loss The second most common presentation is unilateral conductive hearing loss due to the blockage of the eustachian tube opening, leading to unilateral glue ear (serous otitis media). Ophthalmoneurologic symptoms Multiple cranial nerve palsies may occur in nasopharyngeal carcinoma because the nasopharynx lies just below the skull base. The tumor can spread into the cranial cavity through the foramen lacerum. The sixth cranial nerve is most commonly affected, followed by the fifth nerve. Trotter’s triad Neuralgia in the temporal parietal area (fifth nerve involvement) Palatal paralysis (tenth nerve involvement) Unilateral conductive hearing loss (glue ear). Spread of tumor Commonest site of origin in the nasopharynx is the fossa of Rosenmüller. Anterior spread causes blockage of choana and nasal cavity and inferior spread is towards oropharynx and hypopharynx. Lateral spread involves parapharyngeal space and infratemporal fossa through the sinus of Morgagni. Superiorly may spread to involve the intracranial structures. Nasopharynx is rich in lymphatics and an early lymphatic spread is seen in cervical nodes. Lung, bone and liver are the most common sites of distant metastasis. Diganosis Nasal pharyngoscopy to visualise the nasopharynx, followed by biopsy and histopathological confirmation. Treatment The treatment of choice is chemo-radiation (radiotherapy plus chemotherapy). NPC is a radio-sensitive tumor. Chemotherapy often involves cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil. Explanation of other options: Chronic suppurative otitis media (Option A): Chronic suppurative otitis media usually causes purulent ear discharge and does not produce the cervical lymphadenopathy or dull tympanic membrane seen in nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Glomus tumour (Option B): Although glomus tumour can cause tinnitus and middle ear effusion, it would not typically present with cervical lymphadenopathy or eustachian tube dysfunction leading to a type B tympanogram. Sensorineural hearing loss (Option D): Incorrect, since it causes hearing loss but does not explain the cervical lymphadenopathy, dull tympanic membrane, or type B tympanogram indicative of a nasopharyngeal mass.

qText: A patient presents with acute-onset left-sided lower motor neuron (LMN) facial paralysis. Imaging studies show no intracranial or structural abnormalities. What is the next best step in management?
expl: Explanation: The presentation is characteristic of Bell's palsy which is an acute, idiopathic, unilateral LMN facial nerve paralysis . It typically manifests with sudden facial asymmetry , inability to close the eye , and drooping of the mouth . Absence of radiological findings rules out secondary causes (e.g., tumors, stroke, or infection). Bell's palsy is thought to result from inflammation and viral reactivation (most often Herpes simplex virus type 1 ), leading to facial nerve edema and compression within the narrow fallopian canal. Explanation of Other Options: Intravenous antibiotics, and mastoidectomy (Option A): Indicated in acute suppurative otitis media or mastoiditis with facial nerve involvement. This patient has no radiologic evidence of infection , ruling this out. Hence, not appropriate for idiopathic Bell's palsy. Electrical stimulation of facial nerve (Option C): Not part of first-line therapy. Evidence suggests minimal benefit and potential risk of aberrant reinnervation or synkinesis. Focus should be on physiotherapy and muscle retraining Facial nerve decompression (Option D): Not part of first-line therapy. Evidence suggests minimal benefit and potential risk of aberrant reinnervation or synkinesis. Focus should be on physiotherapy and muscle retraining

qText: A 26-year-old woman has become aware of increasing bilateral hearing deficiency. Her eardrums are normal. Her hearing tests show: Rinne test is negative on both sides and BC-normal both sides. What is the the most likely diagnosis?
expl: OTOSCLEROSIS/OTOSPONGIOSIS (EARLY STAGE) It is a fixation of the footplate of stapes. (Piston like movement is slowed) It is a disease of optic capsule. (Bony labryinth) In otosclerosis, the dense endochondral bone of otic capsule is replaced by spongy bone (woven bone) which is later replaced by more of mature bone. Histopathology picture is called Blue mantles It is more common in females (young) mostly 2 nd & 3 rd decade Mostly Bilateral Genetic disease Autosomal Dominant(Involves genes encoding type1 collagen). It is gradually progressive disease, but Pregnancy aggravates it. Most common site of origin is FISSULA ANTE FENESTRAM. It is a point anterior to the oval window. Initial stage of disease is pink in colour, this stage is called otospongiosis. It gradually turns White (this stage is called otosclerosis). In the next few years, the disease will surround the footplate from all-around. Measles viral infection may initiate the conversion of dense bone to spongy bone. (a hypothesis only) Rarely otosclerosis can also involve cochlea which will lead to cochlear otosclerosis. This will lead to mixed hearing loss (CHL+SNHL). CT scan of cochlear otosclerosis shows DOUBLE RING SIGN. Clinical Picture A young female with bilateral gradually progressive CHL Other symptoms- Patients hear better in noisy areas, this is called Paracusis Willisi. Low tone voice. +/- Tinnitus (ringing sensation in the ear). Examination 90% of patients show normal Tympanic Membrane. 10% of patients show Schwartz sign Schwartz sign is in Early stages. It is Flamingo pink appearance behind tympanic membrane. Investigations PTA CHL+ Carhart's Notch (dip at 2000Hz in BC). Tympanometry shows Type As curve. Absent stapedial reflex. Treatment Rx of choice is surgery called Stapedotomy>Stapedectomy. Other treatment for Otosclerosis Hearing aid- is given for patients unwilling for surgery. Sodium fluoride (NaF) oral therapy. It is treatment of choice for Schwartz sign (+) patient. (Early stage of disease) Cochlear otosclerosis. NaF leads to stabilization of disease. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 27, 82, 104.
