qText: A Patient is not able to hear properly from the left ear given an audiogram. What will be finding of Rinne and weber test and which ear is asked?
expl: In this case, the patient is experiencing hearing loss in the left ear. The Rinne and Weber tests are used to assess the patient's hearing and lateralization of sound perception. Right Rinne's positive: When the tuning fork is placed on the mastoid bone (bone conduction) and then moved to the front of the ear (air conduction), the patient can hear the sound better through air conduction (front of the ear) than bone conduction (mastoid bone) in the right ear. Weber lateralized to the right ear: When the tuning fork is placed on the center of the forehead, the patient perceives the sound as being louder or localized to the right ear. This is a case of left side Sensorineural hearing loss. Thus Left Rinne's test positive and weber lateralized to the right ear is the correct option.

qText: Which is the diagnostic investigation of choice in assessing hearing loss in children?
expl: BERA (brainstem evoked response audiometry) is to elicit brainstem responses to auditory stimulation by clicks or tone bursts. It is a noninvasive technique to find the integrity of central auditory pathways through the VIIIth nerve, pons and midbrain. In this method, electrical potentials are generated in response to several click stimuli or tone bursts and picked up from the vertex by surface electrodes. It measures hearing sensitivity in the range of 1000-4000 Hz. ABR is used: As a screening procedure for infants. To determine the threshold of hearing in infants; also in children and adults who do not cooperate and in malingerers. To diagnose retrocochlear pathology particularly acoustic neuroma. To diagnose brainstem pathology, e.g. multiple sclerosis or pontine tumours. To monitor CN VIII intraoperatively in surgery of acoustic neuromas to preserve the function of cochlear nerve. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose & Head and Neck surgery by P L Dhingra, 9 th edition, Pg.no.31,32

qText: A 48-year-old man with a history of trauma to the right ear presents with pain and hearing loss. Examination showed blood clots filling the ear canal. What is the next step in management?
expl: Explanation: The patient is most likely to have sustained traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, resulting in blood clots in the ear canal. In cases of traumatic tympanic membrane perforation with blood clots, the safest initial step is to keep the ear dry and provide analgesics. Traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane usually heals automatically. Its important to keep the ear dry to prevent infections, thus use of ear drops and syringing is best avoided. (Option B, D ruled out). Aspirating the clot, which seals the bleeding, may potentially cause further complications and is usually unnecessary, as the clot typically resolves spontaneously. (Option A ruled out) Overall, conservative management allows for natural healing of the tympanic membrane and pain relief.

qText: A 78-year-old female complaints of vertigo, intermittent weakness of right lower limb since 2 days, severe headache. On physical examination plethoric face and conjunctive injection, over all dusky cyanotic complexion, pulse 60 BPM, regular, BP 250/110 mm Hg. CBC shows RBC count: 7 to 8 million/mm3, Hematocrit - 60 to 70% and also increase in WBCs and platelets. Which of the following statement is true?
expl: Polycythemia Vera (PCV) is a myeloproliferative disorder characterized by increased RBCs, WBCs, and platelets. Erythropoietin levels are reduced in PCV. Erythromelalgia is also seen in PCV. Key findings in PCV include: High RBC count and hematocrit (60-70%). Plethoric appearance (red, flushed face) and dusky cyanosis due to increased blood viscosity. BP 250/110 mm Hg and slowed circulation. Increased blood viscosity leads to complications like headaches, vertigo, and thrombotic events. Why Not Other Options A (Increased blood viscosity, not decreased): Blood viscosity is drastically increased in PCV, causing circulatory issues, not decreased. B (Chronic myeloid leukemia): CML primarily affects WBCs and presents with different clinical features, lacking the characteristic high RBCs and hematocrit seen in PCV. C (Infective lesion in bone marrow): PCV is not caused by infection but by a genetic mutation (JAK2 mutation) in hematopoietic stem cells. Key Takeaways: Correct Diagnosis: Polycythemia Vera (PCV). Main Issue: Increased RBC production, elevated blood viscosity, and associated symptoms like plethoric face and hypertension. Other myeloproliferative disorders: Essential thrombocytosis, CML, Myelofibrosis. Tags: Inicet nov 2019 Tag: Vascular physiology Level: Good to know Reference: Guyton and Hall the text of Physiology, John E Hall & Michael E Hall, 14th Edition, Page No.447

qText: A 20-year-old female patient presented with a complaint of heaviness in her left ear and decreased hearing for 3 months. An endoscopic picture of the affected ear is shown below. Impedance audiometry was performed, suggesting a type B curve. Which of the following statements is true for this condition?
expl: Explanation: Based on the endoscopic findings and the type B curve on impedance audiometry, the diagnosis in this case is serous otitis media. Its management primarily includes antihistamines and decongestants. But if the condition does not resolve even after 3 months, then Myringotomy is performed, followed by placement of a grommet tube or tympanostomy tube to maintain ventilation. The collected fluid in the middle ear impairs the function of impedance matching of the middle ear and usually does not affect the inner ear. Thus, it leads to conductive deafness. Hence, option A is also not true . Since it's a sterile fluid collection, the risk of bone erosion and the development of an intracranial abscess is negligible, and on aspiration of this fluid, no organisms are usually isolated ; thus, options C and D are not true.

qText: A 5-year-old child presents with reduced hearing for the past 2-3 months. The otoscopy finding is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation The otoscopic finding of a dull, opaque, and retracted tympanic membrane with visible fluid behind it points towards serous otitis media (SOM) . It is also called otitis media with effusion and is one of the most common causes of hearing loss in children. Serous Otitis Media (SOM) Symptoms Conductive hearing loss: usually mild to moderate (20-40 dB), gradual, and sometimes fluctuating. Speech delay or impaired speech development. Mild ear discomfort or ear fullness. Children may not complain directly; parents often notice inattentiveness or reduced responsiveness. Signs Tympanic membrane: retracted, dull, opaque, may appear yellowish or bluish. Absence of normal light reflex. Fluid or air bubbles may be seen behind the eardrum. Decreased or absent mobility of tympanic membrane (on pneumatic otoscopy). Diagnostic tests Rinne test : negative (bone conduction > air conduction). Weber test : lateralizes to the affected ear. Schwabach test : prolonged bone conduction in the patient compared to examiner. Absolute bone conduction : normal (bone conduction preserved). Impedance audiometry (tympanometry) : shows flat or dome-shaped curve. Audiometry : conductive hearing loss of 20-40 dB; sometimes mixed if sensorineural component develops. Imaging : X-ray or CT may reveal mastoid air cell opacification. Explanation of Incorrect Options Myringitis bullosa (Option A): This presents with painful, blood-stained blisters on the tympanic membrane, usually associated with viral infection or Mycoplasma. It is not seen as a chronic effusion with retracted drum. Acute otitis media (Option C): Presents with fever, ear pain, irritability, and a red, bulging tympanic membrane. Chronic effusion without bulging is not typical. Pneumo tympanum (Option D): Seen when there is air in the middle ear due to trauma, barotrauma, or blast injury. Tympanic membrane usually looks hypermobile or abnormally inflated, not retracted with fluid levels. Key Takeaway In a child with persistent hearing loss, retracted opaque tympanic membrane, and fluid behind the drum, the diagnosis is serous otitis media .

qText: You see a child with delayed speech development as part of a health visit at a local school. The otoscopic appearance of the ear is shown below. Hearing loss of 20 dB is detected in audiometric tests. What is your diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Serous Otitis Media (SOM) or Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) is characterized by: Fluid in the middle ear without signs of acute infection (otoscopy: dull, retracted TM, possible air-fluid levels or bubbles). Conductive hearing loss (typically mild, 20-40 dB). Delayed speech development is a common consequence in children due to the persistent mild hearing impairment. This is a classic presentation of OME. Otoscopic Findings: Tympanic membrane may appear dull, translucent, or retracted. No purulent discharge (distinguishes it from acute/chronic suppurative OM). Pathogenesis: Eustachian Tube Dysfunction: Failure to aerate/drain the middle ear. Increased Secretory Activity: Of the middle ear mucosa. Aetiology: Mechanical Obstruction: Adenoid hyperplasia. Chronic rhinitis/sinusitis. Chronic tonsillitis (enlarged tonsils). Nasopharyngeal tumours (unilateral SOM in adults warrants investigation). Palatal defects (e.g., cleft palate). Inflammatory/Allergic: Allergies (seasonal/perennial). Unresolved otitis media. Viral infections (adenoviruses/rhinoviruses). Other: Down's syndrome. Inadequate antibiotic therapy (leading to persistent low-grade infection). Treatment First-Line (Initial Management): Observation & Monitoring: Recommended for the first 3 months if no significant hearing loss or developmental concerns exist. Most cases resolve spontaneously. Medical Management (Limited/Selective Use): Autoinflation: (e.g., Otovent®) to promote Eustachian tube opening. Treat Contributing Factors: Nasal corticosteroids for associated allergic rhinitis. Surgical Intervention (If Persistent): Indications: Effusion >3 months with persistent hearing loss (>25-40 dB), speech delay, learning problems, or structural damage. Tympanostomy Tubes: Placement of pressure-equalizing (PE) tubes is the primary and most effective surgical treatment. Adenoidectomy: Considered, especially in cases of nasal obstruction or recurrent OME, typically in children ≥4 years old. Explanation of other options: Acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM) (Option A): Presents with acute symptoms like ear pain, fever, and a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane. It is an acute infection, not a cause of chronic speech delay. Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) (Option C): Involves a chronic perforation of the tympanic membrane with persistent purulent discharge. The TM is not intact. Glomus tumor (Option D): A vascular middle ear tumor that presents with pulsatile tinnitus and a reddish mass behind the TM, not fluid or speech delay. Key Takeaways: OME is a common cause of conductive hearing loss and subsequent speech delay in children. Otoscopic findings are crucial for diagnosis (dull TM, loss of light reflex, fluid).

qText: In a child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with no improvement after using hearing aids, what should be the ideal next line of management?
expl: Explanation: For a child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) who has not experienced improvement with hearing aids, a cochlear implant is the next appropriate step. A cochlear implant bypasses the damaged parts of the cochlea and directly stimulates the auditory nerve, enabling hearing in individuals with severe-to-profound SNHL who derive limited or no benefit from conventional hearing aids. Cochlear implantation is recommended in individuals with Severe-to-profound SNHL as confirmed by audiological assessments. Hearing aids provide insufficient benefit. Speech and language development is at risk due to hearing impairment especially in children. Indications: B/L severe (70-90 dB) to profound (>90 dB) SNHL Prelingual deafness : A child who is born deaf and has not yet developed speech. Post lingual deafness : Child/adult who has become deaf but has already developed speech. Contraindications: Cochlear aplasia 8th nerve abnormality (like aplasia or retro cochlear pathology, conduction via the auditory nerve is dysfunctional) Central auditory lesions Michel aplasia: Complete absence of the bony and membranous labyrinth, including the petrous apex, while the external and middle ears remain unaffected. Prerequisites: Age in prelingual deafness: Minimum age as early as possible, maximum age 7 years There is no age limit for post-lingual deafness Failed trial of hearing aid Intact acoustic nerve and central hearing tract Explanation of other options: Bone-anchored hearing aid (Option A) : This is suitable for patients with conductive or mixed hearing loss, or those with anatomical issues preventing the use of regular hearing aids (e.g., chronic otitis media, atresia). It is not appropriate for severe-to-profound SNHL. Tympanoplasty (Option B) : Tympanoplasty is a surgical procedure to repair the tympanic membrane or middle ear structures and is used in conductive hearing loss, not in sensorineural hearing loss. Normal hearing aid (Option C) : The child has already tried hearing aids without improvement. Recommending a different hearing aid would not be beneficial in cases of severe-to-profound SNHL. Reference: Cochlear Implants - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

qText: A 43 year old mechanical engineer has presented to outpatient clinic with the complaint of right sided hearing loss and Tinnitus. These symptoms have been troubling him for last one year. The hearing loss is progressive in nature. Ear examination of the patient is normal. Pure tone audiometry has shown right sided sensorineural hearing loss. MRI Brain shows space occupying lesion at right cerebellopontine angle. Which of the following is the most likely & earliest clinical finding which can be detected on nervous system examination in this patient?
expl: Vth nerve. This is the earliest nerve to be involved. There is reduced corneal sensitivity, numbness or paraesthesia of face. Involvement of this nerve indicates that the tumour is roughly 2.5 cm in diameter and occupies the cerebellopontine angle. VIIth nerve. Sensory fibres are affected early. There is hypoaesthesia of posterior meatal wall (Hitzelberger's sign), loss of taste (as tested by electrogustometry) and reduced lacrimation on Schirmer test. Motor fibres are more resistant and are affected late. Delayed blink reflex may be an early manifestation. IXth and Xth nerves. There is dysphagia and hoarseness due to palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal paralysis. Other cranial nerves. XIth and XIIth, IIIrd, IVth and VIth are affected when tumour is very large. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose & Head and Neck surgery by P L Dhingra, 9 th edition, Pg.no.132

qText: Which of the following structures are in close proximity to the affected structure in a 70-year-old male patient presenting with decreased hearing in higher frequencies, where the basilar membrane has been affected?
expl: Explanation In presbycusis, high-frequency hearing loss occurs first because the basilar membrane at the base of the cochlea (nearest to the oval window) is responsible for detecting high-frequency sounds. With aging, degeneration of hair cells in this region leads to progressive hearing loss. The oval window lies close to the basal turn of the cochlea and directly transmits vibrations from the stapes into the perilymph of the scala vestibuli. These vibrations initiate movement of the basilar membrane, with the base tuned to high-frequency sounds. Hence, in elderly patients with high-frequency hearing loss, pathology involves the portion of the basilar membrane nearest to the oval window. Explanation of Incorrect Options Modiolus (Option A): The modiolus is the central bony core of the cochlea, housing the spiral ganglion cells and providing support for the cochlear nerve. While important structurally, it is not directly adjacent to the basal basilar membrane where high-frequency sound detection occurs. Stria vascularis (Option B): Located along the lateral wall of the cochlear duct, this structure produces endolymph and maintains the ionic composition necessary for hair cell function. It is not in direct proximity to the basal turn of the basilar membrane affected in high-frequency hearing loss. Helicotrema (Option D): Found at the apex of the cochlea, it connects the scala vestibuli and scala tympani. The apical basilar membrane is sensitive to low-frequency sounds, not high frequencies, and is far from the oval window. Key Takeaway In age-related high-frequency hearing loss, the basilar membrane near the oval window is most affected, as this region is specialized for high-frequency sound detection.

qText: All of the following are features of retrocochlear hearing loss, except?
expl: Explanation: Retrocochlear hearing loss shows tone decay, often markedly so, because the affected nerve cannot maintain continuous firing. Recruitment is seen in cochlear lesions. In retrocochlear pathology, recruitment is typically absent (Option A) . Retrocochlear lesions (especially at the level of the VIII nerve) show normal wave I (generated by the cochlea/auditory nerve periphery) but delayed or absent waves II to V (Option B) . The SISI (Short Increment Sensitivity Index) is low in retrocochlear lesions because small intensity increments are poorly perceived. High SISI is a feature of cochlear lesions (Option C) .

qText: Which of the following tests is the initial test for neonatal screening of hearing of a healthy newborn?
expl: Explanation: The standard initial screening test for hearing in a healthy newborn is Evoked Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE), specifically Transient Evoked Otoacoustic Emissions (TEOAE). Principle of OAE: Otoacoustic emissions are sounds generated by the Outer Hair Cells (OHC) of the cochlea in response to an acoustic stimulus. These "echoes" are recorded by a probe placed in the ear canal. If echoes are recorded (PASS), it indicates the cochlear mechanism is functioning normally. It is objective, non-invasive, rapid, and cost-effective, making it ideal for mass screening of healthy infants. Universal Newborn Hearing Screening Protocol: Healthy Newborns (Well-Baby Nursery): OAE is the first-line screening tool. High-Risk Newborns (NICU, Meningitis, Severe Jaundice, Family History): Automated Auditory Brainstem Response ( AABR/BERA ) is the screening test of choice. This is because high-risk infants have a higher incidence of auditory neuropathy (neural conduction defects) where the cochlea may function normally (OAE Pass), but the nerve does not (Hearing Loss). Types of OAE: Spontaneous OAE (SOAE): Occurs without stimulus. Evoked OAE: Occurs in response to sound. Transient Evoked OAE (TEOAE): Elicited by a click (1 stimulus). This is the type most commonly used for screening. Distortion Product OAE (DPOAE): Elicited by two simultaneous pure tones. Explanation of Other Options: Automated auditory brainstem response (Option A): While highly accurate and testing the entire auditory pathway up to the brainstem, it is more time-consuming and expensive than OAE. It is reserved for high-risk infants (NICU) or as a confirmatory test for babies who fail the OAE screen. Spontaneous Oto acoustic emissions (Option B): These occur without external sound stimulation but are present in only about 50-70% of people with normal hearing. Therefore, the absence of SOAE does not imply hearing loss, making it useless for screening. Pure tone audiometry (Option D): This is a subjective test requiring the patient to respond to sound (raise a hand or press a button). It cannot be performed on newborns. Key Takeaway: Healthy Newborn Screening: Evoked OAE (TEOAE). High-Risk/NICU Screening: BERA/AABR. OAE tests Outer Hair Cell function.

qText: Which of the following statements correctly describes BERA?
expl: Explanation: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) measures the electrical activity of the auditory pathways in response to clicks or tone bursts. It is non-invasive , using surface electrodes on the scalp, and does not require surgery or insertion of instruments. (Option B ruled out). Key Features Objective test: Does not rely on patient feedback. (Option D ruled out) Evaluates auditory pathway up to the brainstem. Shows 7 waves (I-VII); Wave V , generated by the lateral lemniscus, is the most important. Uses Assessment of sensorineural hearing loss , especially in infants, young children, or uncooperative patients. Differentiating cochlear vs retrocochlear hearing loss . Evaluation of malingerers (for medico-legal cases). Considered the gold standard investigation for hearing loss. (Option A ruled out) Limitations Frequency non-specific. Does not assess the auditory cortex.

qText: Cause of decreased bone conduction on audiogram?
expl: Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) results from lesions of the cochlea, VIIIthnerve or central auditory pathways. It may be present at birth (congenital) or start later in life (acquired). The characteristics of sensorineural hearing loss are: A positive Rinne test, i.e. AC > BC. Weber lateralized to better ear. Bone conduction reduced on Schwabach and absolute bone conduction tests. More often involving high frequencies. No gap between air and bone conduction curve on audiometry Loss may exceed 60 dB. Speech discrimination is poor. There is difficulty in hearing in the presence of noise. Other options: Other three options A, C and D give conductive hearing loss on audiogram.

qText: An industrial worker presents with hearing loss. On examination, Rinne's test was negative on the left side and positive on the right side. Weber's test lateralized to the left side. Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) was done with the results as shown below. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The diagnosis is a left conductive hearing loss , which is consistently supported by all the provided findings. Rinne's Test: A negative result on the left (Bone Conduction > Air Conduction) is the classic sign of a conductive hearing loss in that ear. The positive result on the right is normal. Weber's Test: The sound lateralizing to the left ear indicates a conductive hearing loss on that same side. Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA): Right Ear: The audiogram shows hearing thresholds within the normal range (0-20 dB). Left Ear: The audiogram shows normal bone conduction thresholds (upper line, squares) but significantly elevated air conduction thresholds (lower line, crosses). I.e., AC is poor, BC is normal. The difference between these two lines is the air-bone gap , which is the hallmark of a conductive hearing loss. In SNHL, both AC & BC are poor Explanation of Other Options: Right conductive hearing loss (Option A): Incorrect, since Rinne's test was positive on the right and no air-bone gap on the right PTA. Right sensorineural hearing loss (Option C): Incorrect, would cause Weber lateralization to the left , but Rinne would also be positive on the left, not negative. Left sensorineural hearing loss (Option D): A left SNHL would present with a positive Rinne's test (as both AC and BC would be reduced), Weber's lateralizing to the right (better) ear, and an audiogram showing both air and bone conduction thresholds depressed together, with no significant air-bone gap. Key Takeaway:

qText: Most common hearing test done in neonates for screening:
expl: Explanation: Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) is the primary, first-line screening test for neonatal hearing. It is quick, non-invasive, objective , and does not require a behavioral response from the baby. It tests the integrity of the outer hair cells of the cochlea. Pathway: Normal functioning outer hair cells → generate sound vibrations → detected in external ear canal. Absence of OAE suggests outer hair cell damage, as seen in cochlear or middle ear pathologies. Types: Spontaneous OAE: Occur without external stimulation. May be absent in up to 50% of normal individuals. Evoked OAE: Require an external auditory stimulus. Transient Evoked OAE (TEOAE): Elicited by click sounds containing multiple frequencies. Distortion Product OAE (DPOAE): Produced when two pure tones of different frequencies are presented simultaneously, generating distortion products. Clinical Applications: Newborn hearing screening. Assessment in uncooperative or cognitively impaired patients. Differentiates cochlear from retrocochlear hearing loss. Early detection of noise-induced hearing loss . Explanation of other options: Clap & smile (Option A): A subjective behavioral observation, not a reliable screening test. BERA/ABR (Option B): Used as a diagnostic test or for screening in high-risk neonates (e.g., NICU graduates). It is more complex and time-consuming than OAE. PTA (Option D): Requires a conscious behavioral response, which is impossible for a neonate. Key Takeaways: Neonatal Screening: OAE (first line) → BERA/ABR (for confirmation/follow-up).

qText: Which of the following is not an acoustic finding in auditory neuropathy?
expl: Otoacoustic Emissions are useful to diagnose retrocochlear pathology, especially auditory neuropathy. Auditory neuropathy is a neurologic disorder of CN VIII. Audiometric tests, e.g. SNHL for pure tones, impaired speech discrimination score, absent or abnormal auditory brainstem response, show a retrocochlear type of lesion but OAEs are normal. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose & Head and Neck surgery by P L Dhingra, 9 th edition, Pg.no.32

qText: If OAE is absent in a patient, which other screening test can be done? A. BERA B. Tympanometry C. Audiometry D. Speech Audiometry
expl: OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions) is a test that measures sound emissions produced by the cochlea in response to acoustic stimuli. If OAE is absent, it may indicate a problem in the cochlea's function. To further assess the patient's hearing, the following tests can be done: B. Tympanometry: Tympanometry is a test that measures the compliance of the middle ear and the mobility of the eardrum (tympanic membrane). It helps detect conditions such as middle ear effusion (fluid), tympanic membrane perforation, or other disorders affecting the middle ear. D. Speech Audiometry: Speech audiometry evaluates the patient's ability to hear and understand speech at different volumes. It is used to determine the patient's hearing threshold for speech and assess their ability to discriminate speech sounds. A. BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry): It is suitable for assessing cochlear function or detecting OAE since it measures auditory brainstem responses, mainly focusing on the function of the auditory nerve and brainstem pathways. C. Audiometry: It is not a suitable alternative for OAE because audiometry assesses hearing sensitivity at different frequencies but does not directly measure the cochlear emissions detected by OAE.

qText: A 64-year-old female presents with difficulty in comprehension. On examination: fluency intact, poor comprehension, poor repetition. Pure tone audiometry and ABR are normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by fluent speech but impaired comprehension and repetition . Speech may have normal rate and grammar but lacks meaningful content . Most common cause: Ischemic stroke affecting the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere. Normal audiometry and ABR indicate that the auditory apparatus and brainstem pathways are intact; the deficit is cortical (processing and comprehension). Explanation of Other Options: Malingering (Option A): Deliberate feigning or exaggeration of deficits; not supported by clinical pattern. Auditory cortex lesion (Option B): Lesions may cause deficits in sound perception but typically involve ABR changes and additional auditory deficits. Broca's aphasia (Option C): Non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension , impaired speech production, and grammatical errors; does not match this patient's presentation.

qText: All of the following are smell perception tests except?
expl: The Arnold stick test is a test for olfaction that involves the use of a cotton swab dipped in a chemical called amyl acetate. The swab is then waved in front of the patient's nose, and the patient is asked to identify the smell. This test is not a reliable measure of smell perception because the smell of amyl acetate is very strong and can be easily detected even by people with impaired smell. All of the options except Arnold stick test are used to measure smell perception. Arnold stick test is not a reliable measure of smell perception because the smell of amyl acetate is very strong and can be easily detected even by people with impaired smell. A. Smell diskettes Smell diskettes are small, disposable disks that contain a variety of different odors. The patient is asked to smell the diskettes and identify the odors. This test is a measure of the patient's ability to smell. B. UP-SIT UP-SIT stands for Upper Airway Resistance Sensitivity Index Test. This test is used to assess the resistance of the upper airway to airflow. The test is performed by measuring the pressure drop across the upper airway when the patient breathes in and out. C. CC-SIT CC-SIT stands for Conductance Change Sensitivity Index Test. This test is also used to assess the resistance of the upper airway to airflow. The test is performed by measuring the change in conductance of the upper airway when the patient breathes in and out.

qText: Which of the following tests cannot be used to assess nasal mucociliary clearance?
expl: Nasal mucociliary clearance refers to the process by which mucus and debris are cleared from the nasal passages through the action of cilia on the nasal epithelium. Several tests can be used to assess nasal mucociliary clearance, but electron microscopy is not one of them. These are valid methods to assess nasal mucociliary clearance: A. Saccharine Test: This is a simple test in which a small amount of saccharine is placed in the nostril, and the time it takes for the patient to perceive a sweet taste in the mouth is measured. The movement of saccharine through the nasal passages indicates mucociliary clearance. C. Charcoal powder method: In this test, charcoal particles are insufflated into the nasal cavity, and the time it takes for the patient to expectorate the particles is measured. The clearance of charcoal particles indicates mucociliary clearance. D. Scintigraphy: Radioactive particles are used in this test to assess the movement of mucus through the nasal passages and the clearance of radioactive particles indicates mucociliary clearance. Electron microscopy is not a method used for assessing nasal mucociliary clearance. Instead, it is a microscopic technique used to study the ultrastructure of cilia and mucociliary function in certain research settings.

qText: A patient with a history of trauma presents with hearing loss. A High-Resolution Computed Tomography scan was performed. Which of the following structures is not typically visualized on HRCT?
expl: Explanation: HRCT of temporal bone is a specialized imaging technique used to obtain detailed images of the bones and air-filled spaces within the ear . They are useful to evaluate finer structures like ossicles, the bony labyrinth and the internal auditory canal. Vestibule, semicircular canal and cochlea are parts of the bony labyrinth of the internal ear, and can be visualised in an HRCT. The organ of Corti is a neurosensory epithelium responsible for hearing present on the basilar membrane in scala media of the membranous labyrinth and it is difficult to identify on an HRCT. It is better visualised in an MRI.

qText: The framework of the external nose:
expl: Explanation: The external nose is formed by both bone and cartilage. The upper one-third of the structure is bony, while the lower two-thirds are cartilaginous. External nose anatomy: Shaped like a pyramid, with its root directed upward and the base downward. The framework is osteocartilaginous and covered by skin and small muscles. Bony part → nasal bones, frontal bone, and the ascending process of the maxilla. Cartilaginous part → includes upper lateral cartilage, lower lateral (alar) cartilages, sesamoid cartilages, and septal cartilage. Upper lateral cartilages: extend downward from the nasal bones and join the septal cartilage; their lower edge forms the nasal valve (limen nasi). Lower lateral (alar) cartilages: U-shaped with a lateral crus forming the ala and a medial crus forming the columella; they overlap the lower border of the upper lateral cartilages. Lesser alar (sesamoid) cartilages: small accessory cartilages situated above the alar cartilage. Septal cartilage (quadrangular cartilage): supports the cartilaginous dorsum; damage or resection may cause a supratip depression. Explanation of other options: Option B & C: Misrepresent the relative proportions of bony and cartilaginous parts. Option D: Incorrect since the framework is well-defined as 1/3 bony and 2/3 cartilaginous.

qText: A 5-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with bleeding from the nose. Examination reveals trauma to Little's area. Which of the following arteries does not contribute to the vascular plexus in this region?
expl: Explanation: Little's area, or Kiesselbach's plexus, is formed by an anastomosis of several arteries supplying the anterior nasal septum. The posterior ethmoidal artery does not take part in this plexus. Kiesselbach's Plexus Arterial Contributions: Anterior ethmoidal artery (septal branch) Sphenopalatine artery (septal branch) (Option A) Greater palatine artery (septal branch) (Option B) Superior labial artery (branch of facial artery) (Option C) These vessels form a dense vascular network, making Little's area the most common site of anterior epistaxis in children. Posterior Ethmoidal Artery: Supplies the superior and posterior part of the nasal cavity. Does not participate in the anterior septal arterial plexus.

qText: A 75-year-old male who is a known case of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with epistaxis, which does not respond to conservative measures and nasal packing. Which of the following arteries should be prioritised for ligation?
expl: Explanation: The sphenopalatine artery is the main blood supply to the posterior nasal cavity . Posterior epistaxis (especially in elderly hypertensive patients) commonly involves this artery. It is often called the "artery of epistaxis." When packing fails, endoscopic ligation or embolisation of the sphenopalatine artery is the preferred next step. The following arteries are ligated for control of epistaxis. Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation (TESPAL) is done first. If uncontrolled, ligation of the maxillary artery is done. Then, ligation of the external carotid artery above the origin of the superior thyroid artery should be done. If still uncontrolled, ligation of the ethmoidal arteries is done. Explanation of other options: Posterior ethmoidal artery (Option A): supplies the Roof of the nasal cavity, ethmoid sinuses, and has a rare role in epistaxis Anterior ethmoidal artery(Option B): more involved in anterior/superior epistaxis . Greater palatine artery (Option D): supplies the inferior nasal septum and palate and has a Minor, accessory role in epistaxis

qText: Which X-ray view is most appropriate for clearly visualizing the frontal sinuses?
expl: Explanation: The Caldwell view , also known as the occipitofrontal view, is specifically utilized to obtain a clear image of the frontal sinuses. This projection angles the X-ray beam in such a way that the frontal sinuses are visualized without overlapping shadows from other facial bones. This makes the Caldwell view ideal for evaluating the frontal sinuses and detecting any pathology in this region. Explanation of other options: Towne view (Option D): This projection primarily visualizes the occipital bone and the posterior cranial fossa. It is not utilized for assessing the paranasal sinuses.

qText: A child is suffering from goitre and sensorineural hearing loss. He is diagnosed to be the case of Pendred syndrome. This syndrome occurs due to defect in which of the following transporter?
expl: Pendred syndrome is caused by a defect in the iodide-chloride antiporter , also known as Pendrin . Occurs due to mutation in SLC26A4 gene mutation on chromosome 7. This defect leads to: Goitre : due to impaired iodide transport into the thyroid gland, resulting in insufficient iodide for thyroid hormone synthesis. Sensorineural hearing loss : associated with defects in the inner ear due to the malfunction of Pendrin, which is involved in ion transport in the cochlea. Triad of pendred syndrome: congenital sensorineural hearing loss,goitre,impaired ioidide organification. Why Not Others A (Sodium Iodide Symporter): This transporter is essential for iodide uptake in the thyroid but is not the defect in Pendred syndrome. C (Sodium potassium pump): This pump maintains membrane potential and is not directly related to iodide transport or Pendred syndrome. D (Sodium chloride hydride cotransporter): This transporter is not involved in Pendred syndrome. Key Takeaways Correct answer: Option B, the iodide-chloride antiporter (Pendrin) is defective in Pendred syndrome, causing goitre and sensorineural hearing loss. The syndrome highlights the critical role of Pendrin in both thyroid function and auditory health. qText: Name the anterior most ethmoidal cell marked in the figure
expl: The anterior most ethmoidal cell is the Agger nasi cell. It is a small air cell located in the anterior part of the ethmoidal labyrinth, close to the frontal sinus and the nasofrontal beak. It is an important landmark in functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) and plays a role in creating access to the frontal recess . A. Concha bullosa: It refers to the pneumatization or presence of an air-filled cavity within one of the nasal turbinates (conchae). Concha bullosa can be found in the middle or inferior turbinates and is a common anatomical variation. B. Bulla ethmoidalis: Bulla ethmoidalis refers to a rounded, bubble-like prominence or a pneumatized cavity in the middle meatus region of the nasal cavity. It is formed due to the pneumatization of ethmoid air cells. D. Onodi cells: Onodi cells are the part of posterior ethmoid air cells. They line in close proximity to the sphenoid sinus, carotid artery and optic nerve.

qText: Which of the following is true about the T-stage of maxillary sinus carcinoma?
expl: T2 - Tumour causing bone erosion or destruction including extension into the hard palate and/or middle nasal meatus, except extension to posterior wall of maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates. T3 - Tumour invades any of the following: bone of the posterior wall of maxillary sinus , subcutaneous tissues, floor or medial wall of orbit, pterygoid fossa and ethmoid sinuses . T4a - Tumour invades anterior orbital contents, skin of cheek, pterygoid plates, infratemporal fossa, cribriform plate, sphenoid or frontal sinuses . T4b - Tumour invades any of the following: orbital apex, dura, brain, middle cranial fossa , cranial nerves other than maxillary division of trigeminal nerve (V2) , nasopharynx or clivus Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra , 8 th Edition, pg. no – 243

qText: Which structure does the anterior ethmoidal sinus drain into?
expl: Explanation: The anterior ethmoidal sinus drains into the middle meatus. Lateral nasal wall The lateral wall of the nose has three scroll-like bony projections covered by mucous membrane called the inferior, middle, and superior conchae. They extend medially across the nasal cavity, separating it into four air channels: the inferior, middle, and superior meatus and a sphenoethmoidal recess. The nasolacrimal duct and most of the paranasal sinuses open onto the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. The frontal sinus opens into the middle meatus infront of the hiatus semilunaris. The maxillary sinus also opens into the middle meatus, posteriorly within the hiatus semilunaris. The ethmoid sinuses are divided into anterior, middle, and posterior groups, each opening into a different meatus. Anterior ethmoid air sinuses open into the middle meatus within the hiatus semilunaris. Middle ethmoid air sinuses also open into the middle meatus on the ethmoid bulla, a rounded elevation. Posterior ethmoid air sinuses open into the superior meatus. The sphenoid sinus opens above the superior turbinate into the sphenoethmoidal recess. The nasolacrimal duct, carrying tears from the eye, opens into the inferior meatus. Its opening is guarded by a valve called Hasner's valve. The opening of the Eustachian tube (pharyngotympanic tube), connecting the nasopharynx to the middle ear cavity, is located in the nasopharynx just behind the inferior turbinate at the level of the inferior meatus.

qText: Which of the following is not true about physiology of nose
expl: Nasal cycle of rhythmic congestion and decongestion is seen in all normal individuals. The duration of this cycle varies every 2.5 to 4 hours . This occurs because of the autonomic nerve supply of the nose. Nasal mucosa has rich blood supply. Sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction and shrinkage of mucosa, while parasympathetic stimulation causes vasodilation and engorgement. Autonomic system is unstable in cases of vasomotor rhinitis . So the rhythmic congestion and decongestion is disturbed. qText: All of the following investigations are helpful in the diagnostic assessment of a patient of CSF Rhinorrhea except
expl: X ray of paranasal sinuses has no role in the diagnosis of CSF rhinorrhea. Beta-2 transferrin is the best confirmatory test. qText: Occipitomental view with open mouth view to check for nose and paranasal sinus?
expl: The Occipitomental view with an open mouth view is commonly known as the "Pierre view." This imaging technique is used to visualize the nose and paranasal sinuses and is particularly useful in assessing the maxillary sinuses and the nasal bones. Other options: B.Waters view: The Waters view is a radiographic view used to visualize the maxillary sinuses and their relationship to the orbital floor. It does not require the open mouth position. C.Caldwell view: The Caldwell view is an X-ray projection used to evaluate the frontal sinuses and their relationship to the orbits . It is taken with the patient's head tilted backward but does not involve an open mouth view. D.Townes view: The Townes view, also known as the "jug-handle" view, is used for imaging the skull base, including the sella turcica. It is not used to check the nose and paranasal sinuses. It helps to visualize foramen magnum, petrous temporal bone

qText: Identify the structure marked with black arrow on nasal endoscopy
expl: Three and occasionally four turbinates or conchae mark the lateral wall of nose. They are scroll-like bony projections covered by mucous membrane. qText: During a nasal endoscopy, a surgeon observes the opening of the nasolacrimal duct. Into which of the following structures does the nasolacrimal duct drain?
expl: Explanation: The correct answer is the Inferior meatus . The lateral wall of the nasal cavity contains three shelf-like projections called turbinates (or conchae): superior, middle, and inferior. The space beneath each turbinate is called a meatus. These meatuses are clinically important as they are the drainage sites for the paranasal sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct. The nasolacrimal duct , which drains tears from the eye into the nose, opens into the inferior meatus . Drainage into Nasal Meatuses: Explanation of Other Options: Superior meatus (Option A): This is the drainage site for the posterior ethmoidal air cells. Middle meatus (Option B): This is the common and complex drainage pathway for the frontal, maxillary, and anterior/middle ethmoidal sinuses. Sphenoethmoidal recess (Option D): This small area, located above the superior turbinate, is the drainage site for the sphenoid sinus.

qText: A 60-year-old post-COVID male patient came with complaints of one-sided facial swelling, headache, and nasal sinus congestion. He is diabetic and it is uncontrolled. On examination black lesions on the nasal bridge and upper inside of the mouth were observed. Which investigation would you do to confirm the diagnosis of this patient?
expl: Explanation: The patient's presentation- unilateral facial swelling, sinus congestion, black eschar in the nasal and oral cavity, and uncontrolled diabetes post-COVID -is highly suggestive of mucormycosis . The gold standard for confirming mucormycosis is biopsy with histopathologic examination , which demonstrates broad, aseptate fungal hyphae with tissue invasion. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount and fungal culture may also support the diagnosis, but tissue biopsy is definitive. Mucormycosis: Aggressive fungal infection affecting the nose and paranasal sinuses, which rapidly spreads to orbit, brain, and meninges. The fungus invades arteries, leading to thrombosis, necrosis, and tissue destruction. Clinical features: Black necrotic debris in nasal cavity, involvement of septum, turbinates, or palate; "black turbinate sign" on contrast-enhanced MRI. Risk factors: Uncontrolled diabetes (especially ketoacidosis) Prolonged corticosteroid therapy (common in post-COVID patients) Immunosuppression (chemotherapy, neutropenia, HIV, organ transplantation, chronic kidney disease) Diagnosis: Endoscopy: Initially pale mucosa, later black crusting and necrosis. Biopsy: Gold standard; shows angioinvasive broad aseptate hyphae. Imaging: CT : Detects sinus involvement and bony destruction. CECT : Better defines sinus opacification, mucosal thickening, and extent of bone erosion. MRI : Evaluates soft tissue spread, orbital and intracranial extension. Treatment: Antifungals : Amphotericin B (0.6-1 mg/kg/day IV) or Liposomal Amphotericin B (5 mg/kg/day); Posaconazole as step-down oral therapy. Surgery : Endoscopic debridement; in severe cases, maxillectomy or orbital exenteration. Explanation of Incorrect Options: X-ray (Option A): Conventional X-rays are inadequate for diagnosing mucormycosis. They fail to detect early fungal invasion or soft tissue extension. CT and MRI are superior imaging tools. Serum ferritin (Option C): Elevated ferritin and iron overload predispose patients to mucormycosis, but ferritin testing is not diagnostic. It cannot confirm or exclude the infection. HbA1c (Option D): Reflects long-term blood sugar control. Poor control is a risk factor for mucormycosis, but HbA1c has no role in confirming fungal infection. Key Takeaway: -In a post-COVID diabetic patient with black necrotic nasal or palatal lesions, biopsy with histopathology is the gold standard for diagnosing mucormycosis. Imaging supports staging, but tissue confirmation is mandatory to establish the diagnosis and guide urgent antifungal and surgical management.

qText: Obstruction of which sinus drainage is seen in the image provided?
expl: Explanation: The image appears to show a nasal endoscopy view of inflamed and polypoidal mucosa obstructing the middle meatus , which is the drainage site of the maxillary sinus . The maxillary sinus drains into the middle meatus via the ostiomeatal complex (OMC) , which includes the hiatus semilunaris and infundibulum . Any obstruction in this pathway leads to maxillary sinusitis , commonly seen with nasal polyps. The maxillary sinus: The maxillary sinus or the Antrum of Highmore , is the largest of the paranasal sinuses, occupying the body of the maxilla. Shape - Pyramidal Size - 15mL Base - toward the lateral wall of the nose Apex - extends into the zygomatic process of the maxillary bone Relations: Anterior wall: Formed by the facial surface of the maxilla. Posterior wall: Anterior surface of pterygopalatine fossa. Medial wall: Thin and membranous in some areas, this wall borders the middle and inferior meatuses and separates the maxillary sinus from the nasal cavity. Roof: Formed by the floor of the orbit Floor: Located approximately 1 cm below the floor of the nasal cavity, it is formed by the alveolar and palatine processes of the maxilla. Closely related to the roots of the second premolar and first molar teeth. Cavities in these teeth are associated with oro antral fistula. Arterial supply: Branches of the maxillary artery, specifically the infraorbital artery, greater palatine artery, and the posterior superior alveolar artery. Venous drainage: Pterygoid venous plexus and the facial vein. Lymphatic drainage: Submandibular lymph nodes. Nerve supply: Infraorbital nerve, greater palatine nerve, and the posterior superior alveolar nerve, which are branches of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2). Ethmoid Sinus (Option B): is incorrect because the ethmoid sinuses primarily drain into the middle and superior meatus , and their obstruction is associated with frontal or sphenoethmoidal recess involvement. Sphenoid Sinus (Option C): is incorrect because it drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess , located superiorly, which is not prominently obstructed in this image. Frontal Sinus (Option D): is incorrect because it drains into the middle meatus via the frontal recess , and its obstruction is more commonly associated with frontal headaches and pain above the eyes .

qText: Which fungal infection is frequently observed in the maxillary sinus?
expl: Explanation: Aspergillosis is the most common fungal infection of the paranasal sinuses, with the maxillary sinus being the most frequently involved site. It can present in various forms: fungal ball (non-invasive), chronic invasive, or allergic fungal sinusitis. Explanation of other options: Blastomycosis (Option A): A systemic fungal infection endemic to certain regions (e.g., North America); primarily involves the lungs and skin; sinus involvement is rare. Candidiasis (Option C): Typically causes mucocutaneous infections (oral thrush, vaginitis); isolated sinus involvement is very uncommon. Histoplasmosis (Option D): Another systemic fungal infection endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys; primarily involves the lungs; sinus involvement is not characteristic. Key Takeaways: Aspergillus species are the predominant fungi causing sinus infections. The maxillary sinus is the most common location for fungal sinusitis.

qText: Identify the sinus marked in the image.
expl: Explanation: The labelled sinus in the given Xray - Water's view is the maxillary sinus. The maxillary sinus or the Antrum of Highmore , is the largest of the paranasal sinuses, occupying the body of the maxilla. It is pyramid-shaped and lies lateral to the nasal cavity, with its base forming the lateral wall of the nose and its apex extending towards the zygomatic process of maxillary bone. On radiographic or anatomical images, it appears as a large, air-filled cavity inferior to the orbit and lateral to the nasal cavity. Drains into the middle meatus of the nasal cavity through the semilunar hiatus. Commonly involved in sinusitis due to the high location of its drainage opening. Maxillary sinus: Relations Anterior wall: Formed by the facial surface of the maxilla. Posterior wall: Anterior surface of pterygopalatine fossa. Medial wall: Thin and membranous in some areas, this wall borders the middle and inferior meatuses and separates the maxillary sinus from the nasal cavity. Roof: Formed by the floor of the orbit Floor: Located approximately 1 cm below the floor of the nasal cavity, it is formed by the alveolar and palatine processes of the maxilla. Closely related to the roots of the second premolar and first molar teeth. Cavities in these teeth are associated with oro antral fistula. Explanation of other options: Frontal sinus (Option A) : Located above the orbit in the frontal bone; appears superior to the nasal cavity and orbits in images. Pyriform sinus (Option B) : This is a structure in the hypopharynx, not a paranasal sinus. It is unrelated to the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses. Ethmoid sinus (Option C) : Consists of multiple small air cells located between the eyes, medial to the orbit, and posterior to the nasal cavity. These appear as smaller clusters on imaging. qText: Identify the X-ray view shown in the given image.
expl: Explanation: The X-ray shown is the Waters' view, also known as the occipitomental view. Xray Views of Paranasal sinuses: Water's view Water's view is the radiographic projection that provides the best visualization of the maxillary sinus. In this view, the chin touches the X-ray plate. Opening the mouth in Water's view helps visualize the sphenoid sinus from the base of the sphenoid area because the teeth, which are opaque, are moved out of the way. Water's view shows all sinuses except the posterior ethmoid most clearly. Pierre's view Water's view with open mouth is also referred to as Pierre's view. Best view to visualise sphenoid sinus. Caldwell's view Caldwell's view (occipito-frontal view) is the best view for the frontal and ethmoid sinuses. In this view, the forehead touches the X-ray plate. The ethmoid air cells are nicely visible in this view. Lateral View Allows visualization of all sinuses (frontal, maxillary, sphenoid, and ethmoidal). Helps to understand the pneumatization pattern of the sphenoid sinus. Explanation of other options: Towne's view (Option B) : Towne's view is used primarily for imaging the skull, particularly the occipital region, and is not specifically for the maxillary sinus. Law's view (Option C) : Law's view is used to assess the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and not for the maxillary sinus. Stenver's view (Option D) : Stenver's view is used to image the petrous portion of the temporal bone and is not ideal for visualizing the maxillary sinus.

qText: The frontal sinus can be viewed by taking an X-ray at a specific angle, which is depicted in the image below. What is the name of the view depicted?
expl: Explanation: Caldwell's view (Occipitofrontal view) is the standard X-ray projection for visualizing the frontal sinuses . The patient is positioned with the forehead and nose touching the plate, and the X-ray beam is angled 15-20° caudally. This projects the petrous ridges below the orbits, providing an unobstructed view of the frontal and ethmoid sinuses. Explanation of other options: Towne's view (Option B): An anteroposterior view with ~30° caudal tilt used to visualize the occipital bone, petrous pyramids, and foramen magnum, not the frontal sinuses. Law's view (Option C): A lateral oblique view used to image the mastoid air cells . Stenvers view (Option D): An oblique view used to image the petrous part of the temporal bone and internal auditory canal, typically for evaluating conditions like acoustic neuroma. Key Takeaways: Caldwell's view is the primary X-ray projection for assessing the frontal sinuses. Different radiographic views are optimized for visualizing specific skull structures.

qText: Which site is most commonly obstructed by a nasal polyp arising from the maxillary sinus?
expl: Explanation: The most common location for an obstruction caused by a nasal polyp originating from the maxillary sinus is the middle meatus . Nasal polyps are benign, non-cancerous growths that develop in the nasal passages or paranasal sinuses due to chronic inflammation , often associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, or allergies . When arising from the maxillary sinus , these polyps typically expand into the middle meatus , which is the drainage pathway of the maxillary sinus . Obstruction at this site can lead to blocked sinus drainage, recurrent sinus infections, nasal congestion, and difficulty breathing.

qText: The marked structure opens into which of the following spaces ?
expl: The marked structure in the image points to the sphenoid sinus. The sphenoethmoidal recess is a small, anatomical space located in the upper part of the nasal cavity where the sphenoid sinus and the ethmoid sinus meet. It is an important region in the nasal cavity and plays a role in the drainage and ventilation of these paranasal sinuses. Option B. Superior Meatus: The superior meatus is a space in the nasal cavity located below the superior nasal concha. The sphenoid sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess, which is adjacent to the superior meatus. Option C. Middle Meatus: The middle meatus is another space in the nasal cavity located below the middle nasal concha. It is a critical area for the drainage of several paranasal sinuses, including the anterior ethmoidal sinus, frontal sinus, and maxillary sinus. The sphenoid sinus does not open directly into the middle meatus. Option D. Inferior Meatus: The inferior meatus is a space in the nasal cavity located below the inferior nasal concha. It serves as the opening for the nasolacrimal duct, which drains tears from the eyes to the nasal cavity. The sphenoid sinus does not open directly into the inferior meatus.

qText: What is the area marked in the CT shown below?
expl: Explanation: The marked structure in the image is osteomeatal complex which is a final common pathway for drainage of anterior sinus. The OMC is not a single structure but rather a collection of several key anatomical landmarks working together. These include: Uncinate process: A sickle-shaped bone that forms the anterior and inferior border of the hiatus semilunaris. Ethmoid bulla Hiatus semilunaris : lies between the free edge of the uncinate process and the ethmoid bulla; connects the middle meatus into the infundibulum laterally Ethmoidal infundibulum : A channel that lies between the uncinate process and the lamina papyracea Maxillary ostium: The opening of the maxillary sinus into the ethmoidal infundibulum. Middle Turbinate Maxillary Sinus Ostium Explanation of Other Options: Columella (Option B) It is an external, visible anatomical structure of the nose, the narrow strip of skin and cartilage that separates the two nostrils and forms the inferior part of the nasal septum. The uncinate process is a part of the OMC but not the entire complex. It is a thin, curved bony structure that helps form the anterior boundary of the hiatus semilunaris. Maxillary sinus (Option C) The maxillary sinus is a large air-filled space adjacent to the OMC but not the area marked if the arrow is on the narrow drainage pathway. Nasal valve (Option D) The nasal valve is the narrowest part of the nasal airway, located in the anterior nasal cavity. It is unrelated to the osteomeatal complex or sinus drainage. Key Takeaway: The osteomeatal complex is a vital anatomical drainage unit for multiple paranasal sinuses and is a common site of pathology in sinus infections.

qText: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of vertigo that last for several hours, along with tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in her right ear. Over the last few months, she has also noticed a progressive decline in hearing in the same ear. Physical examination reveals sensorineural hearing loss on the right side. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathology?
expl: Meniere's disease is characterized by a triad of recurrent vertigo, tinnitus , and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss . Episodes of vertigo in Meniere's disease last for several hours and are often accompanied by a sensation of fullness in the ear . Hearing loss is typically unilateral and progresses over time, as described in this patient. Why not others: A) Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV): Causes brief vertigo triggered by head movement, usually lasting seconds to minutes . It does not involve tinnitus, ear fullness , or sensorineural hearing loss . B) Acoustic neuroma: Causes gradual hearing loss , tinnitus, and imbalance, but vertigo is less frequent and milder. Recurrent vertigo episodes and ear fullness are more indicative of Meniere's disease . D) Labyrinthitis: Causes continuous symptoms following an infection, including hearing loss and vertigo , but is usually associated with fever and more profound hearing loss rather than recurrent episodes . Key Takeaways: Meniere's disease presents with recurrent vertigo, tinnitus , and sensorineural hearing loss , typically with a feeling of fullness in the affected ear . Other options (BPPV, acoustic neuroma, labyrinthitis) do not fit the pattern of recurrent episodes or the combination of symptoms seen in Meniere's disease. qText: A 40-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of vertigo, nausea, and vomiting that began after a recent upper respiratory infection. She describes feeling unsteady and reports that her symptoms worsen with head movement. On examination, she has horizontal nystagmus but no hearing loss or tinnitus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Vestibular neuritis typically occurs after a viral infection , leading to sudden onset of symptoms such as severe vertigo, nausea , and vomiting . The mechanism involves inflammation of the vestibular nerve, disrupting the balance signals sent to the brain. Patients often report feeling unsteady and experience horizontal nystagmus on examination, a key sign indicating vestibular dysfunction. Key differentiators: There is an absence of hearing loss or tinnitus , which distinguishes it from conditions like labyrinthitis (which presents with both vestibular and auditory symptoms) and Meniere's disease (which includes fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus). Symptoms typically worsen with head movements , reflecting the vestibular system's role in maintaining balance. Why not others: A) Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV): BPPV involves brief episodes of vertigo triggered by specific head positions (like rolling over in bed). The sustained nature of this patient's symptoms and lack of positional triggers make BPPV less likely. B) Meniere's Disease: This condition is characterized by episodes of vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus , and a sensation of fullness in the ear. The absence of these auditory symptoms in this case strongly argues against Meniere's disease. C) Labyrinthitis: Labyrinthitis presents with inflammation of the inner ear structures , typically following an infection, causing both vertigo and hearing loss . The lack of auditory symptoms, particularly hearing loss or tinnitus, suggests that labyrinthitis is not the correct diagnosis. Key Takeaways: The presence of sudden vertigo, nausea , and horizontal nystagmus following a viral illness strongly supports a diagnosis of vestibular neuritis . Other conditions either involve auditory symptoms or have specific positional triggers, reinforcing that vestibular neuritis is the most fitting diagnosis. Tags: Neet 2020 Tag: Special senses Level: May know Reference: Guyton & Hall, Chapter 52, pg. 671; Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26th edition, Page 515

qText: A 55-year-old woman presents to the clinic with complaints of dizziness and balance issues. She describes feeling as though she is spinning when she is stationary. Neurological examination reveals nystagmus and difficulty maintaining her balance while standing. An MRI shows no significant findings, but she is suspected to have vestibular dysfunction. Vestibular system is involved in
expl: Integration of balance and posture information: Role: The vestibular nuclei are essential for integrating sensory information related to balance and posture from the inner ear and other sensory modalities. The signals are integrated by the brain to help control eye movements, stabilize vision, and adjust the body's posture to maintain equilibrium. Function: This integration helps maintain stability and equilibrium, particularly during movement. Its dysfunction will lead to above mentioned Symptoms in the question . Why not the other options? A) Coordination of voluntary motor movements: Explanation: While the vestibular system interacts with motor pathways, the primary control of voluntary movements is handled by the cerebellum and basal ganglia . B) Processing visual information for spatial orientation: Explanation: The vestibular nuclei assist with spatial orientation but do not primarily process visual information; that function is managed by visual centres in the brain. D) Regulation of emotional responses to stimuli: Explanation: Emotional responses are primarily controlled by regions such as the limbic system , not by the vestibular nuclei, which are focused on balance and spatial orientation. Key Takeaways: The vestibular system is critical for the integration of balance and posture information, enabling stability during movement. Understanding vestibular dysfunction can help differentiate it from other neurological issues affecting balance and coordination. Tags: neet 2023 Reference: Kandel, E. R., Schwartz, J. H., & Jessell, T. M., "Principles of Neural Science", Edition: 5 th , Page no 890; Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26 th edition, pg no. 513-515

qText: A patient presents to her GP with recurrent nosebleeds and also complains of facial fullness and facial pain. Over the past 2 months she has developed progressive shortness of breath and on one occasion she coughed up some blood. What would be the most appropriate test to perform?
expl: The mostly likely diagnosis in this case is Wegeners granulamotosis. Sinusitis is the commonest ENT manifestation of this auto immune disorder. Septal perforation (bony and cartilaginous), saddle nose deformity with epistaxis is commonly seen. The multi-system involvement leads to pulmonary symptoms. The biopsy from the nose reveals necrotising vasculitis in this case. ANCA(Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) testing is further helpful for the diagnosis. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8th edition - Volume 1 - Page - 133

qText: 49 year old resident of coastal parts of southern state of India has presented with recurrent epistaxis. He is a catlle bredder and uses ponds for bathing cows. The anterior rhinoscopy picture is given in the image. Which of the following is not an applicable statement in this condition?
expl: This is a case of Rhinosporidiosis. Caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi – aquatic protozoan Most cases from South India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan. The disease is transmitted through contaminated water of ponds CLINICAL FEATURES - Mostly affects nose and nasopharynx Other sites such as lip, palate, conjunctiva, epiglottis, larynx, trachea, bronchi, skin, vulva and vagina may also be affected. Mulberry like polypoidal mass in the nose The mass is very vascular and bleeds easily on touch. Its surface is studded with white dots representing the sporangia. DIAGNOSIS: Biopsy TREATMENT: Complete excision of the mass with a cutting diathermy and cauterization of its base. Medical management: Dapsone is a useful drug to prevent recurrence Option C - Russell bodies and Mikulicz cells are classical histopathological features of Rhinoscleroma. qText: In a patient of resistant epistaxis from left nasal cavity, the bleeding could not be controlled even after the ligation of external carotid artery. What is the possible source of bleeding in this patient?
expl: Think about the blood supply of nose. 80 % is from external carotid artery (ECA). 20 % is from Internal carotid artery (ICA) via the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries . Since ECA has been tied, only remaining circulation is from ethmoidal arteries. They are exposed in the medial wall of the orbit by an external ethmoid (Lynch) incision. Sphenopalatine artery (branch of ECA) is the most common source of epistaxis in hypertensive patients. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 205, 206, 210

qText: Septodermoplasty is a surgery done for the management of recurrent epistaxis in which of the following conditions?
expl: Rendu Osler Weber disease (Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia) Autosomal Dominant . Affects blood vessels in skin, mucous membranes and viscera – presents as telangiectasia, a-v malformations and aneurysms. Presents with recurrent epistaxis due to friable blood vessels in mucosa. qText: Which of the following is not ligated in case of epistaxis control?
expl: Internal carotid artery is a very important source of blood supply to the brain. It is never ligated for control of epistaxis due to the risk of serious cerebral complications and mortality. The following arteries are ligated for control of epistaxis. Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation (TESPAL) is done first. If uncontrolled, ligation of maxillary artery is done. qText: A 62 year old man comes to emergency at 4.00 am with severe epistaxis and high blood pressure (180/110mm Hg). Management of hypertension is started. But the epistaxis could not be controlled on anterior nasal packing and posterior nasal packing. What is the next best management of this patient?
expl: Next Best Management for Severe Epistaxis with High Blood Pressure: B) Endoscopic ligation of Sphenopalatine artery: In the given situation, the patient has severe epistaxis and high blood pressure. If anterior and posterior nasal packing are ineffective, the next step is targeted intervention. Sphenopalatine artery ligation is a minimally invasive procedure. This procedure is performed by an ENT specialist. Sphenopalatine artery supplies the nasal mucosa. Endoscopic ligation involves accessing and tying off the artery to stop bleeding at the source. It's an effective approach for controlling hypertensive epistaxis. Preferred method: TESPAL (Transnasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine Artery Ligation) . Sphenopalatine artery is ligated near the sphenopalatine foramen, close to the posterior end of the middle turbinate. Especially useful for posterior epistaxis . Other Options: A) Ligation of External carotid artery: More invasive and considered after less invasive methods fail. Sequential ligation: Sphenopalatine artery -> Maxillary artery -> External carotid artery -> Ethmoidal artery. C) Foley's catheter placement: Alternative to posterior nasal pack, less effective. D) Electrocauterisation of Little's area: Early measure for anterior epistaxis, less effective for hypertensive epistaxis (usually posterior bleeding). Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no – 208-210

qText: A 35 year old male presents with epistaxis conservative management was done to stop the bleeding but it failed which will be the next step of management
expl: Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (ESPAL) is an effective intervention for severe or refractory epistaxis when conservative management fails. It involves the ligation of the sphenopalatine artery, which is the main source of blood supply to the anterior nasal septum. Other options: B. Maxillary artery: While the maxillary artery is the source of blood supply to the sphenopalatine artery, ligating the maxillary artery is an extensive and invasive procedure not typically performed for epistaxis. C. ICA (Internal Carotid Artery): The internal carotid artery is a major blood vessel supplying the brain. D. ECA (External Carotid Artery): This artery supplies blood to the face and scalp. It is not as likely to be the source of epistaxis.

(Option B) Key Takeaway: Juvenile Angiofibroma - Biopsy C/I & Pre Operative Embolization done: Due to Highly Vascular Tumor. Surgical Excision Mainstay Radiotherapy for Intracranial extension only Post Surgery.

qText: A 22-year-old male presents with recurrent epistaxis. CECT imaging showed findings as shown. Which of the following statements is true regarding the likley cause of epistaxis?
expl: Explanation: The CECT image demonstrates anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, known as the Holman-Miller sign. This finding is characteristic of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma and is supported by the clinical features of young age and recurrent epistaxis. Recurrent bleeding occurs because its highly vascular and the blood vessels in the tumour lack a muscular layer and therefore cannot contract effectively to reduce bleeding after injury. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma Most common benign tumours of nasopharynx predominantly seen in adolescent males. Tumour is seen almost exclusively in males in the age group of 10-20 years. JNA typically originates in the pterygopalatine fossa, a space behind the maxilla, and can extend into the infratemporal fossa and towards the cheek. A highly vascular tumour, with the dominant blood supply to the tumour usually being internal maxillary artery. Clinical features Profuse, recurrent and spontaneous epistaxis. The most common presentation. Progressive nasal obstruction and denasal speech (rhinolalia clausa) Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion due to obstruction of eustachian tube. Mass in the nasopharynx. Tumour is sessile, lobulated or smooth and obstructs one or both choanae. It is pink or purplish in colour with firm consistency is firm but digital palpation should never be done until at the time of operation. Extension of the tumour into the orbit can lead to proptosis (protrusion of the eye), resulting in a frog face deformity. Diagnosis CECT Invetsigation of choice Antral sign or Holman-Miller sign: Pathogonomic sign of angiofibroma. Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of maxillary sinus,. Carotid angiography Shows the extent of tumours, its vascularity and feeding vessels which mostly come from the external carotid system. Biopsy of the tumor is contraindicated due to its high vascularity and risk of severe bleeding. Treatment Surgical excision is the treatmnet of choice. Pre-operative embolization of the internal maxillary artery by an interventional radiologist is often performed to reduce blood loss during surgery. Radiotherapy is generally reserved for cases with intracranial extension or residual/recurrent disease that is not amenable to further surgery.

qText: Sunil, 7 year old child has presented at midnight to emergency with the history of putting a disc battery of his father's wrist watch in his nose few hours back. What would be the ideal management?
expl: Disc batteries contain alkali - sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide and mercury which leaks through them to cause injury. It is observed that a disc battery causes damage to mucosa in 1 hour. Hence disc battery should be urgently removed from the nose. Xylometazoline nasal drops decongest the nose and are used in management of rhinosinusitis. Anterior nasal packing is used in management of epistaxis. Next day removal of foreign body is not suggestive for disc batteries. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no - 409

qText: A 12 year old boy has presenting with recurrent episodes of profuse epistaxis and reddish nasal mass is seen filling nasal cavity. What is investigation best avoided in this patient?
expl: Angiofibroma is a highly vascular tumor and its blood vessels lack elastic tissue and muscle fibres and hence cannot contract. So biopsy of the tumor results in massive hemorrhage and is avoided. CECT is now the investigation of choice for angiofibroma - It shows the extent of tumour, bony destruction or displacements. Antral sign or Holman-Miller sign, is pathognomic of angiofibroma – It is the anterior displacement of posterior wall of maxillary sinus(red arrow). Carotid angiography shows the extent of tumours, its vascularity and feeding vessels which mostly come from the external carotid system. Magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) is complementary to CT scans and shows any soft tissue extensions. qText: A 14-year-old boy presents with a reddish nasal mass, profuse epistaxis & proptosis. What is the possible diagnosis? FMGE DEC 2021
expl: Reddish nasal mass, profuse epistaxis (nosebleeds), and proptosis (forward displacement of the eye) are classic features of a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA). JNA is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumor that primarily affects adolescent males. It arises from the posterolateral wall of the nasopharynx and can cause nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and other symptoms. A.Nasopharyngeal carcinoma - While nasopharyngeal carcinoma can cause nasal symptoms, it is less likely to present with a reddish nasal mass, profuse epistaxis, and proptosis. C.Inverted papilloma -Inverted papilloma is a benign tumor that can cause nasal obstruction and occasional epistaxis but is less likely to present with proptosis. D.Rhinosporidiosis -Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic fungal infection that can cause nasal symptoms but is less likely to present with proptosis.

qText: A 13-year-old boy presents with right-sided nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis for the past 6 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The triad of adolescent male, unilateral nasal obstruction, and recurrent/recurrent epistaxis is highly characteristic of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) . This is a benign but locally aggressive and highly vascular tumor. Explanation of other options: Allergic rhinitis (Option B): Typically causes bilateral nasal symptoms (obstruction, rhinorrhea, sneezing) and itching, not recurrent, profuse epistaxis. Coagulation disorder (Option C): Would likely cause bleeding from multiple sites or generalized bleeding, not isolated, persistent unilateral nasal obstruction. Antrochoanal polyp (Option D): It causes unilateral obstruction and may cause minor bleeding, but recurrent, significant epistaxis is not a hallmark feature.

qText: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of epistaxis, without any history of trauma. On examination, a firm, purplish mass is noted in the left posterior choana. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
expl: Explanation: The described features are consistent with juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) , a benign yet locally invasive vascular tumour that typically affects adolescent males. Recurrent epistaxis along with a firm, purplish mass in the posterior choana are characteristic findings. The preferred management is surgical excision , which enables complete tumour removal while reducing the risk of complications. Staging and Management of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) Staging Systems: JNA is classified based on tumour size, site of involvement, adjacent structure extension, and surgical accessibility. Commonly used systems include: Sessions (1981), Fisch (1983), Chandler (1984), Radkowski (1996), and Janakiram (2017). Preoperative Embolization Carried out with Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) to occlude feeding vessels and minimise intraoperative bleeding. Risks: Stroke, cranial nerve palsies, vision loss. Radiotherapy Indications: Tumours not suitable for surgery due to extent or location Recurrent disease after surgery Intracranial extension involving the internal carotid artery supply Complications: Atrophic rhinitis, facial deformities, and rarely, radiation-induced angiosarcoma. Other Treatment Options Chemotherapy: Reserved for aggressive, recurrent, or residual disease; not curative. Hormonal Therapy: Antiandrogens have been tried but with limited benefit. Recurrence Recurrence occurs in up to 35% of patients . Management includes close observation, repeat surgical intervention, or radiotherapy, depending on accessibility.
