qText: A middle-aged man with a prior history of acne rosacea presents with a deformity in the face as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The image shows an enlarged, red, nodular nose; in a patient with a history of acne rosacea, this is indicative of rhinophyma . Rhinophyma Rhinophyma, also called "potato nose," is a dermatological condition caused by hypertrophy of the sebaceous glands of the skin of external nose. It is usually associated with long-standing acne rosacea. Predominantly affects men past middle age. Presents as a pink, lobulated, sometimes reddish mass with superficial vascular dilation, leading to cosmetic concerns or, in large cases, nasal obstruction. Treatment: Surgical reduction using a sharp knife or carbon dioxide laser, allowing re-epithelialization. In extensive cases, complete excision with skin grafting may be required. Explanation of other options: Rhinoscleroma (Option B) : Rhinoscleroma is a chronic bacterial infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae , leading to granulomatous inflammation of the nasal and upper respiratory tract, without the bulbous nasal deformity seen in rhinophyma. Rhinosporidiosis (Option C) : A chronic granulomatous infection caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi produces polyps rather than the thickened, lobulated nasal skin characteristic of rhinophyma. Scleroderma (Option D): Scleroderma primarily causes skin tightening and fibrosis; it does not produce the redness, lobulation, or bulbous enlargement of the nose seen in rhinophyma.

qText: A 18 year old young male was hit with cricket bat on face and was brought to the ER immediately. X- ray picture is given in image below. What is the ideal treatment of this patient?
expl: This is a case of nasal bone fracture . The nasal bone fracture should be reduced immediately within 1-2 hours before edema starts. This is done using Walsham forceps. If edema is already there, then wait for 7 days for the edema to subside and then reduce the fracture. It is difficult to reduce a nasal fracture after 2 weeks because it heals by that time. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 8 th edition, page 213

qText: A patient presents to OPD with complaints of bleeding from nose and nasal obstruction, and difficulty in breathing. He gave history of bathing in local pool near his house. expl: Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by rhinosporidium seeberi, most cases reported from India (southern states), Sri Lanka and Pakistan, Africa and south America. qText: Which nerve is most likely to be affected in a patient who complains of an inability to close the eye, drooling of saliva, and deviation of the angle of the mouth?
expl: Explanation The symptoms of inability to close the eye, drooling of saliva, and deviation of the angle of the mouth point to facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy) . This occurs because the facial nerve supplies all muscles of facial expression, including the orbicularis oculi (for eyelid closure) and muscles controlling the angle of the mouth. Functions of the Facial Nerve Motor: Muscles of facial expression, stapedius, posterior belly of digastric, stylohyoid Sensory: Taste sensation from anterior two-thirds of tongue (via chorda tympani) Parasympathetic: Lacrimal gland, submandibular and sublingual salivary glands Explanation of Incorrect Options Trigeminal nerve (Option B): Responsible for facial sensation and muscles of mastication. Damage causes numbness of face and difficulty chewing, not inability to close the eye or drooling of saliva. Oculomotor nerve (Option C): Supplies extraocular muscles and levator palpebrae superioris. Lesions cause ptosis, diplopia, and pupillary abnormalities, but not drooling or deviation of mouth. Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option D): Supplies stylopharyngeus muscle and posterior one-third of the tongue. Lesions cause dysphagia and loss of taste posteriorly, not the facial muscle weakness described in this case. Key Takeaway: The facial nerve is the most likely nerve involved when a patient presents with inability to close the eye, drooling of saliva, and deviation of the angle of the mouth - classic signs of facial nerve palsy.

qText: After parotidectomy paralysis of the lower lip occurs due to the injury to which structure
expl: The cervical branch of the facial nerve is a branch of the facial nerve that supplies the muscles of the lower lip and chin region. During parotidectomy, which involves surgical removal of the parotid gland (a salivary gland located near the ear), the cervical branch of the facial nerve can be at risk of injury, leading to paralysis of the lower lip. Main trunk of facial - This is the main nerve that supplies the muscles of the face. It is not injured during parotidectomy. Parotid duct - This is the duct that carries saliva from the parotid gland to the mouth. It is not injured during parotidectomy. Temporal branch of facial - This is a branch of the facial nerve that supplies the muscles of the forehead and temple. It is not injured during parotidectomy.

qText: A patient was admitted with skull base trauma. The doctor was testing the movements of the marked structure. Which of the following nerve is being tested:
expl: The marked structure is the soft palate, and its movements are controlled by the vagus nerve (CN X). The vagus nerve innervates the muscles of the soft palate and plays a crucial role in swallowing and speech. Other options: B. Facial (CN VII): The facial nerve innervates the muscles of facial expression and is not involved in controlling the movements of the soft palate. C. Glossopharyngeal (CN IX): The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue and the oropharynx and does not control the movements of the soft palate. D. Trigeminal (CN V): The trigeminal nerve supplies sensory innervation to the face and controls the muscles of mastication but is not involved in controlling the movements of the soft palate.

qText: After a maxillofacial trauma, the patient cannot be intubated. What is the immediate next step?
expl: Explanation: In a patient with maxillofacial trauma where intubation is impossible and ventilation cannot be achieved, immediate establishment of a surgical airway is required . Emergency cricothyrotomy is the preferred procedure because it provides rapid access to the airway through the cricothyroid membrane, bypassing upper airway obstruction. Explanation of Other Options: Nasopharyngeal airway (Option B): Useful for partial obstruction but inadequate if intubation fails or in severe facial trauma. Laryngeal mask airway (LMA) (Option C): Can provide temporary ventilation, but may not secure the airway definitively in maxillofacial trauma or severe obstruction. Bronchoscopy (Option D): Requires equipment and time; not suitable for immediate airway rescue in a "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" scenario.

qText: A child presents with a history of fever, sore throat and difficulty swallowing. On examination of the oral cavity, the tonsil was found to be enlarged with beads of pus on its surface. What is the correct diagnosis in this child?

qText: Which of the following is not the part of ethmoid bone?
expl: Ans. d. Inferior turbinate Inferior turbinate is not the part of ethmoid bone. `Lateral nasal wall has 3 bony projections called as turbinates or conchae. From below upwards, they are inferior, middle and superior turbinates. The inferior turbinate is a separate bone, while rest of the turbinates are part of ethmoidal labyrinths.' The agger nasi air cells, are the most anterior ethmoidal air cells, lying anterolateral and inferior to the frontoethmoidal recess and anterior and above the attachment of the middle turbinate. They are located within the lacrimal bone and therefore have as lateral relations the orbit, the lacrimal sac and the nasolacrimal duct.' The crista galli is a median ridge of bone that projects from the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. It is where the falx cerebri attaches anteriorly to the skull. The olfactory bulbs lie on either side of the crista galli on top of the cribriform plate.' In the ethmoid bone, a curved lamina, the uncinate process, projects downward and backward from this part of the labyrinth; it forms a small part of the medial wall of the maxillary sinus, and articulates with the ethmoidal process of the inferior nasal concha.'

qText: Which of the following is not a correct statement?
expl: Explanation: The natural opening of the nasolacrimal duct is in the inferior meatus , which is correct anatomically. However, in Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery , performed for chronic dacryocystitis , the surgical opening of the lacrimal sac is made into the middle meatus , not the inferior meatus. This distinction is crucial for ENT surgeons and ophthalmologists during lacrimal drainage procedures. Explanation of Other Options Option A - Sphenoid sinus drains into sphenoethmoidal recess: Correct. The sphenoethmoidal recess is located above the superior concha and receives drainage from the sphenoid sinus. Option C - Anterior ethmoid cells drain into middle meatus: Correct. These cells drain via the ethmoidal infundibulum into the middle meatus. Option D - Posterior ethmoid air cells drain into superior meatus: Correct. These cells open into the superior meatus, located beneath the superior nasal concha.

qText: An ENT surgeon is performing diagnostic nasal endoscopy in a patient of suspected sinusitis. He passes the endoscope at 0 degrees in the middle meatus, what is this pass called?
expl: Diagnostic nasal endoscopy is done in three passes. First pass – Examination of nasopharynx and inferior meatus. Second pass - Examination of the sphenoethmoidal recess, superior meatus and openings of sphenoid sinus and posterior ethmoidal cells. Endoscope is passed medial to middle turbinate. Third pass - Examination of the middle meatus in detail. Endoscope is passed from the front into the middle meatus. Can examine uncinate process, bulla ethmoidalis, hiatus semilunaris, sinus of the turbinate (cavity on lateral side of middle turbinate) and the frontal recess. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no -492- 493

qText: A 10-year-old child presents with throat pain, fever, and earache. He is diagnosed with recurrent tonsillitis. Which cranial nerve is most likely responsible for the referred ear pain in this case?
expl: Explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory and motor innervation to the tongue, pharynx, and middle ear. The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve , also known as Jacobson's nerve, provides sensory innervation to the middle ear cavity and the eustachian tube. In cases of middle ear infections or inflammation, such as those associated with tonsillitis, stimulation of this nerve can cause pain in the ear. Explanation for other options: Greater auricular nerve (Option B) : The greater auricular nerve is a sensory nerve that arises from the cervical plexus and provides innervation to the skin on the side of the head and neck, including the area around the ear. It is not typically involved in ear pain associated with tonsillitis. Auriculotemporal nerve (Option C): The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the trigeminal nerve and provides sensory innervation to the skin of the temporal region, including the area in front of the ear. It is not typically involved in ear pain associated with tonsillitis. Auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Option D): The auricular branch of the vagus nerve is a sensory nerve that arises from the vagus nerve and provides innervation to the skin of the ear canal and outer ear. However, it is not typically involved in ear pain associated with tonsillitis.

qText: You are an ENT resident. A 40 year old man comes to the hospital with complains of nasal stuffiness, headache, sneezing and watery nasal discharge. On examination, polypoid growths are seen in both the nasal cavities. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case.
expl: Killian's polyp or antrochoanal polyp is usually seen in children. It is singular and unilateral. Most commonly arises in response to nasal allergy. Ethmoidal polypi are bilateral and multiple caused by allergic rhinosinusitis and nasal mastocystitis. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no - 200 - 202

qText: What is the most likely diagnosis for an older diabetic woman, who received steroids and remdesivir for COVID, and is now experiencing a malodorous black discharge from her nose? On examination a necrotic black mass, filling the nasal cavity and causing erosion of the septum and hard palate is found.
expl: Explanation: The most likely diagnosis for an older diabetic woman with a malodorous black discharge from the nose, a necrotic black mass filling the nasal cavity, and erosion of the septum and hard palate is mucormycosis . Mucormycosis A severe fungal infection primarily affects the nose and sinuses but can quickly spread to the orbit, cribriform plate, meninges, and brain. The fungus invades arteries, causing endothelial damage, thrombosis, and rapid tissue destruction. Risk Factors Uncontrolled diabetes, especially with ketoacidosis Prolonged steroid use (common in COVID-19 treatment) Conditions causing immunosuppression: Neutropenia, HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, organ transplants, and kidney issues. Early clinical featur es Nasal obstruction. Blood-stained nasal discharge (may be present). Cheek swelling, cheek congestion, cheek pain, cheek heaviness, or sometimes cheek numbness due to involvement of the maxillary sinus. Eye swelling leading to blurred vision, diplopia, or ocular pain (but no black color in the early stage). Loose upper teeth because the maxilla is filled with fungal material. Late features Blackish nasal crust, blackish discoloration around the eye, and black skin necrosis. Diagnosis Endoscopy: Shows pale mucosa early, progressing to black crusts and sloughing. Biopsy: Multiple sites should be sampled for fungal identification; potassium hydroxide preparation is the gold standard for confirming invasive features. Imaging CT : Detects bony destruction and initial assessment of sinus involvement. CECT: CECT provides better delineation of soft tissue structures, allowing for clearer identification of mucosal thickening, sinus opacification, and bony destruction. MRI : Evaluates soft tissue invasion, assesses the extent of extra-sinus disease, and identifies complications, especially in the orbit and brain . Treatment Surgical debridement of ischemic and necrotic tissue to allow drugs to reach the affected areas. The drug of choice is amphotericin B, particularly the liposomal variant, which is safer for the kidneys. Explanation of other options: Aspergillosis (Option A) : Aspergillosis is another fungal infection, but it typically does not present with black necrotic masses. It is more commonly associated with chronic sinusitis or allergic reactions, not with necrosis and tissue destruction seen here. Foreign body (Option C) : A foreign body might cause a localized obstruction and discharge but would not lead to the extensive necrosis and erosion of the nasal cavity, septum, and palate as described in this case. Rhinosporidiosis (Option D) : Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic infection caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi , typically involving the nasal mucosa. It causes polypoidal growths, not necrotic black masses. It is more common in endemic areas, such as India and Sri Lanka.

qText: In a 30-year-old patient with chronic sinusitis and nasal congestion, which anatomical structure is the most likely drainage pathway for the bulla ethmoidalis?
expl: Explanation: The bulla ethmoidalis is one of the largest and most consistent anterior ethmoidal air cells. It produces a rounded elevation on the lateral nasal wall and typically drains into the middle meatus . This meatus is a key channel for the outflow of several paranasal sinuses, including the anterior ethmoidal and maxillary groups. Components of the Middle Meatus: Uncinate Process : Curved bony projection extending obliquely downward and backwards. It forms the anterior boundary of the hiatus semilunaris inferior (the gap between the uncinate process and bulla). Subdivides the lower middle meatus into membranous areas called fontanelles. Infundibulum : A curved passage bordered medially by the uncinate process and laterally by the lamina papyracea. Receives the natural opening of the maxillary sinus near its lower end. Bulla Ethmoidalis : A prominent ethmoidal cell is located just behind the uncinate process. Defines the posterior margin of the hiatus semilunaris. It may be air-filled (pneumatized) or present as a solid bulge. Hiatus Semilunaris : Inferior cleft: space between the uncinate process and the bulla. Superior cleft: lies between the bulla and the skull base. Ostiomeatal Complex : A critical anatomical region within the middle meatus where the frontal, anterior ethmoidal, and maxillary sinuses open. Blockage in this area is a major cause of recurrent or chronic sinusitis. Explanation of Other Options: Middle concha (Option D): The middle concha (middle turbinate) is a bony projection of the ethmoid bone that extends into the nasal cavity. Its role is mainly structural, helping to regulate airflow and support the lateral wall. It is not involved in sinus drainage and therefore does not act as a pathway for the bulla ethmoidalis.

qText: A 25-year-male patient presented with complain of immobile swelling over the cheek region since 2 months. Nasal endoscopy was performed was found to be normal. CT PNS showed presence of mass in left maxillary sinus. The mass has ground glass appearance on CT. What is most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Based on the clinical picture and CT scan findings the probable diagnosis in this case is Fibrous dysplasia. This is an idiopathic benign tumour where medullary bone is replaced by poorly organized fibro-osseous tissue. Most common site of involvement is maxilla. It presents as an asymmetrical painless enlargement of one side of cheek. CT scan is the investigation of choice. CT scan shows characteristic ground glass appearance. Management is by surgical Resection and repair of maxillary bone. Mucocele is non tender non inflammatory chronic complications of sinusitis. It occurs due to cystic dilation of mucous glands of sinus (Option A). Osteoma is benign bone growth which are hard and lobulated with ivory like appearance often mixed with coarse granular component (Option B). Inverted papilloma/Schneiderian/Ringertz Tumor is MC benign tumour of nasal cavity. It's Premalignant, recurrent, locally invasive, arises lateral wall of nose. It shows papillary appearance on histology. No role of radiotherapy, rx is with wide excision (Option D). Key Takeaway: Fibrous dysplasia benign bone Tumour present with asymmetric painless enlargement in maxilla. In CT scan shows ground glass appearance and managed with surgical excision.

qText: A 55 year old male patient known case of chronic rhino sinusitis presented with a complain of painful, firm swelling at the forehead region. Picture Is given below. Patient is also a known case of diabetes mellitus. What is the pathology involved in this condition?
expl: Explanation: Based on the clinical picture and history the most probable diagnosis in this case will be Pott's puffy tumour. Pott's puffy tumour is not an actual tumour. It is an osteomyelitis of the frontal bone which later leads to abscess formation in the subperiosteal plane. It affects the anterior table of the frontal bone. It is mainly seen in adults and in immunocompromised states. Osteosarcoma is aggressive Malignant Tumour with bony destruction and Hard in consistency (Option A). Aspergillosis a fungal infection involves sinus and shows sinus walls thickening and double density sign (Option B). Fibrous Dysplasia due to excessive bone growth present with facial deformities unlike abscess (Option D). Key Takeaway: Pott's puffy tumour is soft doughy swelling over the forehead. It is an osteomyelitis of the anterior table of frontal bone which later leads to abscess formation in the subperiosteal plane in Immunocompromised adults.

qText: False about Caldwell-Luc operation: a. Infraorbital nerve damage may occur as complication b. Opening of maxillary antrum through gingivobuccal incision c. Used for the treatment of chronic maxillary sinusitis & for obtaining biopsy for antral malignancy d. Sublabial approach leading to opening of mandibular antrum may be done under local anaesthesia with nerve block
expl: Caldwell–Luc Operation (Anterior Antrostomy): Definition: The Caldwell–Luc operation involves opening the maxillary antrum through the canine fossa using a sublabial approach. It's also known as anterior antrostomy as it provides access to the maxillary sinus through the anterior wall. Indications: Chronic Maxillary Sinusitis: When there are irreversible changes in sinus mucosa. Suspected Neoplasm: To biopsy suspected tumors in the antrum. Maxillary Artery Ligation: Approaching the pterygopalatine fossa for ligation of the maxillary artery. Operational Procedure: Incision: A horizontal incision is made below the gingivolabial sulcus , from lateral incisor to second molar. Mucoperiosteal Flap: The mucoperiosteal flap is then raised from the canine fossa to the infraorbital nerve, ensuring nerve protection. Objective: The goal is to provide access to the maxillary sinus through the canine fossa for various procedures mentioned. Anesthesia General Anesthesia with Cuffed Endotracheal Tube and Pharyngeal Pack: The procedure is performed under general anesthesia . A cuffed endotracheal tube is inserted into the trachea to secure the airway and facilitate mechanical ventilation during surgery. A pharyngeal pack is used to minimize the risk of blood or fluids entering the throat or trachea. Reference: – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8th Edition, pg. no – 485

qText: A 20-year-old male patient known case of fracture of maxilla was undertaken for reduction through Caldwell luc approach. Picture Is given below. What is the most common complication of Caldwell Luc approach?
expl: Explanation: Caldwell luc operation is the procedure of opening the maxillary antrum by making an opening on its anterior wall by giving a sub labial It is defined as a sublabial approach to the maxillary sinus through the canine fossa wherein the maxillary mucosa is radically excised and drainage is established by creating an intranasal antrostomy. With advent of FESS it is no longer done for chronic maxillary sinusitis and AC polyp. I ndications are: Reduction of maxillary fractures Elevation of fracture of floor of orbit in blow out fracture. Opening of posterior wall of maxillary sinus for approaching sphenopalatine fossa. Taking a biopsy in suspected malignancy of maxilla. Complications are: Anaesthesia or paraesthesia of the cheek, teeth and gingiva because of stretch injury of infraorbital nerve. Trauma to tooth Oro antral fistula (Option A) Haemorrhage (Option C) Injury to orbit Although all listed complications occur but infraorbital nerve injury is most common. Key Takeaway: Most Common Complication of Caldwell luc operation is infraorbital nerve injury which present with anaesthesia of cheek, teeth & gingiva.

qText: What is the preferred diagnostic procedure prior to performing functional endoscopic sinus surgery?
expl: Explanation: The preferred diagnostic procedure before functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) is a CT scan. FESS is a minimally invasive surgery used to treat chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps, and other sinus disorders. CT scan provides high-resolution, cross-sectional images of the sinus anatomy. I It helps identify sinus pathology such as chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps, blockages, or anatomical variations that may influence the surgical approach. Preoperative CT imaging is crucial for accurate surgical planning, ensuring a clear understanding of sinus structures and pathology while minimizing the risk of intraoperative complications. Explanation of other options: MRI scan (Option A): MRI is primarily used to evaluate soft tissue or neurological structures. It is less effective than CT for assessing sinus anatomy and bony structures, which are essential for preoperative planning of FESS. X-ray (Option B): X-ray imaging provides less detailed views of the sinuses and cannot adequately show complex sinus anatomy or pathology Antral lavage (Option C): Antral lavage is primarily a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure to irrigate the maxillary sinus in chronic sinusitis. It does not provide the detailed anatomical information required for preoperative planning of FESS.

qText: What is the preferred initial management for a patient presenting with CSF rhinorrhea?
expl: Explanation: The initial management for CSF Rhinorrhea is bed rest with head elevation and avoidance of straining activities. Management of CSF Rhinorrhea The treatment of choice for CSF rhinorrhea is initially conservative management for 7 to 10 days. Conservative Management: Bed rest with elevation of the head to promote venous return and decrease intracranial pressure. Stool softeners, avoidance of nose blowing, sneezing, and straining to minimise increases in CSF pressure. Prophylactic antibiotics to prevent meningitis Acetazolamide to decrease CSF formation Lumbar drain if indicated Surgical repair Indicated only if the leak does not stop after 10 days of conservative treatment. (Option D ruled out) Surgical repair can be performed by neurosurgeons (open approach) or ENT surgeons (endoscopic approach), given the proximity of the nasal roof to the skull base. Surgical Repair Approaches: Neurosurgical Intracranial Approach Extradural Approaches (rarely used): External ethmoidectomy for cribriform plate and ethmoid area. Transseptal sphenoidal approach for sphenoid. Osteoplastic flap approach for frontal sinus leaks Trans nasal Endoscopic Approach: Preferred for anterior cranial fossa and sphenoid sinus.

qText: A 5-year-old child presents with chronic nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, and recurrent ear infections. Clinical examination suggests significant adenoid hypertrophy. Based on these findings, which type of tympanogram is most likely to be observed?
expl: Explanation: Type B is the most likely tympanogram seen in this child. The child has chronic nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, and recurrent ear infections , which are classic signs of adenoid hypertrophy . Adenoid hypertrophy can obstruct the Eustachian tube , leading to negative middle-ear pressure and eventually middle ear effusion . This results in fluid accumulation in the middle ear , impairing tympanic membrane movement. A Type B tympanogram is flat , indicating no compliance , commonly seen with middle ear effusion . Therefore, Type B is the most likely tympanogram pattern in this child. Explanation of Other Options: Type A (Option A) is seen in normal middle-ear pressure with a peak at 0 daPa. This is not expected in a child with chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction due to adenoid hypertrophy. Type As (Option C) shows reduced peak compliance and is typically seen in ossicular chain fixation, such as otosclerosis, not in middle-ear effusion caused by adenoid hypertrophy. Type Ad (Option D) reflects increased compliance due to ossicular chain discontinuity or tympanic membrane scarring; again, this is unrelated to the child's symptoms.

qText: What would be the next step in managing the symptoms of a 7-year-old child who underwent a tonsillectomy and now presents with snoring, palpitations, mouth breathing, a slight hearing loss, a high arched palate, and a decline in school performance, causing concern to the mother?
expl: Explanation: In the given clinical scenario, the symptoms point to persistent adenoid hypertrophy causing: Airway obstruction: Snoring, mouth breathing, palpitations (from sleep-disordered breathing), high arched palate (long-term mouth breathing). Eustachian tube dysfunction: Conductive hearing loss due to middle ear effusion (Otitis Media with Effusion - Glue Ear), leading to poor school performance. Since a tonsillectomy has already been performed, an adenoidectomy is needed to relieve the nasal obstruction. The concomitant hearing loss necessitates grommet (ventilation tube) insertion to aerate the middle ear and resolve the effusion. (Option A ruled out) Explanation of other options: Myringoplasty (Option B): This procedure repairs a perforated tympanic membrane, which is not present in this case. The hearing loss is due to fluid, not a perforation. Conservative management (Option D): Given the significant symptoms affecting breathing, sleep, and school performance, active intervention is required. Watchful waiting is unlikely to resolve the issue. Key Takeaways: Adenoid hypertrophy can cause both upper airway obstruction and Eustachian tube dysfunction. The management of associated Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) often requires grommet insertion alongside adenoidectomy.

qText: What is the preferred management for a pediatric patient with symptomatic adenoid hypertrophy causing chronic nasal obstruction and sleep apnea?
expl: Explanation: The preferred management for a pediatric patient with symptomatic adenoid hypertrophy causing nasal obstruction and sleep apnea is adenoidectomy. Management of Adenoid Hypertrophy: For mild symptoms Breathing exercises Decongestant nasal drops Antihistamines for any nasal allergies Topical Nasal Steroids may reduce adenoid size and improve related symptoms. For severe cases Treatment for choice is adenoidectomy. Traditional adenoidectomy involved using a curette (like the ST Clair Thomson's Adenoid curette) in a blind surgical technique. This method has a higher risk of bleeding, damage to the Eustachian tube opening, and incomplete removal. Newer, better methods for adenoidectomy include coblation (controlled ablation of tissue with less bleeding) and suction diathermy/microdebrider with endoscopic guidance. Endoscopic adenoidectomy is considered safer with less bleeding and fewer complications. Explanation of other options: Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion (Option B): In a child with adenoid hypertrophy, adenoidectomy with grommet insertion is indicated only in the presence of recurrent otitis media, glue ear or hearing loss. Antibiotic therapy (Option C): Antibiotics are not effective for adenoid hypertrophy unless there is acute infection. Watchful waiting (Option D): Watchful waiting may be considered in mild, asymptomatic cases , but not in children with sleep apnea or significant obstruction .

qText: A 6-year-old female malnourished patient presented with complain of throat pain and fever. On examination of oral cavity tonsil shows presence of ulcer and greyish black membrane. Picture Is shown below. Which of the following antibiotics should be used in this case?
expl: Explanation: Based on the picture shown above the diagnosis in this case is Vincent's angina. It is also known as trench mouth. This is an Acute necrotizing ulcerative lesion caused by Borrelia Vincenti (spirochete) and fusiformis (anaerobe). Other predisposing factors: Caries teeth, pyorrhea, poor diet. Clinical features: Sudden onset Sore throat Pain is usually severe Fetor oris High grade fever Cervical adenitis Associated area is covered with greyish membranous slough , which on separation is associated with considerable loss of tissue. Base of the ulcer usually bleeds and the slough reforms after removal. Though the acute symptoms subside in 4 to 7 days, the ulcers may persist for few weeks. The infection starts in the interdental papillae and then spreads to the surface of gingiva and tonsil forming the ulcer and greyish black necrotic membrane. Management: Penicillin and metronidazole. Antiseptic mouthwash Antiseptic paint over fauces and gums Key Takeaway: Vincent's Angina Management: Penicillin (Covers Spirochete) & Metronidazole (Covers Anaerobes)

qText: A patient presented with complain of persistent post nasal drip, occipital headache. Nasal endoscopy was done which showed presence of a blind and inflamed sac in the nasopharynx in the midline. Picture given below. Which of the following is false about the condition?

qText: An adult man in a restaurant suddenly begins choking on his food. He is conscious. The following procedure was performed. Identify the procedure.
expl: Explanation The Heimlich maneuver is the recommended first-aid procedure for conscious adults with airway obstruction. The rescuer stands behind the victim and applies quick, forceful, upward abdominal thrusts between the ribcage and umbilicus. This creates an artificial cough by rapidly increasing intrathoracic pressure, which helps expel the obstructing object. Explanation of Incorrect Options Back slap (Option B): Used primarily in infants with choking, where the rescuer delivers firm blows between the shoulder blades while the infant is supported prone. It is not appropriate for adults, as it can worsen airway obstruction or cause trauma. Chest thrusts (Option C): Typically used during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) or for choking in unconscious individuals. It involves applying pressure over the lower half of the sternum, but it is not the correct approach for a conscious adult. Blind insertion of finger (Option D): Not recommended, as blindly sweeping the finger in the mouth may push the foreign body deeper into the airway and also risks injuring the oropharynx. Key Takeaway The Heimlich manoeuvre is the procedure of choice for relieving airway obstruction in a conscious choking adult . Other methods are either reserved for infants, unconscious patients, or are unsafe

qText: Nucleus ambiguus is not associated with which cranial nerve:
expl: Ans. D: XII Nucleus Ambiguus Function: * Motor innervation of ipsilateral muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, larynx and upper esophagus. Pathway: * Axons of motor neurons in the nucleus ambiguus course with three cranial nerves: C.N. IX (glossopharyngeal), C.N. X (vagus), C.N. XI (the rostral or cranial portion of spinal accessory) to innervate striated muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, larynx and upper esophagus. Deficits: * Lesion of nucleus ambiguus results in atrophy (lower motor neuron) and paralysis of innervated muscles, producing nasal speech, dysphagia, dysphonia, and deviation of the uvula toward the opposite side (strong side). * No affection of the Sternocleidomastoid or Trapezius. These muscles are innervated by cells in the rostral spinal cord (caudal portion C.N. XI).

qText: The most common malignancy of the oropharynx:

qText: Name the structure marked in the figure:
expl: Pyriform Fossa The marked structure is pyriform fossa. The pyriform fossa is an anatomical structure located in the hypopharynx. It is a recess or groove on each side of the larynx, bordered by the thyroid cartilage and arytenoid cartilage. The pyriform fossae are important landmarks in evaluating and diagnosing various conditions, such as laryngopharyngeal reflux and tumors of the hypopharynx. Other options are: Post cricoid: The post cricoid area is located below the level of the vocal cords, at the level of the cricoid cartilage. It is an important anatomical region in the pharynx. Vallecula: The vallecula is a small depression or groove between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis. It is an important anatomical landmark in the oropharynx. Pharyngeal pouch: A pharyngeal pouch, also known as Zenker's diverticulum, is an outpouching or herniation of the mucosa through the posterior pharyngeal wall. It typically occurs in the hypopharynx, above the cricopharyngeal muscle.

qText: A patient presents with a fishbone stuck in the pyriform sinus. During its endoscopic removal, which of the following nerves is most susceptible to injury?
expl: Explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve (ILN) is a sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve It provides sensation to the mucosa of the larynx above the vocal cords , pyriform sinus , and epiglottis The pyriform sinus is anatomically close to the path of the ILN , making it vulnerable during instrumentation or foreign body removal Injury to the ILN can lead to loss of sensation , increasing the risk of aspiration and diminished cough reflex The external laryngeal nerve (ELN) is motor and supplies the cricothyroid , unrelated to the pyriform sinus (Option B ruled out) The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) supplies motor innervation to the rest of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles and is located deeper, lower in the tracheoesophageal groove (Option C ruled out) The glossopharyngeal nerve innervates the pharynx and posterior third of the tongue , not the pyriform sinus (Option D ruled out)

qText: A child with a mild cold who also has adenoid facies has been identified as having chronic adenoid hypertrophy. Which is the best surgical management for this condition?
expl: Explanation: For a child with chronic adenoid hypertrophy and adenoid facies, the preferred surgical management is coblation adenoidectomy. This method allows precise tissue removal with minimal collateral damage, resulting in less postoperative pain and quicker recovery. Management of Adenoid Hypertrophy: Medical Management (for mild cases, first-line): Breathing exercises (Option D ruled out) Decongestant nasal drops Antihistamines if nasal allergies are present Topical nasal steroids to reduce adenoid size and relieve symptoms Surgical Intervention (Adenoidectomy): Traditional Methods: Blind curettage adenoidectomy (Option C ruled out) is still widely practiced but has limitations, such as unpredictable bleeding and inadequate access to choanal adenoids. Endoscopic techniques are therefore preferred. Direct Vision Techniques: Suction diathermy Endoscopic coblation or microdebridement, which allow precise excision of obstructive tissue under visualization Laser Approaches: KTP laser carries a higher risk of nasopharyngeal stenosis, whereas the gold laser does not show this complication. Explanation of Other Options: Microdebrider (Option B): A microdebrider is a powered instrument that combines suction with a rotating blade to excise tissue and is another technique used for adenoidectomy. Although it allows precise tissue removal, it carries a higher risk of postoperative bleeding compared to coblation. Microdebrider-assisted adenoidectomy remains an effective option for managing chronic adenoid hypertrophy.

qText: A neonate suffering from bilateral complete choanal atresia has respiratory distress since birth. What is the cause of respiratory difficulty in this neonate?
expl: Nose is the natural pathway for breathing. Mouth breathing is an acquired act through learning. The nose also permits breathing and eating to go on simultaneously.

qText: Treatment of choice in a case of Retropharyngeal abscess in a child 2 years of age presenting with stridor and respiratory distress is:

qText: A 5-year-old girl presents with difficulty breathing through her nose. Her face appears elongated with an open mouth and reduced facial expression. Examination reveals a high-arched palate and crowded upper teeth. An X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The child's symptoms of nasal obstruction, elongated face, open-mouth posture, high-arched palate, and crowded upper teeth are characteristic of adenoid hypertrophy . The X-ray image shown also demonstrates enlarged adenoid tissue in the nasopharynx. Adenoid hypertrophy The nasopharyngeal tonsil, commonly called adenoids is situated at the junction of the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx. Adenoid tissue is present at birth, shows physiological enlargement up to the age of 6 years, and then tends to atrophy at puberty and almost completely disappears by the age of 20. Adenoids are subject to physiological enlargement in childhood. Causes of adenoid hypertrophy include frequent colds and upper respiratory infections, leading to chronic inflammation and permanent enlargement of the lymphoid tissue. Clinical features Explanation of other options: Lingual tonsils (Option A) : Lingual tonsils are located at the base of the tongue, not the nasopharynx, and thus do not cause chronic nasal obstruction. Quinsy (Option B) : Quinsy refers to a peritonsillar abscess, typically presenting with severe throat pain, fever, and trismus, not with chronic nasal obstruction and facial deformities. Tonsillar hypertrophy (Option C) : Tonsillar hypertrophy is the enlargement of the palatine tonsils , which is more likely to cause throat-related symptoms like difficulty swallowing , rather than the nasal obstruction seen in this case.

qText: Bowed down vocal cords are seen in paralysis of which of the following nerves?

In unilateral palsy, anterior commissure is rotated towards normal side which is called Askew Glottis . qText: A 30-year-old female patient underwent thyroidectomy. Recurrent laryngeal nerve is encountered during the surgery. All of The following are the common sites of injury to nerve during the surgery except?
expl: Explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve run in or lateral to the tracheoesophageal groove. It has a variable relation with the branches of inferior thyroid artery. On the left side, the nerve hugs the tracheoesophageal groove as it ascends from the chest. However on the right side the nerve is more superficial being 45 degree to the tracheoesophageal groove. The three most common sites of injury are: Near the lower pole in case of anterior displacement (Option A) At The point of entry of nerve Near cricothyroid joint. (Option C) At the point of crossing of inferior thyroid artery. (Option B) Surgical landmark of the recurrent laryngeal nerve is the Baehr's triangle. It is formed by common carotid artery inferiorly, inferior thyroid artery laterally and recurrent laryngeal nerve medially. Key Takeaway: Most common sites of RLN Injury Near the Lower pole Near Cricothyroid Joint At Crossing of Inferior Thyroid artery.

qText: A 55-year-old male patient has been diagnosed with SCC supraglottis. His CT scan shows a tumour extending from the right valleculae and involving the epiglottis. Vocal cords are mobile. expl: Explanation: Tumour Grading: T1 - Tumour is limited to one subsite of the glottis. T2 - Tumour extending to adjacent subsites, normal vocal cord mobility. T3 - Vocal cord fixation or spread to pre-epiglottic or paraglottic space with minor thyroid cartilage invasion. qText: What is the best Treatment of choice for T3 stage of Laryngeal cancer
expl: The entire larynx including the hyoid bone, pre-epiglottic space, strap muscles and one or more rings of trachea are removed. Pharyngeal wall is repaired and lower tracheal stump sutured to the skin for breathing. Laryngectomy may be combined with block dissection for nodal metastasis. Total laryngectomy is indicated in the following conditions: T3 lesions (i.e. with cord fixed) All T4 lesions Invasion of thyroid or cricoid cartilage Bilateral arytenoid cartilage involvement Lesions of posterior commissure Failure after radiotherapy or conservation surgery Transglottic cancers, e. tumors involving supra-glottis and glottis across the ventricle, causing fixation of the vocal cord. It is contraindicated in patients with distant metastasis. Radiotherapy. Curative radiotherapy is reserved for early lesions which neither impair cord mobility nor invade cartilage or cervical nodes. Cancer of the vocal cord without impairment of its mobility gives a 90% cure rate after irradiation and has the advantage of preservation of voice. Superficial exophytic lesions, especially of the tip of epiglottis, and aryepiglottic folds give 70-90% cure rate. Radiotherapy does not give good results in lesions with fixed cords, subglottic extension, cartilage invasion and nodal metastases. These lesions require surgery. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.363

qText: Laryngeal videostroboscopy helps to differentiate benign from early malignant lesions of vocal cord by -
expl: Mucosal wave is the pattern of light traveling mediolaterally along the superior surface of the vocal fold during vibration under illumination. It is a correlate of the pliable cover (epithelium and superficial lamina propria) of the vocal fold being displaced relative to the body of the vocal fold (vocalis muscle). Focal abnormalities of mucosal wave help to localize pathology in the vocal fold . This helps to differentiate benign from malignant lesion. The following parameters can also be assessed using stroboscopy: The fundamental speech frequency of the patient Periodicity : It refers to the regularity of the successive vocal fold movements Symmetry : Normal vocal folds vibrate in a symmetric manner Glottic closure : During normal vibratory phase the membranous portion of the vocal cord firmly apposes, while the posterior glottic chink may be open. REFERENCE- Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery – 8 th edition – Volume 3 – Page number – 945, 946, 902, 906

qText: While otoscopy, the patient started coughing. Stimulations of which nerve leads to cough?
expl: Arnold's nerve, also known as the auricular branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), supplies sensory innervation to the external acoustic meatus . Stimulation of Arnold's nerve can lead to a cough reflex as the vagus nerve is involved in the regulation of the respiratory system and can initiate a cough response to protect the airway. Other options: Jacobson's nerve:This is a tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve that supplies sensation to the posterior tongue and the tonsils. It also supplies middle ear .It doesn't causes cough reflex. Nerve of Wrisberg: It is also known as the intermediate nerve , is a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). It supplies skin of the posterior superior part of external auditory canal .It contains sensory and parasympathetic fibers that supply the tympanic membrane. The nerve of Wrisberg arises from the facial nerve in the geniculate ganglion. The tympanic branch supplies sensory innervation to the tympanic membrane and the middle ear. The lesser petrosal nerve supplies parasympathetic innervation to the parotid gland. Vidian nerve: This is a branch of the trigeminal nerve that supplies sensation to the pterygopalatine fossa. It does not supply sensation to the middle ear, so it would not cause a cough reflex when the eardrum is stimulated. qText: A 40-year-old woman presents with difficulty swallowing. She has no history of fever, sore throat, or smoking, but her father has Marfan's syndrome. Oral examination reveals unilateral tonsillar swelling with pulsation. What is the most probable cause of the tonsillar swelling?
expl: Explanation: The unilateral tonsillar swelling with pulsation points toward a vascular cause . Given the family history of Marfan's syndrome , there is an increased risk of aneurysm due to connective tissue weakness. An extracranial internal carotid artery (ICA) aneurysm is a rare but recognized cause of tonsillar swelling and can mimic a mass lesion. Extracranial Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) Aneurysm Occurs due to weakening of the ICA wall due to atherosclerosis, connective tissue disorders (Marfan's syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome), infections, or trauma. Location: Medial to the tonsil; identifiable by pulsation on oral examination . Symptoms: Unilateral tonsillar swelling Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) Pulsation on oral exam Absence of infection or inflammatory signs Risk Factors: Connective tissue disorders (Marfan's, Ehlers-Danlos), atherosclerosis, hypertension Complications: Rupture, thrombosis, stroke, cranial nerve compression Diagnosis: CT/MR angiography, Doppler ultrasound Treatment: Surgical repair or endovascular stenting Explanation of other options: Intracranial External Carotid Artery Aneurysm (Option B), Extracranial External Carotid Artery Aneurysm (Option C): The extracranial external carotid artery runs laterally in the neck, while the intracranial segment does not pass near the tonsils. Therefore, aneurysms in either segment do not present as tonsillar swelling. Intracranial Internal Carotid Artery Aneurysm (Option D): Intracranial ICA aneurysms typically present with stroke-like symptoms such as headache, visual disturbances, or cranial nerve palsies, rather than tonsillar swelling. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6703024/ https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5853199/

qText: Which nerve is responsible for ear pain following a tonsillectomy procedure?
expl: Explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx and tonsillar region. It also has referred sensory pathways to the ear through its tympanic branch also known as the Jacobson's nerve. This referral pathway explains the ear pain commonly experienced after a tonsillectomy. Explanation of other options: Facial nerve (Option B) : The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) is primarily involved in motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression and does not provide sensory innervation to the tonsillar or pharyngeal region. Trigeminal nerve (Option C) : The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) provides sensory innervation to the face, including the external ear via its auriculotemporal branch, but it is not directly involved in tonsillar pain. Vagus nerve (Option D) : The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) provides sensory innervation to parts of the larynx and pharynx, but it is less commonly associated with referred ear pain in tonsillectomy cases.

qText: Lakshaya, a 7-year-old school-going child underwent a tonsillectomy. He was shifted to the ward after an uneventful post-operative recovery period. In the evening, the nursing sister notices the patient is profusely bleeding from her mouth. What is the best further management?
expl: The most common serious complication of tonsillectomy is delayed hemorrhage. If a patient is actively bleeding, the patient should be taken urgently for control of the hemorrhage. Until the patient is transferred to the operating room, if hemorrhaging is significant, direct pressure, either with a throat pack or gauze, should be applied to the tonsillar fossa if the patient is cooperative. Control of hemorrhage was historically managed with suture ligation, but suction cautery is more routinely performed

qText: A 6 year old child was operated for Adeno-tonsillectomy under general anaesthesia. In the evening, patient develops neck spasm and is excessively crying. MRI Neck shows Atlantoaxial subluxation. What is the possible diagnosis in this case?
expl: This is a case of Grisel syndrome. Non traumatic subluxation of the atlanto-axial joint(C1- C2) Observed after adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy due to over extension of neck. qText: Which of the following is the main arterial supply to the palatine tonsils?
expl: Explanation: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the primary arterial supply to the palatine tonsils. Palatine Tonsils: Blood and Nerve Supply Arterial Supply: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery (main supply) Ascending pharyngeal artery Ascending palatine artery Dorsal linguae branches of the lingual artery Descending palatine branch of the maxillary artery. Venous Drainage It drains into the paratonsillar vein , which joins the common facial vein and the pharyngeal venous plexus. Sensory Nerve Supply Lesser palatine branches of the sphenopalatine ganglion (CN V) and the glossopharyngeal nerve . Explanation of other options: Descending palatine branch of maxillary artery (Option B) : Mainly supplies the palate, including the soft and hard palates, but it is not the main source of blood supply for the palatine tonsils. Buccal branch of maxillary artery (Option C) : This artery primarily supplies the buccinator muscle and cheek mucosa, not the palatine tonsils. Ascending palatine branch of facial artery (Option D) : Although it contributes to the vascularisation of the pharyngeal region, it is not the primary blood supply to the tonsils.

qText: A child 5 year old patient is scheduled for tonsillectomy. On the day of surgery he had running nose, temperature 37.5°C and dry cough. Which of the following should be the most appropriate decision for surgery?
expl: Presence of acute infection in upper respiratory tract, even acute tonsillitis is a contraindication to tonsillectomy. Bleeding is more in the presence of acute infection. qText: Which is the most common source of bleeding during tonsillectomy?
expl: Paratonsillar vein : After tonsillectomy (tonsil surgery), postoperative bleeding can occur, and the bleeding source is commonly the paratonsillar vein (peritonsillar vein). qText: A 6-year-old unimmunized child is brought to the ER with fever, cough, and difficulty in breathing. On examination, there is a greyish-white membrane over the tonsils which bleeded on attempts to remove, along with marked cervical lymphadenopathy producing a bull-neck appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
expl: Explanation: The described clinical presentation is most consistent with diphtheria , a bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. A hallmark feature of diphtheria is the greyish pseudomembrane that adheres firmly to the underlying tissue and bleeds upon removal. Swelling of the neck due to bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and soft tissue oedema is a classic sign of diphtheria, which leads to bull-neck appearance. Fever, cough, and difficulty breathing are the common systemic and respiratory symptoms of diphtheria. Diagnosis can be aided by Albert stain. The lack of vaccination increases susceptibility to diphtheria, which is preventable through the DPT vaccine. Common causes of membrane over the tonsils: Moniliasis (Candidiasis) Diphtheria (pseudo membrane) Vincent's angina (pseudo membrane) Infectious mononucleosis Malignancy of tonsil Trauma Aphthous ulcers Leukemia Agranulocytosis Explanation of other options: Infectious mononucleosis (Option A) : While it may cause tonsillar swelling and pharyngitis, it does not cause a pseudomembrane over the tonsil or bull-neck appearance. Tonsillitis (Option B) : Tonsillitis can cause fever and difficulty swallowing, but it does not produce a pseudomembrane or bull-neck swelling. It is usually due to bacterial (e.g., Streptococcus pyogenes ) or viral infections. Candidiasis (Option D) : Oral candidiasis can cause white patches on the mucosa, but these are easily scraped off without bleeding, unlike the pseudomembrane in diphtheria.

qText: A 12-year-old unimmunised girl presents with sore throat fever and pain in the throat. Throat examination reveals membrane over tonsils, which bleed on removal as shown in the picture below. Most probable diagnosis in this case is?

qText: Which among the following conditions does not result in the development of a grey-white membrane over the tonsils ?
expl: Explanation: Ludwig's angina does not produce a grey-white membrane over the tonsils. Ludwig's angina is a deep neck space infection involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces. Source infection: Usually dental caries or dental infection (often of the lower molars). Clinical Presentation: Starts with a dental infection. Midline chin swelling. Trismus (difficulty in opening mouth). Sometimes respiratory distress if the swelling is significant and pushes the tongue upwards. Explanation of other options: Streptococcal tonsillitis (Option A) : Although rare, severe forms can lead to exudative tonsillitis, with grey-white deposits on the tonsils. However, this is not as adherent or classic as the membrane seen in diphtheria. Diphtheria (Option B) : Diphtheria is a hallmark condition associated with the formation of a grey-white pseudomembrane over the tonsils, which is firmly adherent and bleeds upon removal. Infectious mononucleosis (Option D) : Caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, it can produce white or greyish exudates on the tonsils, especially in severe cases, alongside fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy.

qText: A young male, who is a professional trumpet player, presents with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, compression of the swelling produces a gurgling sound. The neck X-ray was inconclusive, so a CT scan of the neck was performed (image provided). What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: In a trumpet player presenting with a neck swelling that produces a gurgling sound on compression , the most likely diagnosis is a laryngocele . The given CT scan shows a characteristic air-filled structure adjacent to the larynx , confirming the diagnosis. Laryngocele A laryngocele is an air-filled dilation of the laryngeal saccule that may communicate with the laryngeal lumen. It is commonly seen in individuals performing activities that increase intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure, such as trumpet players or wind instrument musicians. Classification: Internal laryngocele: Confined to the larynx. External laryngocele: Extends outside the larynx into the neck. Clinical features Neck swelling , which may produce a gurgling sound on compression due to air or fluid within the sac. Hoarseness Diagnosis Bryce's sign: Air escape sound on pressing the neck swelling. Imaging: CT scan: Gold standard, shows a well-defined air-filled structure adjacent to the larynx. X-ray with Valsalva maneuver: Air-filled neck swelling becomes more prominent. Management: Surgical excision is the treatment of choice to remove the sac and prevent recurrence. Explanation of other options: Pharyngeal pouch (Option A): Pharyngeal pouch, also known as the Zenker's diverticulum , typically presents with dysphagia, regurgitation of food, and aspiration, not a gurgling sound on neck compression. Moreover, it is located in the sterior pharyngeal wall, not adjacent to the larynx as seen in a laryngocele. Tracheoesophageal fistula (Option C): Tracheoesophageal fistula is a congenital connection between the trachea and oesophagus, usually diagnosed in infancy. In adults, it does not present as a neck swelling with a gurgling sound. On CT imaging, it would show a direct connection between the trachea and oesophagus. Tonsillar swelling (Option D): Tonsillar swelling usually results from infection or tumours of the tonsils. It does not produce a gurgling sound on neck compression, nor does it show the air-filled structure adjacent to the larynx seen on CT imaging in laryngocele.

qText: A child, following tonsillectomy, ate a packet of chips, 2 days after surgery, and now came to the hospital with bleeding. What is the next ideal step in management?
expl: Explanation: Bleeding 2 days after surgery indicates secondary haemorrhage, commonly caused by infection or slough separation. In this case, hard food disturbed the slough casing bleeding and minor bleeding are managed conservatively with antibiotics and a soft/semi-solid diet. Post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage Primary hemorrhage: Occurs during surgery; main source is the paratonsillar vessels. Bleeding is controlled with pressure, ligation, or electrocautery . Reactionary hemorrhage: Occurs within 24 hours due to slippage of a ligature. It is a surgical emergency requiring clot removal, vessel re-ligation under general anaesthesia, IV fluids , and possible blood transfusion . Secondary hemorrhage: Occurs 5-10 days after surgery , usually from infection or premature slough separation , and is typically Managed with hospital admission, IV antibiotics, and a semi-solid diet .

qText: A 14-year-old male presents with a recurrent history of epistaxis and associated with nasal block and excessive nasal discharge. On examination, a solid purplish growth was observed on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. What is the probable underlying cause?
expl: Explanation: The given clinical history of recurrent epistaxis and nasal obstruction, along with a mass in the posterior nasopharynx in a child is likely suggestive of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma A benign but locally aggressive vascular tumour occurring predominantly in adolescent males. Site of origin: Posterior nasal cavity, near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen, where the sphenoid and palatine bones meet. Gross Appearance Reddish-purple, lobulated, sessile mass covered by mucosa; lacks a capsule despite being benign. Microscopic Appearance Vascular Tissue: Endothelium-lined spaces with incomplete/absent muscle coats, leading to bleeding; peripheral vessels are thin-walled, central vessels hyperplastic. Stromal Cells: Stellate or spindle-shaped cells that produce collagen, affecting tumor firmness. I mmunohistochemistry Fibroblasts, collagen, myofibroblasts, mast cells, and occasionally giant cells are present. Reactivity to smooth muscle actin and beta-catenin, suggesting beta-catenin's role in growth. Explanation of other options: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Option A): This malignant tumour usually occurs in older adults and is rare in this age group. It often presents with neck lymphadenopathy, nasal obstruction, or ear symptoms but is unlikely to present with a solid, vascular growth in a young male. Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option B): This is a malignant soft tissue tumour that can occur in the nasopharynx but is rare and less likely to cause repeated epistaxis without systemic signs like weight loss or fatigue. Pyogenic granuloma (Option C): This is a vascular lesion but typically occurs on the nasal septum or oral mucosa, not in the nasopharynx. It is usually smaller, friable, and more superficial.

qText: Which of the following is incorrect about juvenile angiofibroma
expl: Explanation: Biopsy done under local anesthesia is the incorrect statement. Definition and Epidemiology: Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumor that occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males aged 10-20 years . It arises from the posterior nasal cavity near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen . The tumor originates from a hamartomatous vascular nidus that proliferates under the influence of testosterone , making it a hormone-dependent tumor . Clinical Features: The tumor can expand into the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pterygomaxillary fossa, infratemporal fossa, orbit, cheek, or even intracranial space , producing characteristic signs and symptoms: Profuse, recurrent, spontaneous epistaxis - the most common symptom Progressive nasal obstruction and denasalized speech due to mass effect in the postnasal space Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion from Eustachian tube blockage Nasopharyngeal mass that may appear sessile, lobulated, or smooth Additional features: broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis, cheek swelling , and possible involvement of cranial nerves II, III, IV, and VI In advanced cases, frog-face deformity may develop Diagnosis: Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical examination and imaging studies . Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice. A pathognomonic sign is the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus , known as the Holman-Miller sign (Antral sign) . Surgery is the treatment of choice.

qText: Rhinolalia clausa occurs in all of the following except:
expl: Explanation: Rhinolalia clausa is not seen in cleft palate. Instead, a cleft palate causes velopharyngeal insufficiency , leading to hypernasal speech (rhinolalia aperta) due to excessive nasal resonance, rather than the nasal obstruction characteristic of rhinolalia clausa. Rhinolalia clausa Rhinolalia clausa or hyponasality is the lack of nasal resonance for sounds that are normally resonated in the nasal cavity, such as m, n, and ng . It manifests as a nasal or blocked voice caused by obstruction of the nasal passages or nasopharynx. Common causes of hyponasality Common cold Nasal allergy Nasal polyp Nasal growth Adenoid hypertrophy Nasopharyngeal mass (Option A, B, D ruled out)

qText: A 12-year-old male presents with recurrent, profuse nasal bleeding and right-sided nasal obstruction. Endoscopy reveals a globular, vascular mass in the right nasal cavity occupying the posterior choanae and nasopharynx. A CT scan shows anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation : The combination of clinical and radiological findings is pathognomonic for a Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) . Angiofibroma: The most common benign tumor of the nasopharynx Arises from the sphenopalatine foramen Exclusive in adolescent males Clinical features Presents with profuse epistaxis and nasal obstruction, hyponasality( Rhinolalia clausa) On examination, a red and fleshy mass was seen in the nasal cavity As Eustachian tube obstruction occurs, serous otitis media can occur, and the patient can present with conductive type hearing loss The tumor can spread into Laterally- pterygopalatine fossa, causing pressure over the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, causing it to bow anteriorly, called the Holman Miller sign or Antral sign, seen in contrast CT Orbit- through the inferior orbital fissure, causing proptosis, diplopia, with involvement of II, III, IV, and VI cranial nerves, depending on the extent of the tumor Infratemporal fossa- through the pterygomaxillary fissure, and appears as cheek swelling Intracranial extension can occur Nasal bridge broadening, proptosis, and cheek swelling give rise to frog face deformity Explanation of other options: Antrochoanal polyp (Option B): While this also presents as a unilateral nasal mass, it is an inflammatory polyp that is typically pale and avascular. It causes nasal obstruction but does not typically cause profuse bleeding. On CT, it opacifies and expands the maxillary sinus ostium, but does not cause the characteristic bony bowing seen in JNA. Rhinoscleroma (Option C): This is a chronic granulomatous bacterial infection caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It leads to hard, nodular infiltrations ("woody" feel) of the nasal mucosa, not a distinct globular, vascular mass. Rhinosporidiosis (Option D): This is a chronic fungal infection caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi that presents as a friable, polypoidal, "strawberry-like" mass that bleeds easily on touch, but it does not cause the specific bony erosion pattern of JNA.

qText: A 20-year-old male patient presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent bleeding for the past 1 year. Trans nasal endoscopic results are shown below. A contrast-enhanced CT revealed a mass extending from the posterior choana to the nasopharynx. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation The presentation of a young male with unilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, and imaging showing a vascular mass extending into the nasopharynx is classic for Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) . It is a benign but highly vascular tumor arising from the posterolateral wall of the nasal cavity near the sphenopalatine foramen. Clinical Features of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA): Nasal and Nasopharyngeal Symptoms Recurrent, profuse epistaxis due to fragile thin-walled vessels. Progressive nasal obstruction causing a nasal, hyponasal voice. Secondary nasal discharge from sinus obstruction or infection. Otologic Symptoms Conductive hearing loss from Eustachian tube obstruction . Otitis media with effusion and possible ear pain. Ophthalmic and Neurological Symptoms Proptosis from orbital invasion. Diplopia due to cranial nerve compression (III, IV, VI). Other cranial nerve palsies (II, V, IX, X). Facial Features Broadening of nasal bridge or cheek swelling from tumor extension. " Frog-face deformity" in advanced cases with bilateral proptosis and facial distortion. Demographics Occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males (10-20 years) . Very rare in females. Endoscopic Appearance Smooth or lobulated reddish-purple mass in nasopharynx. Firm in consistency but must not be palpated due to high bleeding risk. Explanation of Incorrect Options Antrochoanal polyp (Option B): Arises from the maxillary sinus (antrum) and extends posteriorly into the choana. It presents with nasal obstruction but typically does not cause recurrent severe epistaxis or such vascular mass extension into the nasopharynx. Rhinoscleroma (Option C): Chronic granulomatous condition caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (Frisch bacillus) . It progresses through three stages-catarrhal, granulomatous, and sclerotic. Patients develop nasal obstruction, discharge, and deformity, but recurrent severe epistaxis and a vascular nasopharyngeal mass are not characteristic. Histology shows Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies . Concha bullosa (Option D): This is an anatomical variation where the middle turbinate is pneumatized (air-filled). It may cause obstruction but does not present with epistaxis or extension into the nasopharynx. Key Takeaway Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) should be suspected in a young male presenting with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis , especially when imaging shows a vascular mass extending into the nasopharynx.

qText: The investigation shown in the picture is used in which of the following diseases?
expl: A CT scan of the head with contrast enhancement is the investigation of choice. It shows the extent of the tumour, bony destruction or displacement . Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus , often called the antral sign or Holman-Miller sign , is pathognomonic of angiofibroma . MRI helps assess soft tissue extensions (intracranial, infratemporal fossa, orbit). Carotid angiography defines tumour vascularity and feeding vessels, mainly from the external carotid. Embolization is done before surgery to reduce intraoperative bleeding (ideally within 24-48 hrs). Blood should be arranged even after embolization (2-3 units in reserve). Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a highly vascular tumour seen in adolescent males. Classical radiologic feature: Holman-Miller sign Surgery is the mainstay of treatment; pre-op embolization is critical. Explanation of other options: Capillary Haemangioma of the septum (Option B): Usually diagnosed clinically or with nasal endoscopy. Not associated with the Holman-Miller sign. Cancer of the Maxillary sinus (Option C): CT may show destruction but not the characteristic anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary wall. D) Inverted Papilloma of Nose (Option D): Appears as a soft tissue mass on imaging but lacks the typical vascular and bony features of angiofibroma. Key Takeaways: The Holman-Miller sign is diagnostic of JNA on contrast-enhanced CT. Embolization must be followed by timely surgery (within 24-48 hours). JNA is a vascular tumour requiring special perioperative planning. Reference: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat, 7th Edition, Page Numbers: 292-293

qText: A 30-year-old man presents with nonaxial proptosis of the left eye. He reports a remote history of a road traffic accident that occurred 15 years ago. Based on the findings in the accompanying CT scan, what is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The diagnosis based on clinical features and CT is frontal mucocele . A mucocele is a cyst-like structure that forms when the lining of a sinus cavity becomes inflamed or blocked. When a mucocele forms in the frontal sinus, it can cause proptosis (bulging) of the eye. This commonly occurs as a result of obstruction to the frontal ostium due to chronic disease of the frontal recess or due to postsurgical/ traumatic fibrosis, causing blockage. Symptoms of a frontal mucocele include: Proptosis (bulging) of the eye Headache or facial pain Vision changes or double vision Nasal congestion or discharge Sinus pressure or pain Swelling or tenderness in the forehead Explanation for other options: Frontal meningioma (Option B): A meningioma is a tumour that arises from the lining of the brain or spinal cord. When a meningioma forms in the front of the head, it can cause eye proptosis. However, meningiomas are relatively uncommon in young adults, and a history of trauma may not be associated with developing a meningioma. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (Option C): Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a rare and benign tumour, typically in adolescent males. It arises from the back of the nose or upper throat and can cause eye proptosis as it grows. However, the history of trauma 15 years prior is not usually associated with developing a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Pseudotumor of the orbit (Option D): Pseudotumor of the orbit, also known as an idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome, is a condition in which the tissues around the eye become inflamed and swollen, causing eye proptosis. The cause of the pseudotumor of the orbit is unknown, but it is thought to be related to an abnormal immune response. While a history of trauma is not typically associated with developing pseudotumor of the orbit, the condition can occur at any age.

qText: The main vessel involved in bleeding from juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
expl: The main feeding vessels of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma are the terminal branches of Maxillary Artery( which is a branch of External Carotid Artery) This artery is subjected to pre-operative embolization to reduce the blood loss during surgery. Resection of tumour should not be delayed beyond 24–48 h of embolization to avoid revascularization from the contralateral side. In very large tumors or those with intracranial extension, bloody supply may come from branches of Internal Carotid Artery. But these are not embolized. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 292

qText: What is the ideal surgical approach for limited Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma(Radkowski Stage 1)
expl: Limited Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma(Fisch stage 1) – In this the tumor is limited to the nose and the nasopharyngeal area. Transpalatal endoscopic approach is the best for such tumors. If unavailable, Wilson's transpalatal approach can be used. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 294

qText: A 52 year adult patient presenting with right sided hearing loss has been subjected to audiological investigations and was found to have a type B tympanogram. What will be the priority in further management of this patient?
expl: This is a suspected case of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma(NPC). Type B tympanogram is suggestive of glue ear(serous otitis media). The unilateral serous otitis media(presenting as conductive hearing loss) in an adult patient should always arise the suspicion of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Hence, nasopharyngoscopy should be done and biopsy of any suspicious area should be taken. Nasopharyngeal cancer is the occult hidden primary. Cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common presentation of NPC. Myringotomy and grommet insertion will be done for glue ear at a later date when NPC is ruled out. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 297

qText: A 50-year-old male presents with right-sided serous otitis media and a history of cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: In an elderly patient presenting with serous otitis media and cervical lymphadenopathy, the most likely diagnosis is nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma Nasopharyngeal cancer is a multifactorial disease most common in China. Mostly affects people aged 50 to 70 years, although younger patients can also be affected. Aetiology Epstein-Barr (EB) virus is closely associated with nasopharyngeal cancer. Genetics, particularly HLA-A2 and B47, also play a supportive role. Air pollution, smoking of tobacco and opium, nitrosamines from dry salted fish, smoke from burning of incense and wood have all been incriminated. Most common site of origin: Fossa of Rosenmuller. Nasopharynx is rich in lymphatics and an early lymphatic spread is seen in cervical nodes. Clinical features Cervical lymphadenopathy The most common presentation is metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy (secondary neck node). Hearing loss The second most common presentation is unilateral conductive hearing loss due to the blockage of the eustachian tube opening, leading to unilateral glue ear (serous otitis media). Ophthalmoneurologic symptoms Multiple cranial nerve palsies may occur in nasopharyngeal carcinoma because the nasopharynx lies just below the skull base. The tumor can spread into the cranial cavity through the foramen lacerum. The sixth cranial nerve is most commonly affected, followed by the fifth nerve. Trotter's triad Neuralgia in the temporal parietal area (fifth nerve involvement) Palatal paralysis (tenth nerve involvement) Unilateral conductive hearing loss (glue ear). Diganosis Nasal pharyngoscopy to visualise the nasopharynx, follwed by biopsy and histopathological confirmation. Treatment The treatment of choice is chemo-radiation (radiotherapy plus chemotherapy). NPC is a radio-sensitive tumor. Chemotherapy often involves cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil. Explanation of other options: Angiofibroma (Option A): Angiofibroma is seen in the juvenile age group and presents with recurrent epistaxis. Adenoid hypertrophy (Option C): Adenoid hypertrophy is seen in children and presents with mouth breathing, nasal obstruction and recurrent ear infections, but is not associated with cervical lymphadenopathy Peritonsillar abscess (Option D): A peritonsillar abscess is a collection of pus in the peritonsillar space, located between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle. It most commonly affects adults and presents with severe throat pain, odynophagia, hot-potato voice, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

qText: Which clinical test is being shown in the image?
expl: Explanation: The given image shows Cottle's test. Cottle's Test Cottle's Test is a diagnostic procedure used to evaluate nasal obstruction and the function of the nasal valve. During the test, the examiner gently pulls the lateral nasal wall outward while the patient breathes in. If airflow improves, it indicates nasal valve collapse or dysfunction, commonly seen in cases of deviated septum or nasal valve stenosis. T This test helps guide decisions for surgical interventions like septoplasty or rhinoplasty. Heimlich maneuver (Option B) : The Heimlich maneuver is an emergency procedure used to relieve airway obstruction caused by a foreign body (choking). It works by generating a sudden increase in intra-abdominal and intrathoracic pressure to expel the obstructing object from the airway.
