qText: Identify the structure marked in the given endoscopic view of the nasopharynx.
expl: Explanation: The marked structure in the endoscopic image is the fossa of Rosenmüller . It is a common site for nasopharyngeal carcinoma and is located posterior to the torus tubarius on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx. On endoscopic examination, it appears as a deep recess lateral to the Eustachian tube opening . Nasopharynx The nasopharynx is the uppermost part of the pharynx, located posterior to the nasal cavities , extending from the base of the skull to the soft palate (level of the hard palate). It is functionally a posterior extension of the nasal cavity and is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium . Walls of the Nasopharynx Roof: Formed by the basisphenoid and basiocciput . Posterior wall: Formed by the arch of the atlas , covered by prevertebral muscles and fascia . Floor: Formed anteriorly by the soft palate , posteriorly deficient. Anterior wall: Formed by the posterior nasal apertures (choanae) , separated by the posterior border of the nasal septum . Lateral walls: Each wall contains the pharyngeal opening of the Eustachian tube , about 1.25 cm behind the inferior turbinate. Bounded above and behind by the torus tubarius , raised by the cartilage of the tube. Posterior and superior to torus tubarius lies the fossa of Rosenmüller , a common site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma . A salpingopharyngeal fold extends from the lower torus tubarius to the lateral wall, raised by the salpingopharyngeus muscle . Important Structures in the Nasopharynx

qText: Which is the most common site for head and neck cancer in India?
expl: Explanation: In India, the oral cavity is the most common site for head and neck cancer. This high prevalence is largely attributed to the widespread use of tobacco in various forms (smoking, chewing, betel quid) and alcohol consumption. Poor oral hygiene and HPV infection are also contributory factors. Explanation of other options: Nasopharynx (Option A) : While nasopharyngeal carcinoma is relatively common in some regions (e.g., Southeast Asia), it is not the most common site of head and neck cancer in India. Oropharynx (Option B) : Oropharyngeal cancers, including those involving the tonsils and base of the tongue, are associated with HPV infection but are less common than oral cavity cancers in India. Hypopharynx (Option D) : Hypopharyngeal cancers are associated with smoking and alcohol use but are less frequent than oral cavity cancers in the Indian population.

qText: A 30-year-old male patient presented with complain of swelling over left side of neck. Biopsy of the swelling revealed well differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. The patient also developed pain in the lower jaw, conductive type of deafness and palatal palsy. What is the most probable diagnosis based on it ?
expl: Explanation: The most common presentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is unilateral neck swelling (enlarged neck lymph nodes at presentation). Neoplastic infiltration of sinus of Morgagni can lead to the development of Trotter's triad : Ipsilateral conductive hearing loss Ipsilateral trigeminal neuralgia Ipsilateral soft palate palsy. Conductive deafness develops due to compression of Eustachian tube . Palatal palsy occurs secondary to the akinesia of Levator veli palatini . Trigeminal neuralgia occurs due to close proximity of sinus of Morgagni to the foramen ovale . Mnemonic: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma NPC: N euralgia of ipsilateral head P alatal palsy C onductive hearing loss. Juvenile Angiofibroma ( Option A ): Present in young male patient with recurrent epistaxis. Acoustic Neuroma ( Option B ): Present with Tinnitus with UL SNHL in elderly Patients. Glomus Tumor ( Option D ): Present with Pulsatile Tinnitus with CHL. Key Takeaway: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma most common presentation - Unilateral Deep Cervical Lymphadenopathy. If it Involves Sinus of Morgagni - Trotter triad of Neuralgia, Palatal Palsy & CHL occurs.

qText: Identify the most common location of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma:
expl: Explanation: The most common site of origin of nasopharyngeal cancer is the Fossa of Rosenmuller, which in the image is marked as 2. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma Nasopharyngeal cancer is a multifactorial disease most common in China. Mostly affects people aged 50 to 70 years, although younger patients can also be affected. Aetiology Epstein-Barr (EB) virus is closely associated with nasopharyngeal cancer. Genetics, particularly HLA-A2 and B47, also play a supportive role. Air pollution, smoking of tobacco and opium, nitrosamines from dry salted fish, smoke from burning of incense and wood have all been incriminated. Clinical features Cervical lymphadenopathy The most common presentation is metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy (secondary neck node). Hearing loss The second most common presentation is unilateral conductive hearing loss due to the blockage of the eustachian tube opening, leading to unilateral glue ear (serous otitis media). Ophthalmo-neurologic symptoms Multiple cranial nerve palsies may occur in nasopharyngeal carcinoma because the nasopharynx lies just below the skull base. The tumour can spread into the cranial cavity through the foramen lacerum. The sixth cranial nerve is most affected, followed by the fifth nerve. Trotter's triad Neuralgia in the temporal parietal area (fifth nerve involvement) Palatal paralysis (tenth nerve involvement) Unilateral conductive hearing loss (glue ear). Spread of tumor Commonest site of origin in the nasopharynx is the fossa of Rosenmüller. Anterior spread causes blockage of choana and nasal cavity and inferior spread is towards oropharynx and hypopharynx. Lateral spread involves parapharyngeal space and infratemporal fossa through the sinus of Morgagni. Superiorly may spread to involve the intracranial structures. Nasopharynx is rich in lymphatics, and an early lymphatic spread is seen in cervical nodes. Lung, bone and liver are the most common sites of distant metastasis. Diagnosis Nasal pharyngoscopy to visualise the nasopharynx, followed by biopsy and histopathological confirmation. Treatment The treatment of choice is chemo-radiation (radiotherapy plus chemotherapy). NPC is a radio-sensitive tumour. Chemotherapy often involves cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil.

qText: In nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which of the following is a component of trotter's triad?
expl: Explanation: Trotter's triad is a classic presentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) involving: Conductive hearing loss Due to obstruction of the Eustachian tube by the tumour, leading to middle ear effusion. Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia Caused by tumour infiltration into the base of the skull, affecting branches of the trigeminal nerve. Palatal paralysis Resulting from involvement of the pharyngeal plexus or cranial nerves IX and X.

qText: A patient presents with a persistent red lesion on the lateral border of the tongue. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following viral infections is most strongly associated with this malignancy?
expl: Explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity is associated with human papillomavirus . Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) constitutes up to 80% of SCCs in this region, most commonly involving the tonsils, base of tongue, and pharynx, and is frequently associated with oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) , particularly HPV-16. The incidence of HPV-associated SCC of the oropharynx has more than doubled in recent decades, and these tumours often arise in the reticulated epithelium of the tonsillar crypts, presenting as nonkeratinizing, basaloid cell proliferations in nests and cords accompanied by sheets of lymphocytes, as shown below. Clinically, HPV-associated SCCs may lack obvious mucosal lesions but are notable for significant cervical lymphadenopathy , and p16 protein overexpression is a useful marker for diagnosis, with PCR or in situ hybridization serving as confirmatory tests. In contrast, keratinizing SCCs , more often linked to smoking and alcohol , usually originate as dysplastic lesions that may progress to full-thickness dysplasia (carcinoma in situ) before invading the underlying stroma. They can vary from well-differentiated to anaplastic forms, and histologic differentiation does not correlate with behaviour. These tumours tend to infiltrate locally before metastasising, with cervical lymph nodes as common sites for local spread, and lungs, liver, and bones as frequent sites for distant metastases. Long-term outcomes are generally better in HPV-positive cases. A significant concern in SCC of the oropharynx is field cancerization , where patients, particularly those with classic SCC, face a high risk of developing new primary tumours due to widespread mucosal carcinogen exposure . Explanation of other options: Epstein–Barr virus (Option A): Hairy leukoplakia is an EBV-associated oral lesion typically seen on the lateral border of the tongue in immunocompromised individuals, notably those with HIV, but also in cases of cancer therapy, transplant-related immunosuppression, and advanced age. It appears as white, confluent, hyperkeratotic patches that cannot be scraped off, with histology showing hyperparakeratosis, acanthosis with balloon cells, and detectable EBV RNA and proteins in lesional cells. Malignancies associated with EBV include nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and other B-cell lymphomas. Cytomegalovirus (Option B): In immunocompetent individuals beyond the neonatal stage, CMV infection most often presents as an infectious mononucleosis syndrome , characterised by fever, atypical lymphocytosis, lymph node enlargement, and hepatitis with hepatomegaly and abnormal liver function test results. Herpes simplex virus (Option C): Oral herpes, most often due to HSV-1, commonly presents in children as acute gingivostomatitis and in adults as acute pharyngitis , with vesicles and ulcerations that may be accompanied by fever, lymphadenopathy, and anorexia. Lesions range from small vesicles to large bullae containing clear fluid, which rupture to form painful shallow ulcers. Histology shows intracellular and intercellular oedema with intranuclear viral inclusions or multinucleated giant cells, demonstrable by the Tzanck test.

qText: The ideal treatment for T1N0M0 glottic cancer larynx is
expl: T1N0M0 glottic malignancy - Tumour limited to vocal cord(s) with normal mobility. Carcinoma of the mobile membranous vocal cord is traditionally treated with radiotherapy. qText: Which is the narrowest part of the adult larynx airway?
expl: Explanation: The adult laryngeal airway is divided into three regions: supraglottis, glottis, and subglottis . The glottis , which includes the true vocal cords and the space between them, is the narrowest part of the adult airway. In contrast, the pediatric airway has its narrowest point at the cricoid cartilage (subglottis). Knowledge of the narrowest airway region is crucial for airway management, endotracheal intubation, and recognizing potential sites of obstruction. Explanation of Other Options: Supraglottis (Option A): Includes epiglottis, arytenoids, false cords, and ventricles; wider than the glottis. Subglottis (Option C): Area below the vocal cords to the cricoid; narrowest in children. Trachea (Option D): Continues below the subglottis; larger than glottis in adults. Reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33232069/

qText: Croup can be caused by which of the following?
expl: Explanation: Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis) is an acute viral infection of the upper airway that causes inflammation and narrowing of the subglottic region of the larynx and trachea, leading to a characteristic barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness. It commonly affects children between 6 months and 3 years of age , with a higher incidence in boys and during the late fall and winter months. Etiology: The most common cause is Parainfluenza virus type 1 , followed by types 2 and 3. Other viruses include Influenza virus , Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) , Adenovirus , and Measles virus . Pathophysiology: Viral infection leads to inflammation and edema of the laryngeal, tracheal, and bronchial mucosaespecially the subglottic area. This narrowing increases airway resistance during inspiration, producing stridor . Clinical Features: Croup typically begins with nonspecific upper respiratory symptoms (coryza, low-grade fever, and sore throat), progressing to barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor . Symptoms worsen at night and may be associated with varying degrees of respiratory distress. Diagnosis: Usually clinical, based on characteristic symptoms. Neck X-ray (AP view) may show the "steeple sign" tapering of the subglottic tracheal shadow. Treatment: Mild cases: Humidified air, hydration, and reassurance. Moderate to severe cases: Nebulized epinephrine for rapid relief and systemic corticosteroids (dexamethasone or budesonide) to reduce airway inflammation. Severe airway obstruction: Hospitalization and oxygen support may be needed. Explanation of other options: Streptococcus (Option A): May cause bacterial tracheitis, which is a different, more severe condition. Hemophilus Influenza (Type B) (Option B): The classic cause of Acute Epiglottitis , a medical emergency distinct from croup. N.Gonorrhoea (Option D): It causes sexually transmitted infections and neonatal conjunctivitis, not croup. Key Takeaways: Croup = Viral (Parainfluenza, Influenza, RSV) . Epiglottitis = Bacterial (H. influenzae type B) .

qText: Dohlman's procedure is performed for which of the following conditions?
expl: Explanation: Dohlman's procedure is a minimally invasive endoscopic technique used for the treatment of Zenker's diverticulum - a pharyngoesophageal pouch resulting from cricopharyngeal muscle dysfunction. The procedure involves an endoscopic diverticulotomy, in which the cricopharyngeal bar is divided to facilitate smooth passage of food into the oesophagus."\ Zenker's Diverticulum A false diverticulum caused by herniation of the pharyngeal mucosa through Killian's dehiscence. Killian's dehiscence is a weak area between the oblique and transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus muscle. Pathophysiology: Dysfunction of the cricopharyngeal muscle leads to increased intraluminal pressure during swallowing, resulting in posterior outpouching (diverticulum) of mucosa. Clinical Features: Dysphagia Regurgitation of undigested food Halitosis Aspiration pneumonia due to regurgitation into the airway Diagnosis: Barium swallow X-ray: Demonstrates a posterior pharyngeal pouch arising from Killian's dehiscence. Treatment: Endoscopic diverticulotomy (Dohlman's procedure): Preferred for small to moderate pouches. Open diverticulectomy: I ndicated for large diverticula or recurrent cases. Explanation of other options: Meckel's diverticulum (Option A): Meckel's diverticulum is a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct located in the small intestine. It is treated surgically by Meckel's diverticulectomy, not by Dohlman's procedure. Bochdalek hernia (Option C): A congenital diaphragmatic hernia resulting from the failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close. Management involves surgical repair of the diaphragmatic defect , not Dohlman's procedure. Menetrier's disease (Option D): Menetrier's disease is a rare hypertrophic gastropathy characterized by protein loss and excessive mucus secretion . Treatment includes medical management and, in severe cases, gastrectomy.

qText: Which vitamin deficiency leads to Laryngismus stridulus?
expl: Explanation: Laryngismus stridulus is associated with Vitamin D deficiency as in rickets. Laryngismus stridulus is a condition in which stridor (a high-pitched, wheezing sound during breathing) is caused by spasmodic contraction of the adductor muscles of the larynx. It is usually a manifestation of a broader disorder, namely tetany or spasmophilia, often secondary to rickets. Thus, it can result from calcium or vitamin deficiency. Explanation of other options: Vitamin K (Option A): Vitamin K is involved in blood clotting; its deficiency causes bleeding disorders like hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. Vitamin E (Option B): Vitamin E a cts as an antioxidant and is not associated with laryngospasm. Vitamin A (Option D): Vitamin A is essential for epithelial integrity and vision. Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia and keratomalacia, not laryngismus. Reference: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/003591575204500605

qText: A child presented with stridor, barking cough and difficulty in breathing since 3 days. He also had low grade fever with increased leukocyte count. All of the following are true except:
expl: This is a case of acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup). Treatment includes: Hospitalization & IV fluids I/v steroids : to reduce edema especially when child is in distress Humidified air to soften crusts Racemic Adrenaline via a respirator - Bronchodilator Intubation / tracheostomy may be needed Antibiotics are only given to prevent secondary infection. Croup is usually caused by viral infections, and antibiotics are not the mainstay of treatment. Supportive care, such as humidified air, hydration, and sometimes corticosteroids, is more commonly used. Antibiotics are not effective against viral infections. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no – 339, 340

qText: Which of the following treatment options is not recommended for a 4-year-old boy presenting with low-grade fever, inspiratory stridor, and barking cough for the past 5 days? The examination shows a hoarse voice, a moderately inflamed pharynx, and a slightly increased respiratory rate. The chest x-ray reveals subglottic narrowing resembling a steeple.
expl: Explanation: The clinical picture barking cough, stridor, hoarseness, and the steeple sign on X-ray is classic for viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus. Antibiotics like cefotaxime have no role in the treatment of uncomplicated viral croup. The management of this condition involves a multi-faceted approach. Antibiotic therapy, typically with Ampicillin at a dosage of 50 mg/kg/day, is administered to target bacterial pathogens such as influenzae . Humidification is employed to loosen and clear obstructive crusts and thick secretions from the tracheobronchial tree. Steroids are added to the regimen to reduce inflammatory edema, while racemic epinephrine is used for its bronchodilatory effects to relieve airway constriction. If the obstruction persists or worsens beyond 72 hours despite these measures, intubation or tracheostomy must be considered to secure the airway. Explanation of other options: Nebulized racemic epinephrine (Option A): Used for moderate to severe croup to provide temporary relief of airway edema via vasoconstriction. Helium oxygen mixture (Heliox) (Option C): Can be used in severe croup to reduce airway turbulence and work of breathing due to its low density. Intramuscular dexamethasone (Option D): A single dose of corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) is the cornerstone of treatment for all severities of croup to reduce inflammation and edema. Key Takeaways: Croup is a viral illness; antibiotics are not indicated unless there is strong evidence of a secondary bacterial infection (e.g., bacterial tracheitis). Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment.

qText: A neonate with a history of respiratory difficulty and stridor since birth has been evaluated by microlaryngobronchoscopy. The laryngeal image is shown in the picture. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Subglottic Hemangioma: Though congenital, a patient is asymptomatic till 3-6 months of age when the haemangioma begins to increase in size. About 50% of the children have associated cutaneous haemangiomas. Patient may present with a stridor but has a normal cry. Agitation of the patient or crying may increase airway obstruction due to venous filling. Direct laryngoscopy shows reddish-blue mass below the vocal cords. Biopsy is sometimes, not always, associated with hemorrhage. Some patients have associated mediastinal haemangioma. Depending on individual case, the treatment is: Tracheostomy and observation, as many haemangiomas involute. Steroid therapy. Dexamethasone 1 mg/kg/day for 1 week and then prednisolone 3 mg/kg in divided doses for 1 year. CO2 laser excision, if the lesion is small. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page Number 344-345.

qText: A 3 year old child has been brought to paediatric emergency with the history of fever, respiratory difficulty, stridor and drooling of saliva since yesterday. The child is in a very critical situation with Sp02 level of 80 %. What would be your immediate management?
expl: This is a case of acute epiglottitis . It is an acute inflammatory condition confined to supraglottic structures, i.e. epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds and arytenoids. There is marked oedema of these structures - which may progress rapidly and prove fatal unless relieved immediately. Acute Epiglottitis is an airway emergency. In any airway problem, the first treatment is to establish the airway first. Indirect laryngoscopy is avoided for fear of precipitating complete obstruction. It is better done in operation theatre where facilities for intubation are available. REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 338, 339

qText: A 6-month-old baby presented with complain of stridor. Which of the following is not true about this condition?
expl: Explanation: Based on the clinical features and the picture, the diagnosis is It is the most common congenital anomaly of the larynx and also the most common cause of stridor in infants. (Option A) The main presentation is of stridor, which is inspiratory in nature and peaks around 6 months of age. The stridor worsens on crying and in supine position and improves in prone position. qText: A 3-year-old child presented with hoarseness voice and stridor. Following a normal vaginal delivery, this child received all the routine immunization. Endoscopic picture of larynx is given below. Most probable diagnosis is:
expl: Explanation: Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis is the most common benign tumour seen in children 2 to 5 years of age. It is caused by the human pailloma virus (HPV), subtypes 6 and 11, HPV 11 being more aggressive. Transmission to neonate occurs through contact with mother's birth canal during vaginal delivery . The papilloma starts at the true vocal cords, as seen in the endoscopic picture, and later on spreads to involve the whole of the larynx. They are multiple and even reach the mouth, pharynx, trachea and lower respiratory tract. Management involves microlaryngoscopic excision/ debulking by microdebrider, CO2 laser, cup forceps or cryosurgery. The most accepted and gold standard means is the microdebrider. Chances of recurrence are very high, so repeated excision is required. In the postoperative period, alpha interferon, bevacizumab, and cidofovir have been shown to decrease the chance of recurrence.

qText: Which of the following statements regarding laryngomalacia is true?
expl: Explanation: It is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx and the most common cause of stridor in newborns. Also known as congenital laryngeal stridor. It is characterised by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx, which is sucked in during inspiration, producing an inspiratory stridor and sometimes cyanosis. (Option A ruled out) The stridor increases with crying and breastfeeding due to increased negative pressure causing more supraglottic collapse. The stridor improves in the prone position because the floppy supraglottic structures fall away from the vocal cords, increasing the breathing space. Direct laryngoscopy shows elongated epiglottis, curled upon itself (omega-shaped Ω), floppy aryepiglottic folds and prominent arytenoids. Management Mostly, treatment is conservative. 90% of babies improve by 12 to 18 months of age. (Option D ruled out) Severe laryngomalacia may necessiate the need for supraglottoplasty or epiglottoplexy.

qText: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a barking cough and noisy breathing. An anteroposterior neck X-ray reveals a steeple sign. Which type of stridor is most commonly associated with this condition?
expl: Explanation: The presence of barking cough, noisy breathing, and a steeple sign on X-ray in a 2-year-old child is indicative of croup , which typically presents with biphasic stridor . Croup Also known as laryngotracheobronchitis, it is an inflammation of larynx, trachea, and bronchi. Commonly caused by parainfluenza virus. Typically affects infants and yound children aged 3 months to 3 years. Clinical presentation Low grade fever Barking cough: Due to bronchospasm. Biphasic stridor: Due to the subglottic involvement. Diagnosis Anteroposterior soft tissue xray of neck shows th steeple sign due to subglottic stenosis resembling the steeple of a church. Management Antibiotics against secondary infections due to Gram-positive cocci and H. influenzae. Humidification helps to soften crusts and tenacious secretions which block tracheobronchial tree. Steroids may be useful to relieve oedema. Adrenaline, racemic adrenaline administered via a respirator is a bronchodilator and may relieve dyspnoea and avert tracheostomy. Intubation/tracheostomy is done, if respiratory obstruction increase in spite of the above measures. Explanation of other options: Inspiratory Stridor (Option A): Typically occurs in inflammatory or obstructive conditions above the vocal cords (supraglottic) as seen in laryngomalacia. Expiratory Stridor (Option B): Associated with subglottic or lower airway involvement, such as inflammation in the trachea or bronchi.

qText: A child presents with noisy breathing. On examination, inspiratory stridor is noted, and the laryngeal findings are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Laryngoscopy reveals an omega-shaped epiglottis, which, along with the clinical presentation of inspiratory stridor in a child, is characteristic of laryngomalacia . Laryngomalacia Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital anomaly of the larynx and the leading cause of stridor in newborns . It is also referred to as congenital laryngeal stridor . The condition is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic structures , particularly the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds. During inspiration, these structures collapse inward, leading to inspiratory stridor and, occasionally, cyanosis . Clinical Features: Inspiratory stridor, appearing at birth or soon after. Stridor worsens with crying or feeding due to increased negative intrathoracic pressure. But improves in the prone position , as the floppy supraglottic tissues fall forward, increasing airway space. Usually resolves spontaneously by 12-24 months of age. Laryngoscopic Findings: Omega-shaped epiglottis Floppy aryepiglottic folds Redundant arytenoid mucosa collapsing into the airway during inspiration. Management: Conservative in most cases: 90% resolve by 12-18 months of age. Surgical intervention (supraglottoplasty or epiglottoplexy) is indicated for severe cases with feeding difficulty, cyanosis, or growth failure. Explanation of other options: Vocal cord paralysis (Option A): Vocal cord paralysis presents with biphasic stridor and a weak or breathy cry, unlike laryngomalacia, which causes purely inspiratory stridor with a normal cry. Subglottic stenosis (Option B): Subglottic stenosis also typically produces biphasic stridor and is commonly associated with a history of prolonged intubation , which is not seen in laryngomalacia. Laryngeal papilloma (Option C): Laryngeal papilloma leads to progressive hoarseness and voice changes due to involvement of the vocal cords, whereas laryngomalacia primarily causes stridor without affecting the voice.

expl: Acute epiglottitis in children is most commonly caused by Streptococcus Pneumoniae Onset of symptoms is abrupt with rapid progression. qText: Stridor in a newborn is commonly seen in which of the following conditions? 1.Laryngomalacia 2.Subglottic stenosis 3.Laryngeal papilloma 4.Hemorrhagic polyp
expl: Explanation: Subglottic stenosis and Laryngomalacia are the causes of stridor in neonates. Stridor is an abnormal, harsh respiratory sound caused by turbulent airflow through a narrowed segment of the airway . It can occur during inspiration, expiration, or both . Inspiratory stridor: Typically results from obstruction above the vocal cords , such as in the supraglottic region or pharynx . Common causes include laryngomalacia and retropharyngeal abscess . Biphasic stridor: Heard during both inspiration and expiration , usually due to narrowing at the glottis, subglottis, or cervical trachea . Examples include laryngeal papillomas, bilateral vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis . Expiratory stridor: Occurs with obstruction of the lower airway , such as the thoracic trachea or bronchi , and is seen in conditions like tracheal stenosis or a bronchial foreign body . Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis presents with stridor in children and not in neonates. Haemorrhagic polyp may present with obstruction but not with stridor. Key takeaway: Noisy breathing/ Acute stridor

qText: A patient with prolonged intubation complained of respiratory distress. Which of the following staging systems is used to stage the condition shown in the image?
expl: Explanation: The Cottom-Meyer classification is used for staging post-intubation tracheal stenosis , which can develop due to prolonged intubation, leading to respiratory distress. This classification helps assess the severity of tracheal injury and stenosis caused by mechanical ventilation. Cotton-Meyer Classification of Subglottic Stenosis Used to classify subglottic stenosis based on cross-sectional airway obstruction. Originally developed for pediatric patients but now applied in adults. Can be supplemented with letters (a-d) based on the number of laryngeal subsites involved. Severe comorbidities or congenital abnormalities are marked with a '+' sign . Idiopathic laryngotracheal stenosis (iLTS) commonly presents as Grade I-II stenosis . iSGS (idiopathic subglottic stenosis) often occurs in women and presents with a higher grade of stenosis . Radkowski classification (Option B): Incorrect because the Radkowski classification is used for tracheal injuries , but it is not the primary staging system for post-intubation tracheal stenosis. TNM classification (Option C): Incorrect because TNM is a staging system used for cancers (such as lung cancer) and is not applicable to respiratory issues caused by prolonged intubation. AJCC classification (Option D): Incorrect because the AJCC classification is primarily used for cancer staging and does not apply to conditions like tracheal stenosis caused by intubation. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7139051/ https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8892813/

qText: Foreign body entry in the laryngeal inlet, prevented by cough reflex. Reflex is sluggish in alcohol ingestion and some other conditions. Which nerve is likely injured/damaged?
expl: Internal laryngeal nerve (ILN): Above the vocal cords, The sensory supply of the larynx is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve- a branch of superior laryngeal nerve. So as mentioned in the question when a foreign body enters in the laryngeal inlet coughing reflex occurs as a preventive measure. In cases of alcohol it affects the sensitivity of the laryngeal inlet as the ILN may be affected, leading to a sluggish reflex. Option A: ELN (External laryngeal nerve): innervate the cricothyroid muscle and is not involved in the cough reflex. Option C: RLN (Recurrent Laryngeal nerve): is responsible for the innervation of the intrinsic muscles of the larynx and the sensory innervation to the larynx below the vocal cords. It does not produce a cough reflex. Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve: is responsible for the sensory innervation to the oropharynx and the posterior 1/3 rd of the tongue but is not involved in the cough reflex. KEY TAKEAWAY - Internal laryngeal nerve which is a branch of superior laryngeal nerve gives sensory supply to pyriform fossa and supraglottis.

qText: A 6 year old male child comes to emergency with stridor and respiratory distress for last 6 hours. On Direct laryngoscopy, the vocal cords are found to be immobile and lying in median position. Which of the following would not be part of the management strategy of this patient?
expl: This is a case of bilateral abductor palsy of vocal cords of idiopathic origin. Injection thyroplasty is done in the case of bilateral adductor palsy . Various temporary fillers with varying duration of efficacy are available. These cause swelling of the cord and help in its medialization. Calcium hydroxyapatite (1-2 years) Collagen (6-9 months) Hyaluronic acid (4-9 months) Carboxymethylcellulose (2-3 months) Autologous fat, Teflon, silicon – used in past. The remaining three methods are used in the management of bilateral abductor palsy. Emergency tracheostomy is done first to secure the airway. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 350

qText: Warthin's tumour is also called?
expl: Explanation: Warthin's tumour is a benign salivary gland tumour , most frequently seen in the parotid gland . It is also referred to as adenolymphoma or papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum , owing to its characteristic histology. Histological features: Composed of oncocytic epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Shows a bilayered epithelial lining . Contains a prominent lymphoid stroma . Clinical features: Appears as a painless, cystic swelling. More common in older men . Strongly linked with cigarette smoking . Pleomorphic adenoma (Option B): This is the most common benign salivary gland tumour, but it differs from Warthin's tumour in its microscopic appearance. It is termed a mixed tumour because it shows both epithelial structures (ductal/glandular elements) and mesenchymal-like areas, which may resemble myxoid tissue, cartilage, or even bone. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (Option C): This is a malignant salivary gland tumour, unlike the benign Warthin's tumour. It is made up of three main cell types - mucous-producing cells, squamous cells, and intermediate cells - and is known for its variable grade and clinical course. Acinic cell carcinoma (Option D): This is also a malignant salivary gland tumour , originating from the acinar cells that normally produce serous secretions. It usually presents as a slow-growing mass but carries malignant potential, which sets it apart from benign entities like Warthin's tumour.

qText: An 72-year-old man presents with painless swelling below the right ear that has been growing slowly for about a year. Physical examination confirms a cystic lesion. Fine- needle aspiration returns scanty brown fluid, which microscopically consists of a mixture of lymphoid cells and epithelial cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. A biopsy of the mass is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Warthin tumor is a benign neoplasm of the parotid gland, composed of cystic glandular spaces embedded in dense lymphoid tissue. This tumor is the most common monomorphic adenoma. Although the neoplasm is clearly benign, it can be bilateral (15% of cases) or multifocal within the same gland. Warthin tumor is the only tumor of the salivary glands that is more common in men than in women. These lesions generally occur after the age of 30, with most arising after age 50 years. Pleomorphic adenoma (choice c) has a biphasic appearance, which represents an admixture of epithelial and stromal elements. Acinic cell carcinoma (choice a) is an uncommon malignancy. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (choice b) is a slow-growing malignant neoplasm of the salivary gland, which invades locally and tends to recur after surgery.

qText: A seven year old child patient has mild hearing loss along with nasal obstruction, crowding of upper teeth and dull voice. The otoscopy examination finding is given in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: GLUE EAR (OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION-OME) It is most common cause of hearing loss. Glue ear is also called SEROUS OTITIS MEDIA or SECRETORY OTITIS MEDIA. (SOM) Its new name is OME (OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION). It is collection of sterile thick glue-like fluid in middle ear. Basic aetiology of glue ear is ET blockage. Very rarely bluish tympanic membrane . Treatment : Surgery Myringotomy in (Anteroinferior quadrant) + Grommet insertion (also called as middle ear ventilation tube ) + Adenoidectomy. qText: Oropharyngeal picture of a patient with Trismus, hot potato voice and dysphagia is shown in the given image. What is the possible diagnosis?
expl: The clinical scenario suggests quinsy. Quinsy/peritonsillar abscess – Tonsil is pushed medially and uvula is deviated to other side. This is classical feature of quinsy. qText: A patient presented with fever, plummy voice and difficulty in swallowing. The oropharyngeal picture is shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?
expl: uvula is pushed to the other side and tonsil is pushed medially.It is a typical finding in peritonsillar abscess also known as quincy. The oropharyngeal picture shown indicates the presence of a peritonsillar abscess. A peritonsillar abscess is a collection of pus located between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle. It can cause symptoms such as fever, severe sore throat, "hot potato" voice (muffled voice), and difficulty swallowing. Other options: B. Parapharyngeal abscess: A parapharyngeal abscess is a deep neck infection involving the spaces around the pharynx, and it would not typically present with the specific oropharyngeal appearance seen in the image. It presents with neck swelling or swelling near the angle of mouth C. Retropharyngeal abscess: A retropharyngeal abscess is an infection located in the retropharyngeal space, but it would not produce the distinct bulging seen in the tonsillar area in the image. It produces swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall. D. Ludwig's angina: Ludwig's angina is a severe infection involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces of the neck, which can cause significant swelling and elevation of the tongue , but it would not present with a peritonsillar appearance as seen in the image.

qText: A professional singer presents with difficulty in raising the pitch of her voice following thyroid surgery. There is no hoarseness. Which nerve is likely injured?
expl: Explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (ELN) supplies the cricothyroid muscle , which tenses and elongates the vocal cords This function is essential for modulating pitch , particularly for producing higher frequencies in professional voice users Injury to the ELN , commonly during thyroid surgery , may not cause hoarseness but results in the inability to raise pitch or project the voice Singers and other voice professionals are often the first to notice this subtle voice change The ELN lies close to the superior thyroid vessels , putting it at risk during thyroid procedures ILN and RLN injuries typically cause hoarseness or loss of voice, which is absent in this case (Option A & C ruled out) Glossopharyngeal nerve involvement would affect swallowing and pharyngeal sensation, not pitch (Option D ruled out)

qText: A patient who is a teacher by profession presents to the clinic with hoarseness of voice. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
expl: Explanation: The most probable diagnosis in a teacher presenting with hoarseness of voice is a vocal nodule . This is because vocal nodules are the most common benign lesions of the vocal cords in individuals who rely heavily on their voice, such as teachers, singers, and actors. They develop due to vocal abuse or misuse , where repeated trauma to the vocal folds causes small, benign swellings to form. Clinical Features Hoarseness of voice Voice fatigue after prolonged speaking Difficulty producing high-pitched sounds Explanation of Other Options: Vocal polyp (Option A): Unlike vocal nodules, which are typically bilateral and symmetric, vocal polyps are usually unilateral, larger, and more vascular . They are often associated with acute voice trauma (e.g., shouting, sudden excessive vocal use) rather than chronic overuse. Patients may present with sudden hoarseness following a single vocal strain episode. Vocal cysts (Option B): These are fluid-filled sacs that develop on the vocal folds, typically due to blockage of a mucous gland. Reinke's edema (Option D): This condition involves swelling and fluid accumulation within the vocal folds, most often linked to chronic irritant exposure such as smoking or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). While it can also lead to hoarseness, it is less likely to be the underlying cause in a teacher presenting with voice changes, where vocal nodules are more common.

expl: Explanation: Based on the clinical picture and symptoms, the diagnosis in this case is Rienke's oedema. This is a chronic and irreversible oedema of the Rienke's space. qText: A 20 year old male patient has high pitch voice. His fiberoptic laryngoscopy is normal. The clinician has advised him for speech therapy in which he is asked to phonate while pulling the thyroid cartilage downwards and pressing it backwards. What is the name of this manoeuvre for speech therapy?
expl: This is a case of Puberphonia. Normally, childhood voice has a higher pitch. When the larynx matures at puberty, vocal cords lengthen and the voice changes to one of lower pitch. This is a feature exclusive to males. Failure of this change leads to persistence of childhood high-pitched voice and is called puberphonia Treatment - pressing the thyroid prominence in a backward and downward direction relaxes the overstretched cords and low tone voice can be produced (Gutzmann’s pressure test). Prognosis is good. If patient is not relieved with speech therapy, then Type III thyroplasty is done. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra , 8th Edition, pg. no – 367, 351

qText: A 20-year-old male patient presented with complaints of persistence of a boy-like high-pitched voice. All his friends have developed adult-like low-pitched voices. expl: Explanation: The test described in the question is called Gutzmann pressure test. The condition in which it is performed is called At puberty, the high-pitched voice of a boy changes to the low-pitched voice of an adult male. This occurs due to lengthening and relaxation of the vocal cords. If the low-pitched voice fails to develop, the adult male continues to have a high-pitched voice. This is usually seen in introverts and emotionally insecure males. If these patients produce a low pitch voice on pressing the thyroid prominence downwards and backwards then they should be treated with surgical method. This is known as Gutzmann pressure test. Surgical management includes type 3 thyroplasty which is procedure of relaxing the vocal cords by shortening it anteroposteriorly. Explanation of other options: Option B: Androphonia has characteristic low pitch sounds. Option C: Hysterical Aphonia Presents in mostly Female pt. Patient present with No VC adduction on speech & VC movement on cough. Managed with Psychotherapy and reassurance. qText: A 45-year-old teacher presents with complaints of progressive hoarseness and voice fatigue that worsens by the end of the day. She has no history of smoking or alcohol use. Flexible laryngoscopy findings are shown in the given image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The laryngoscopic image shows nodular lesions at the anterior-middle third junction of the vocal cords. In the context of hoarseness and vocal fatigue in a teacher, these findings are indicative of vocal nodules . Vocal nodules Also known as singer's or screamer nodes. Most common cause of vocal abuse. These nodules appear symmetrically on the free edge of vocal cord at the junction of anterior 1/3 rd and the posterior 2/3, which is the area of maximum vibration of the cord and thus subject to maximum trauma. Vocal nodules are the result of vocal trauma in form of misuse or abuse; mostly affects teachers, actors, singers. A contributory risk factor is laryngopharyngeal reflux or gastroesophageal reflux disease. Presenting complaints Hoarsness Vocal fatigue Pain in neck on prolong phonation. Treatment Early cases of vocal nodules can be treated conservatively by speech therapy to teach proper vocal techniques. If speech therapy is not an option, voice rest is the second-best treatment. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are also recommended due to the role of reflux. Surgery is required for large nodules or nodules of long standing in adults. They are excised with precision under operating microscope either with cold instruments or laser avoiding any trauma to the underlying vocal ligament. Explanation of other options: Reinke's oedema (Option B): It is ch aracterized by bilateral diffuse swelling of the vocal cords. It results from vocal abuse (excessive talking or shouting) and smoking. Vocal polyp (Option C): The etiology and site of vocal polyps are the same as vocal nodules, but the key difference from nodules is that vocal polyps are usually unilateral. Keratosis larynx (Option D): Commonly results due to chronic irritation by smoking, tobacco chewing, excessive voice abuse, and reflux. This presents as a whitish keratinous coating on the vocal cords.

qText: What is the most common site of a ranula?
expl: Explanation: A ranula is a mucus retention cyst that arises in the floor of the mouth. It results from obstruction or rupture of the sublingual gland duct, leading to saliva pooling in the surrounding tissues. Clinically, it presents as a bluish, dome-shaped, fluctuant swelling beneath the tongue. Larger ranulas can cause discomfort and may interfere with speech, mastication, or swallowing.

qText: Which of the following symptoms is most characteristic of Reinke’s oedema?
expl: Explanation : The hallmark symptom of Reinke's edema is diplophonia , often described as a 'double voice.' This occurs when the vocal cords vibrate irregularly, producing two different pitches simultaneously. The condition is strongly linked to chronic irritation of the vocal cords. Aetiology / Risk Factors: Chronic smoking (hence also called smoker's larynx ). Prolonged vocal abuse or strain. Laryngopharyngeal reflux. Endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism. Clinical Presentation: Hoarseness and a low-pitched, rough voice. Diplophonia (classic sign). Swollen, translucent, fusiform vocal cords on laryngoscopy. False vocal cord hypertrophy may obscure the true cords. Management: Microlaryngeal surgery (cord decortication) is performed in stages. Voice rest post-surgery. Speech therapy to restore proper voice function. Explanation of Other Options: Dysphonia (Option B): Refers to any general voice change and can occur, but it is not specific. Dysphagia (Options C & D): Difficulty swallowing liquids or solids is not associated with Reinke's oedema.

qText: Post complete laryngectomy all advised/done except?
expl: After a complete laryngectomy, the patient will need a way to produce speech. The most common methods are an electrolarynx , a tracheo-esophageal fistula , or esophageal speech . Supra tracheal prosthesis / fistula is not a method of speech production that is used after a complete laryngectomy. A. Electrolarynx: An electrolarynx is an electronic device held against the neck that produces sound when activated, providing an artificial voice. B. Tracheo -Esophageal fistula (TEF): TEF is a surgical technique that creates a connection between the trachea (windpipe) and the esophagus. This allows air to be diverted into the esophagus, and the patient can use the upper esophageal sphincter to create speech sounds. It is a common method of post-laryngectomy voice rehabilitation. D. Esophageal speech: Esophageal speech is a technique where the patient swallows air and then regurgitates it while shaping the mouth and pharynx to produce speech sounds.

qText: Given below is the image of a patient who underwent laryngectomy. Which mode of speech is he using?
expl: In the image, a laryngectomy has been performed, which means the patient's larynx (voice box) has been removed. In such cases, patients often use alternative methods to produce speech. Tracheoesophageal speech is a common method used by laryngectomy patients. It involves the surgical creation of a small opening between the trachea and the esophagus, through which air can be redirected from the lungs into the esophagus. By expelling air from the esophagus, patients can produce speech sounds and communicate.

qText: A 45 year old female was operated for emergency appendectomy under general anesthesia. After surgery she is complaining of hoarseness of voice. What can be the most probable etiology?
expl: This patient was given general anaesthesia which implies that she has been intubated. Therefore intubation granuloma is the most probable cause of this situation. It is an iatrogenic entity. Intubation granuloma Due to injury to vocal processes of arytenoids due to rough intubation, use of a large tube or prolonged presence of tube between the cords. Mucosal ulceration is followed by granuloma formation over the exposed cartilage. Bilateral involving posterior thirds of true cords. Present with hoarseness and if large, dyspnoea as well. Treatment is voice rest and removal by microlaryngeal surgery. REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no - 354

qText: Biology after taking a long vigorous 8 hour class for 6 years began to have hoarseness in his voice. Which of the following condition is associated with this:
expl: The above picture depicts vocal nodules over both the vocal folds. History of a teacher with gradual hoarseness of voice also supports the diagnosis. Vocal fold nodules are small bilateral swellings (less than 3 mm in diameter) that develop on the free edge of the vocal fold at approximately the mid-membranous portion The etiology of vocal nodules is not known, but traditionally they are thought to be due to 'voice abuse' rather than overuse. Voice abuse is characterized by forced voice production due to strain in the neck and shoulder region producing a harsh quality to the voice. It may be precipitated by talking for prolonged periods in a loud voice as in teachers, repeated shouting and/or singing above one's natural range and occasionally repeated coughing and throat clearing. The repeated trauma of the mid membranous portions leads to localized swelling and epithelial thickening. The mainstay of treatment for persistent vocal nodules is voice therapy with the aim of modification of lifestyle and vocal behavior, providing information and guidance on voice care, producing the voice more effectively with less strain and coping strategies. Surgery is reserved for those who fail voice therapy and remain symptomatic. If surgery is performed, the aim must be precise excision of the nodule alone with no exposure or damage to the underlying ligament

qText: A 19 year old college going girl has presented to emergency with sudden loss of voice. Her cough sound is normal. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Functional aphonia is a voice disorder that occurs when someone is unable to use their voice normally, despite being physically healthy. It can be caused by a number of factors, including: Improper breathing : The respiratory system powers the voice, so breathing problems can make it difficult to speak. Lack of coordination: Using the voice normally requires coordination between the respiratory system, larynx, throat, nose, and mouth. Underlying psychiatric condition : Functional aphonia can be a symptom of an underlying psychiatric condition. There are two types of functional aphonia: Habitual aphonia : Can be caused by any factor and may continue even after the cause is gone. Psychogenic aphonia : Occurs when someone loses their voice in response to a traumatic or stressful life event. Misophonia: A strong reaction to specific sounds.Misophonia may cause a reaction to sounds such as dripping water, chewing, snapping gum, or repetitive noises, such as pencil tapping or clicking sounds. Phonasthenia is a voice disorder that refers to a functional weakness or fatigue of the voice.

qText: A patient suffering from chronic recurrent heartburn, epigastric pain has developed a hoarse voice for the last one month. The laryngeal fiberoptic laryngoscopy has revealed the congestion and mamillation of mucosa in the interarytenoid area. What is the possible diagnosis in this case?
expl: Chronic recurrent heartburn and epigastric pain are suggestive of gastro-oesophageal reflex. qText: A 72-year-old female smoker presents with a long history of hoarseness of voice, difficulty swallowing, and difficulty breathing. The patient was diagnosed with laryngeal cancer and underwent surgical management. The post-operative picture is shown below. Which of the following surgeries was most likely performed on the patient?
expl: Explanation: The image shows a permanent end tracheostomy , which is the definitive result of a total laryngectomy . Indications of total laryngectomy: Advanced laryngeal cancer (e.g., T4a stage with thyroid cartilage invasion ). Stage 3 or 4a tumours in patients unfit for chemoradiation . Recurrent tumours after previous treatments. Bilateral arytenoid involvement affects vocal cord mobility. Permanent End Tracheostomy (Post-Total Laryngectomy) Seen after total laryngectomy , performed for advanced laryngeal cancers when organ preservation is not feasible. Entire larynx (including vocal cords, thyroid cartilage, and cricoid cartilage) is removed. Pharynx is closed and the trachea is brought forward and sutured to the skin, creating a permanent stoma for breathing. This permanently separates the airway from the digestive tract . Patients lose natural voice production , and require voice rehabilitation (esophageal speech, tracheoesophageal puncture, or electronic larynx). Explanation of Other Options: Partial laryngectomy (Option A): Involves removal of part of the larynx (e.g., hemilaryngectomy, supraglottic laryngectomy) with preservation of voice and no permanent tracheostomy. The picture does not match. Standard tracheostomy (Option C): Involves creation of a temporary opening in the trachea for airway access. The upper airway remains intact, and tracheostomy tubes are usually present, unlike the permanent end stoma seen here. Percutaneous tracheostomy (Option D): Minimally invasive tracheostomy done at the bedside, temporary and not equivalent to laryngectomy. It does not result in permanent separation of airway and digestive tract.

qText: Which of the subsequent laryngeal cartilages is least prone to calcification?
expl: Explanation: Epiglottis is least prone to calcification because it is composed of elastic cartilage , which resists calcification compared to hyaline cartilage. Elastic cartilage maintains its flexibility and does not undergo the age-related ossification seen in other laryngeal cartilages. Epiglottis: Unpaired Elastic Cartilage Shape: Leaf-shaped yellow elastic cartilage. Location: Forms the anterior wall of the laryngeal inlet. Attachments: Connected to the hyoid bone by the hyoepiglottic ligament , dividing it into suprahyoid and infrahyoid Portions. The petiole attaches it to the thyroid cartilage just above the vocal cords. Anterior Surface: Pre-epiglottic Space: Located in front of the epiglottis, between the anterior surface and the thyrohyoid membrane/upper thyroid cartilage. Filled with fat, it may be involved in supraglottic cancers or the base of tongue carcinomas. Posterior Surface: Tubercle of Epiglottis: A bulge that may obstruct the view of the anterior commissure during indirect laryngoscopy. Contains pits for mucous glands and occasional perforations, which may facilitate cancer spread to the pre-epiglottic space. Clinical Significance: Cancer Spread: Supraglottic cancers can invade the pre-epiglottic space through epiglottic perforations. Non-Essential for Swallowing: The epiglottis can be safely amputated in cases of cancer or trauma without significant risk of aspiration. Explanation of other options: Thyroid (Option A) : The thyroid cartilage is made of hyaline cartilage , which tends to calcify with age, especially after the third decade of life. Cricoid (Option B) : Like the thyroid cartilage, the cricoid cartilage is also composed of hyaline cartilage and is prone to calcification as part of the normal ageing process. Arytenoid (Option C) : The arytenoid cartilage consists of hyaline cartilage in its base and elastic cartilage in its apex, but the hyaline portion is susceptible to calcification over time. qText: A surgeon has planned for a biopsy procedure for a supraglottic lesion. Before the procedure, he placed a cotton soaked in Xylocaine in the Pyriform Sinus region. Which nerve is being anesthetized?
expl: The superior laryngeal nerve, a branch of a vagus nerve produces two branches: the internal laryngeal nerve (its sensory branch) which supplies sensory fibers to the laryngeal mucosa, and the external laryngeal nerve (its motor branch) which innervates the cricothyroid muscle. Local anesthetic injections to block the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN) can anesthetize the supraglottic region, down to the bottom of the epiglottis, and block the cricothyroid muscle, which relaxes the vocal cords.

qText: If the pyriform fossa is injured due to a fish bone, which nerve is likely to be damaged?
expl: Explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is responsible for irritation. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve courses beneath the mucosa along the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus . When a foreign body becomes lodged in this area, it can irritate the nerve. Because the nerve is superficial here, it can be readily targeted for local anesthesia . Pain from carcinoma of the pyriform sinus is often referred to the ear through this nerve. The pyriform fossa lies on each side of the larynx, forming a lateral food channel that extends from the pharyngoepiglottic fold down to the upper end of the esophagus . Its boundaries are: Medial: Aryepiglottic fold and the posterolateral surfaces of the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages Lateral: Thyrohyoid membrane and thyroid cartilage Explanations for other Options: Vagus nerve (Option A): The vagus gives off the internal superior laryngeal nerve but its main trunk lies much deeper in the neck , well protected by surrounding structures. A superficial injury inside the pyriform fossa is unlikely to reach the main vagus. Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option C): This nerve ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and enters the larynx below the thyroid cartilage , far away from the mucosal surface of the pyriform sinus.Damage here would cause vocal-cord paralysis, but its location is too inferior and medial to be injured by a fish bone in the fossa. Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option D): The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the oropharynx and posterior third of the tongue and passes high in the parapharyngeal space.It does not course through the pyriform sinus , so a local mucosal injury there would not affect it.

qText: Which structures pass between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle?
expl: Explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle (derived from the 3rd pharyngeal arch) and the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) (the nerve of the 3rd arch) pass through the gap between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors. Explanation of other options: Internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery (Option B): Pass through the thyrohyoid membrane in the gap between the middle and inferior constrictor muscles. Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option C): Enters the larynx deep to the inferior constrictor muscle . Ascending palatine artery (Option D): A branch of the facial artery that passes through the sinus of Morgagni , the gap between the base of the skull and the superior border of the superior constrictor muscle. Key Takeaways: Between Superior & Middle Constrictor: Stylopharyngeus & CN IX. Between Middle & Inferior Constrictor: Internal Laryngeal Nerve & Vessel.

qText: A anaesthetic was performing the procedure of superior laryngeal nerve block. Picture given below. What will be the landmark he will use for superior laryngeal nerve block?
expl: Explanation: The larynx is supplied by the vagus nerve. It gives 2 branches to the larynx The superior laryngeal nerve and the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The superior laryngeal nerve arises from the Inferior ganglion of vagus just below the base of the skull and descends down In the neck, at the level of the greater cornu of hyoid bone, it gives off two branches The external laryngeal nerve, as the name suggests, lies externally deep to the superior thyroid artery and supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which is the only intrinsic muscle of the larynx lying externally. qText: Delphian nodes are
expl: Explanation: The Delphian node is a Level VI node which lies in the central/anterior compartment of the neck. These are prelaryngeal lymph nodes located just above the thyroid isthmus, on the cricothyroid membrane. Mainly drains the subglottic region of larynx and pyriform sinuses. qText: Laryngeal crepitus is absent in which of the following conditions?
expl: Explanation: Normally, the larynx moves during deglutition and can also be shifted laterally, producing a characteristic grating sound called laryngeal crepitus . Fixity of the larynx indicates inflammation or infiltration by a growth into surrounding structures, leading to loss of laryngeal crepitus . Loss of laryngeal crepitus most reliably indicates a prevertebral abscess or advanced post-cricoid carcinoma . In prevertebral abscess, l aryngeal crepitus is absent because the infection fixes the larynx to the spine. Explanation of other options: Post-cricoid malignancy (Option A): In post-cricoid malignancy, early-stage tumours do not fix the larynx. Laryngeal crepitus is preserved in initial stages and is lost only when the malignancy advances and invades surrounding tissues. Hypopharyngeal abscess (Option B): Hypopharyngeal abscess, although it may partially restrict laryngeal movement, laryngeal crepitus is usually preserved and is absent only in cases of a very large abscess. Parapharyngeal abscess (Option C): A parapharyngeal abscess is located lateral to the larynx and rarely causes fixation. While extensive abscesses may slightly restrict movement, laryngeal crepitus is usually preserved.

qText: A 55-year-old individual presents with hoarseness and dysphagia and is subsequently diagnosed with laryngeal carcinoma. Surgical treatment is performed, and a post-operative image is provided. Based on the clinical background and image findings, which surgical procedure was most likely carried out?
expl: Explanation: A total laryngectomy is a surgical procedure in which the entire larynx is removed. This procedure is typically performed in advanced laryngeal cancer cases that have not responded to other treatments, such as radiation therapy or chemotherapy. During a total laryngectomy, the trachea is rerouted to the front of the neck to create an opening called a stoma, which serves as the new airway. This procedure has significant implications for speech and swallowing, and patients typically require extensive rehabilitation to learn new communication and eating methods. Indications for total laryngectomy: T4a with thyroid cartilage invasion. Stage 3 and 4 patients who cannot tolerate chemotherapy. Stage 3 and 4 recurrent tumours Bilateral arytenoid involvement. Explanation for other options: Partial laryngectomy (Option A) : A partial laryngectomy is a surgical procedure in which only a part of the larynx is removed, leaving the rest of the organ intact. Percutaneous tracheostomy (Option B) : Percutaneous tracheostomy is a minimally invasive procedure where a tube is inserted into the trachea via a small neck incision. It's commonly used for temporary or permanent airway support in conditions like obstructive sleep apnea or chronic respiratory failure, but it's not suitable for treating laryngeal cancer. Standard tracheostomy (Option C): A standard tracheostomy involves creating a neck incision to access the trachea, commonly used for temporary or permanent airway support in breathing difficulties. However, it's typically avoided in laryngeal cancer cases as it doesn't address the cancerous tissue in the larynx.

qText: A patient presents with hoarseness of voice. On examination, there is an ulceroproliferative mass on the right vocal cord, but the cord remains mobile. There is no regional lymph node involvement or distant metastasis. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
expl: Explanation: In this patient, the ulceroproliferative mass is confined to the right vocal cord and the vocal cord remains mobile. There is no regional lymph node involvement and no distant metastasis. These findings indicate an early-stage laryngeal carcinoma (T1–T2) . For such localized tumors, radiotherapy is the treatment of choice. It effectively eradicates the tumor while preserving voice function and avoiding more invasive surgery . Laryngeal Carcinoma A major risk factor is smoking due to carcinogenic chemicals like benzopyrene . Laryngeal carcinoma is classified based on the site of origin within the larynx into three main types : Supraglottic, glottic and subglottic. Simplified tumor staging of laryngeal cancer T1: I nvolves only one named structure of the larynx T2: Involves more than one named structure T3: Fixed or immobile vocal cord. Also includes invasion of the pre-epiglottic space or paraglottic space. T4: Indicates the tumor has expanded beyond the larynx. T4a: Involves invasion of the thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, or extra-laryngeal extension into neck structures like the thyroid gland or neck muscles (strap muscles). T4b: Involves carotid artery involvement or invasion of the prevertebral space. These are considered very advanced and often inoperable. Management based on tumour staging Explanation of other options: Conservative laryngectomy (Option C): Conservation laryngeal surgery aims to preserve voice and avoid a permanent tracheal opening. However, only carefully selected cases are suitable for this approach. In the present case, conservative laryngectomy is not done as radiotherapy is the preferred first-line treatment for early-stage vocal cord cancer (T1 N0 M0) with no lymphatic spread. Chemotherapy (Option D): For stage III and IV laryngeal cancers, induction chemotherapy with radiotherapy or concurrent chemoradiation offers effective organ preservation with better locoregional control compared to surgery. However, since concurrent chemoradiation has higher toxicity, proper case selection is crucial.

qText: A 60-year-old male patient with carcinoma larynx presented 6 months after completion of his radiotherapy. The patient’s case sheet showed that he was given radiation in the dose of 1.8 to 2.25 Gy. It was given once a day for five days in a week. What kind of fractionation was used in this patient?
expl: Explanation: The paramount goal of patient care is to optimize treatment efficacy, while minimizing toxicity. It was seen that instead of giving a single large dose of radiation if the dose is divided into multiple fractions, it improved the recovery of the normal tissue. This is called Conventional fractionation: It implies a dose per fractionation of 1.8 to 2.25Gy, given once a day, five fractions in a week. (Option B) Hypo fractionation: Dose per fractionation is more than 2.25 Gy given once daily five fractions a week. (Option A) Hyper fractionation: Total number of doses are increased, but are delivered using multiple fractions per day. The dose per fraction Is slightly reduced. (Option C) Accelerated fractionation: Overall treatment time is significantly reduced. The total dose per fraction and the number of fractions are either unchanged or sometimes reduced. (Option D)

qText: A patient presents to the emergency department with significant nasal trauma after a fall. Examination reveals a deviated nasal pyramid, and palpation confirms crepitus and mobility of the nasal bones. A lateral nasal bone X-ray confirms a displaced nasal bone fracture. Which of the following instruments is specifically designed for the closed reduction of a displaced nasal bone fracture?
expl: Explanation: Walsham forceps are specifically designed for closed reduction of nasal bone fractures . qText: The image below depicts a surgical procedure performed on the patient. Identify the procedure.
expl: Explanation: The image depicts a tracheostomy procedure, in which a surgical opening is created in the trachea to establish an airway. Tracheostomy A tracheostomy is a surgical procedure in which an opening is created in the neck directly into the trachea to provide an airway when the upper airway is blocked or compromised. The procedure involves making an incision below the vocal cords and inserting a tracheostomy tube. Complications of Tracheostomy Immediate complications: Hemorrhage: Most common; bleeding from vessels like the anterior jugular or thyroid vessels. Surgical emphysema: Air collects under the skin if tracheal air leaks or skin sutures are too tight. Apnea: Temporary cessation of breathing due to rapid CO 2 washout. Pneumothorax: Rare; more common in children due to injury to the apical pleura. Loss of voice: Air bypasses the vocal cords, preventing normal phonation. Late complications: Infection: At the tracheostomy site due to poor hygiene or dressing care. Subglottic stenosis: Narrowing of the airway below the vocal cords from trauma or infection. Explanation of other options: Endotracheal intubation (Option A): Endotracheal intubation involves placing a tube into the trachea via the mouth or nose, without any surgical neck incision. Needle cricothyroidotomy (Option B): An emergency procedure in which a needle is inserted through the cricothyroid membrane to provide temporary airway access, not a permanent opening like a tracheostomy. Oropharyngeal airway (Option D): It is a mouth-inserted device that maintains airway patency in unconscious patients, without any surgical incision or permanent airway creation.

qText: What is the probable cause of surgical emphysema in a patient following an emergency tracheostomy?
expl: Explanation: Surgical emphysema (subcutaneous air) post-tracheostomy occurs when air leaks from the airway into the subcutaneous tissues of the neck. The most common cause is a tear in the posterior tracheal wall created during the procedure. This allows air from the trachea to escape into the paratracheal fascia and then dissect through the subcutaneous planes of the neck and chest. Explanation of other options: High tracheostomy (Option A): A high incision (above the 2nd tracheal ring) risks injury to the cricoid cartilage and subglottic stenosis, but it is not a direct cause of surgical emphysema. Block in tracheostomy (Option C): A blocked tube would cause respiratory distress and failure to ventilate, not subcutaneous air. Tight suture around tracheostomy site (Option D): Over-tight skin sutures can cause skin necrosis or impair healing but do not typically allow air to track into subcutaneous tissues. Key Takeaways: Surgical emphysema after tracheostomy suggests an air leak, most commonly from an iatrogenic injury to the posterior tracheal wall. The posterior tracheal wall is vulnerable as it is thin and lies immediately anterior to the esophagus.

qText: A child is brought to the ER with sudden onset of respiratory distress, cough, inability to speak after consumption of apple. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
expl: Explanation: A child with sudden onset of respiratory distress and cough after consumption of apple likely has Foreign Body Aspiration. The most appropriate first step in management of this patient would be Heimlich Maneuver. Management of Foreign Body Aspiration is as follows: Conscious Patient (Partial Obstruction): Encourage coughing to clear the airway. Conscious Patient (Complete Obstruction): Infants ( Children (>1 year) & Adults: Abdominal thrusts ( Heimlich maneuver). Pregnant/Obese: Sternal thrusts. Unresponsive Patient: Immediately start CPR (chest compressions); check airway after 30 compressions. Medical Intervention (if basic measures fail): Direct laryngoscopy with Magill forceps or suction for visible objects. Cricothyrotomy for supraglottic obstruction. Endotracheal intubation to push object into mainstem bronchus for temporary ventilation (if subglottic). Bronchoscopy (rigid) is the definitive procedure for diagnosis and removal, especially for suspected partial obstructions or if basic measures fail. Explanation of Other Options: CPR (Option A) CPR is reserved for unconscious patients who are not breathing or have no pulse . In this case, the child is still conscious. Endoscopy (Option B) Endoscopic removal of foreign bodies is definitive management , but not the first step . It should be done after initial resuscitation or if Heimlich fails . Blind finger sweep (Option D) Dangerous and outdated . Blind sweeps can push the object further into the airway and should never be performed , especially in children. Key Takeaway: In a conscious child with complete airway obstruction after food ingestion (inability to speak/cough), the Heimlich maneuver is the immediate life-saving intervention . qText: What is the first investigation performed when a child is suspected of inhaling a foreign body?
expl: Explanation: After a child is suspected of having inhaled or swallowed a foreign body, the first-line investigation is usually a chest X-ray. qText: Following a building collapse, a male patient was brought to the emergency department with a copious amount of debris in the mouth, making endotracheal intubation impossible. The emergency procedure shown in the image was performed. Which of the following statements regarding this procedure is true?
expl: Explanation: The image depicts a needle cricothyroidotomy , a rescue procedure for a "Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate" (CICO) airway emergency. This is a temporary, life-saving measure that is not a definitive airway; therefore, it must be converted to a formal surgical airway, such as a tracheostomy , as soon as the patient is stabilized. This procedure allows for emergency oxygenation but is inadequate for effective ventilation (CO 2 removal) and can only be used for a very short duration (30-45 minutes), not hours (Option A ruled out). It accesses the airway through the cricothyroid membrane and has no connection to the central venous system, so it cannot be used to measure central venous pressure (Option B ruled out). As it is performed to bypass a complete upper airway obstruction where bag-and-mask ventilation has failed, it dramatically decreases the work of breathing (Option D ruled out).
